item.title: What Does a Kilogram of Coffee Really Cost?
item.description: From productive trees and farm costs through moisture, processing yield, grade recovery and the true cost of saleable green coffee.
item.content:encoded:
← All writingCoffee Pricing Engine researchRSS

RESEARCH / COFFEE PRICING ENGINE

Kenneth S. Legesi, CFA · 29 October 2026 · Research essay

What Does a Kilogram of Coffee Really Cost?

The denominator matters as much as the numerator.

Coffee businesses often discuss cost per kilogram without first agreeing on which kilogram they mean.

Is it freshly harvested cherry? Dried cherry (Kiboko)? Parchment? Hulled FAQ? Clean green beans? A particular screen grade accepted by an export buyer? These are not interchangeable products. Nor do they have the same weight, moisture, processing losses or price.

Before we calculate the true cost of coffee, we must first reconcile its physical journey.

Begin with the productive tree

Consider a purely illustrative coffee plot with 450 productive trees and 600 kilograms of saleable green-coffee-equivalent output per acre. That is approximately 1.33 kilograms of green equivalent per productive tree. This is not a claimed Uganda yield standard; it simply shows how a farm-level assumption becomes a unit-cost denominator.

If attributable farm costs are UGX 6 million per year and the plot produces 600 saleable green-equivalent kilograms, the arithmetic cost is UGX 10,000 per kilogram. With the same costs but 400 kilograms, unit cost rises to UGX 15,000.

The exercise is simple; doing it correctly is not. Establishment costs, tree age, unpaid family labour, depreciation, land opportunity cost and planting losses must be classified consistently. An annual cash break-even measure and a full economic cost are both useful, but answer different questions.

One input kilogram does not become one export kilogram

The next challenge is physical conversion. Coffee loses weight as moisture is removed, hulls are separated, defects rejected and beans sorted into saleable grades.

Suppose a hypothetical mill buys 1,000 kilograms of a dry input form, recovers 550 kilograms of green output, and only 495 kilograms meet a specified target grade. The remaining output may still have saleable value. Charging all input costs against 495 kilograms without accounting for other saleable grades can distort profitability; dividing the purchase price by 1,000 kilograms understates the cost of target-grade output.

A proper costing system needs an input-output mass balance, a recorded moisture basis, grade-by-grade recovery and an explicit method for allocating joint costs or crediting by-product revenue. No blanket conversion factor can substitute for an actual mill-batch reconciliation.

From production cost to commercial quote

The farmer's sale price becomes the trader's purchase cost. The trader adds sourcing, handling, transport, processing, storage, cost of money and contract performance risk. The exporter must consider grade, named delivery place, buyer payment, logistics and currency. A farmer's sale in Kampala is not the same economic proposition as delivery under an ocean-freight contract.

The fully loaded cost is one number. The relevant incremental cost of accepting a particular buyer offer can be another. The market price might be above or below either.

That is why the proposed Coffee Pricing Engine separates the cost-based minimum and target quote from a comparable, dated buyer price. A software-generated number should not be confused with an executable trade.

The research question

We are developing a Uganda-first unit-cost framework that starts at the tree and follows the coffee through farm, mill, lot, grade and sale. The aim is to expose assumptions, test them against records and explain where price and cost diverge.

A useful pricing engine should make its assumptions contestable — not hide them.

See the Coffee Pricing Engine prototype. All example calculations here are synthetic and for explanation only.

Invitation: help establish real unit costs

We seek farm cost and harvest records, anonymised milling batch/outturn schedules, moisture and grade recovery data, logistics invoices and dated buyer quotations. Researchers and practitioners are also invited to challenge unit definitions and costing methodology. Contribute via Connect; share no confidential material without consent and suitable terms.

Explore the research and contribute →

item.title: Coffee Is Traded, Not Just Grown
item.description: Why origin-side coffee producers and traders need cost, quality, conversion and financing intelligence alongside market prices.
item.content:encoded:
← All writingCoffee Pricing Engine researchRSS

RESEARCH / COFFEE PRICING ENGINE

Kenneth S. Legesi, CFA · 29 October 2026 · Research essay

Coffee Is Traded, Not Just Grown

The challenge for coffee-producing economies is not simply to produce more coffee. It is to understand — and capture — more of the economics of the coffee they produce.

A farmer sees a price per kilogram. A trader sees an inventory position. An exporter sees a grade, a shipment, a payment date and a buyer obligation. A large international trading house sees all of these at once, alongside futures prices, origin differentials, currency, credit exposure and the cost of carrying stock.

They may be trading the same coffee, but they are not operating with the same information.

This is one of the reasons I have begun work on the Coffee Pricing Engine: a public-facing tool that seeks to connect the physical economics of coffee production with the financial economics of coffee trading.

A market price is not a business model

Suppose a coffee producer hears that Robusta is selling for UGX 24,000 per kilogram in Kampala. Is that a good price? It is impossible to answer without specifying the coffee form, grade, moisture, buyer, date and delivery terms — and knowing how much it cost the seller to produce or acquire that kilogram.

For a farmer, the right denominator begins with productive trees, the yield of a plot, inputs, labour, losses and actual saleable output. For an aggregator, the farmer's selling price becomes an acquisition cost. For a processor, the question becomes how much acceptable green coffee emerges from each kilogram of cherry, dried cherry or parchment. For an exporter, the costs extend into quality assurance, storage, finance, freight, compliance and payment risk.

In each case, the headline price is only one variable.

The invisible economics between tree and trade

A shipment's apparent spread can disappear through poor milling outturn, slow inventory turnover, a stronger purchasing currency, delayed buyer settlement or a quality claim.

Conversely, an enterprise can create value without taking an outsized price view: through better farm yield, more consistent quality, lower losses, faster turnover, cheaper working capital or more disciplined contracting.

The goal is not to predict every movement in London Robusta futures. It is to make the enterprise's own cost and risk structure legible.

An open methodology, not another mysterious price signal

The Coffee Pricing Engine begins with a simple question: what does one saleable kilogram really cost? The answer must be reconcilable from farm records, processing outturns and documented transaction expenses. It must then be tested against the price the market will actually pay for the same product, quality, place and date.

A cost-based target is not a market-clearing price. Where the achievable market netback falls below cost, the engine should show the economic gap rather than conjure a margin.

Our current calculator is an illustrative prototype, not a live market quotation service. The research programme is developing validated conversion tables, costing principles, finance schedules and buyer-price comparisons before stronger claims can be made.

Why this matters

Improved access to market prices helps. But it is insufficient if the producer cannot calculate cost per tree, the huller cannot reconcile saleable outturn, or the trader cannot quantify what 45 days of borrowed capital does to a deal.

The ambition is to move from prices heard and repeated to costs measured and decisions explained.

Know your cost before you quote.

Research and prototype: Coffee Pricing Engine. Methodology and validation programme in development. Illustrative inputs are not verified market quotations.

Contribute to the research

We welcome anonymised farm-year cost and yield data, real milling outturn sheets, grade-recovery measurements, dated physical coffee bids and exporter cost schedules. Particularly valuable are observations that challenge the model. Share the type of data, coffee form, units, observation date, region and permission to use it through the site's Connect route. Do not send confidential personal, commercial or customer information without permission or an agreed data-sharing arrangement.

Explore the research and contribute →

item.title: Economic Opportunity Is Not Investability
item.description: The Africa Investability Index begins with a distinction between economic opportunity and the conditions for deploying, protecting and recovering capital.
item.content:encoded:
Home← All writingAfrica Investability IndexRSS

RESEARCH / AFRICA INVESTABILITY INDEX

Economic Opportunity Is Not Investability

Kenneth S. Legesi, CFA · 28 October 2026 · Foundational essay

The existence of an investment opportunity does not establish that capital can be deployed, protected or recovered on workable terms.

Africa is often presented through the language of potential: expanding markets, demographic growth, mineral wealth, urbanisation and unmet demand. These may all point to opportunities for enterprise. But the existence of an opportunity is not the same as its investability.

An investor does not commit capital to a demographic projection. Capital is committed through a legal and financial arrangement, in a currency, within a jurisdiction, to an enterprise or asset whose future cash flows remain uncertain. The investor must be able to enter, finance, govern, protect and ultimately realise the investment. Each of those steps depends on institutions and market arrangements that growth statistics alone do not capture.

From potential to executable capital

Consider two economies with similarly promising demand. In one, foreign exchange is accessible, contracts are enforceable, financing is available for appropriate tenors and investors can exit through credible mechanisms. In the other, financing is short-term, currency conversion is unpredictable and remedies for non-payment are difficult to enforce. Their economic potential may look comparable while the conditions for investment differ materially.

This does not imply that difficult markets are uninvestable, or that stronger institutions guarantee superior returns. Investors may earn high returns by structuring around constraints, bearing risks others avoid or accessing opportunities unavailable to competitors. It does mean that opportunity and the mechanisms that convert opportunity into recoverable capital deserve separate analysis.

Five provisional dimensions

The Africa Investability Index (AII) research programme begins with five candidate dimensions: political and institutional durability; domestic capital formation; market accessibility and capital mobility; enterprise durability; and capital protection and recovery.

These dimensions are not yet an index, and their importance has not been empirically established. They form a set of hypotheses about the conditions under which productive capital can be mobilised and sustained. The research will test whether they are distinct, measurable and useful beyond established country-risk and governance frameworks.

Whose investability?

Investability is not necessarily a single national characteristic. A pension fund purchasing local-currency government bonds, a venture investor backing a technology business and an infrastructure lender financing a power project face different constraints. Country-level conditions matter, but transaction structure, asset class, investor eligibility and legal remedies may matter just as much.

The programme therefore distinguishes ex-ante investability—conditions observable before capital is committed—from transaction feasibility and ex-post investment outcomes, including recoveries, exits and realised returns. This separation matters: an index cannot credibly claim to predict investment outcomes if those outcomes are built into the same explanatory score.

What the research must prove

The ambition is not to publish another league table of African countries. It is to test whether a disciplined account of institutional and financial mechanisms adds information that investors and policymakers do not already obtain from growth, governance, sovereign-risk or financial-development indicators.

The programme will examine competing methods, including a multidimensional dashboard rather than a single composite ranking. It will prioritise transparent definitions, data provenance, comparisons against existing benchmarks and out-of-time validation. Where data are missing or the evidence is inconclusive, the limitations should remain visible.

Economic opportunity is the starting point. Investability concerns the conditions under which that opportunity can become a durable financial claim. Understanding the difference is the research agenda.

Research status: This essay introduces a working conceptual framework. It does not report validated AII country scores or investment recommendations. The underlying research repository is private; publication of methods and findings will follow source review and editorial approval.

Explore the Africa Investability Index research programme.

item.title: Africa's Enduring Enterprises: Evidence Update, 26 October 2026
item.description: Three longevity cases: Nigerian Breweries at 80, New KCC's 1925 lineage and Ethiopian Airlines' operational anniversary.
item.content:encoded:
WRITING / AFRICA'S ENDURING ENTERPRISES / RESEARCH DISPATCH

Eight decades, a century-old lineage, and the problem of institutional identity

Nigerian Breweries, New Kenya Co-operative Creameries and Ethiopian Airlines show why a founding year is only the beginning of the investigation.

Kenneth S. Legesi · 26 October 2026 · Research status: provisional evidence update, not a definitive longevity ranking

Three developments worth recording

Nigerian Breweries turns 80. The company dates its incorporation to 1946 and marked the milestone with an anniversary campaign in September 2026. Its founding arrangement involved UAC and HEINEKEN, making this an example of a Nigeria-incorporated enterprise—not evidence of indigenous Nigerian founding. The company reports that its shares began trading on 5 September 1973. Anniversary history · Investor relations.

More revealing than the anniversary is the governance record: company disclosures put HEINEKEN's shareholding at 56.13% in September 2020 and 72.9% in December 2025. That is a 16.77 percentage-point increase, but the precise transactions behind it still need reconciliation. An exchange-filed notification dated 15 May 2025 records Hans Essaadi's departure on 30 June and Thibaut Boidin's appointment from 1 July 2025. It also describes a NGN 550 billion rights issue; the allotment and dilution history need separate examination.

New KCC carries a 101-year lineage—but is not a 101-year-old legal company. The original Kenya Co-operative Creameries is dated to 1925 in the Kenya Yearbook. Yet the company's Treasury-hosted annual financial statements record a new cooperative registered on 24 June 2003 and a distinct company incorporated on 19 November 2004 with 100% Government of Kenya ownership. Brand and asset lineage survived; the legal entity and ownership form changed. This distinction is central to any credible list of Africa's oldest companies and cooperatives.

Ethiopian Airlines marked 80 years of flying on 8 April 2026. Its official overview separates 21 December 1945 (founding) from 8 April 1946 (first operations) and identifies the Ethiopian government as the sole owner. The 8 April 2026 announcement marks the anniversary of operations, not the original founding date.

Selected feature under development

Who Owns an 80-Year-Old Company? Nigerian Breweries and the Institutions Beyond Its Founders

Thesis: Eight decades of existence do not tell us who founded an enterprise, who now controls it, or which governance systems enabled successive managers to keep it operating.

  1. Founding versus nationality: the 1946 UAC–HEINEKEN arrangement and why Nigerian incorporation differs from indigenous founding.
  2. Capital-market institution: the 1973 listing, later acquisitions and the ability to raise new equity.
  3. Ownership change: HEINEKEN's reported 56.13% and 72.9% stakes, with transaction-level reconciliation still required.
  4. Succession: the July 2025 chief executive transition and the board's role in leadership renewal.
  5. What actually endured: test whether governance, capital access and management systems explain survival rather than simply assuming that they do.

Evidence boundary: 1946 is company-reported, but the original incorporation certificate and exact date have not been obtained. The 2003/2004 New KCC transitions are documented in official financial statements; the 1925 predecessor date comes from a government historical account. Neither ownership concentration nor executive succession alone proves causal drivers of survival.

Research agenda

The next documents to secure are Nigerian Breweries' original incorporation certificate, complete 2024 rights-issue allotment and post-issue shareholder register, and New KCC's original predecessor registration and transfer instruments. The public candidate directory is a provisional evidence register, not a ranking of legally continuous centenarian firms.

For full citations, continuity notes and editorial questions, see the research log and feature outline.

item.title: Three Models of Institutional Continuity
item.description: Comparative research on a cooperative, a bank and an airline.
item.content:encoded:
WRITING / AFRICA'S ENDURING ENTERPRISES

Three Models of Institutional Continuity: Cooperative, Bank and Airline

Bugisu Co-operative Union, Banque Misr and Ethiopian Airlines pose three different questions about how organisations endure.

Kenneth S. Legesi · 19 October 2026 · Original editorial feature

Why comparison matters

The search for Africa's oldest enterprises is most useful when it becomes a comparison of institutional design. A cooperative, a bank and a national airline operate under different incentives, legal forms and capital requirements. The purpose of comparing them is not to crown a universal model but to identify what each arrangement must do to remain viable after its founders or first managers depart.

Bugisu: continuity through member institutions

Bugisu Co-operative Union's official history places its registration in July 1954, after the consolidation of four local unions. An earlier Bugisu Coffee Board dates to 1933, but that predecessor should not be treated as the union's own incorporation date. The cooperative model raises questions about how primary societies elect leadership, discipline management, accumulate capital and represent members whose interests evolve. Original registration and audited financial records remain necessary to establish full continuity.

Banque Misr: continuity through changes of control

Banque Misr traces its establishment to 1920 under Mohamed Talaat Harb. The bank's own historical publications report the founder's resignation in 1939 and nationalisation in 1960. The analytical issue is what survived these transitions: a legal entity, banking franchise, deposit relationships, managerial routines, public mandate or all of them. A founding date alone cannot answer that question; historical shareholder and statutory records are needed.

Ethiopian Airlines: continuity through organisational capability

Ethiopian Airlines reports founding on 21 December 1945 and commencement of operations on 8 April 1946, with government ownership. In 2022, the airline announced the appointment of Mesfin Tasew as group CEO after a long internal career. This makes the depth of the management pipeline an attractive hypothesis, but it does not prove that internal succession caused performance. A serious test would compare strategic continuity, governance decisions and financial results across leadership transitions.

The institutional common denominator

All three cases highlight the need to separate continuity of purpose from continuity of people. Member ownership can fail without accountable governance. State ownership can fail without commercial discipline. Professional management can fail without reliable oversight and capital allocation. The more promising research question is how each institution makes decisions, replenishes leadership, mobilises capital and corrects mistakes over time.

Evidence before rankings

The Africa's Enduring Enterprises directory is a provisional research register, not a definitive ranking. We publish uncertainty where records are incomplete and distinguish original corporate claims from independently corroborated legal and financial evidence. The aim is to learn how enduring African institutions are built, not to manufacture a league table from incomparable dates.

Part of Africa's Enduring Enterprises. Research is provisional; documentary corrections welcome. Explore sources and methodology.

item.title: Kakira: The Company That Had to Be Rebuilt
item.description: Institutional continuity through expropriation, reconstruction and development finance.
item.content:encoded:
WRITING / AFRICA'S ENDURING ENTERPRISES

Kakira: The Company That Had to Be Rebuilt

Madhvani’s commercial lineage survived, but the story of Kakira is one of rupture, restructuring and rehabilitation—not uninterrupted corporate life.

Kenneth S. Legesi · 19 October 2026 · Original editorial feature

The problem with anniversary arithmetic

The Madhvani Group traces its Ugandan commercial origins to 1914. That date is an important part of the group's history, but it cannot be assigned automatically to every present subsidiary as a legal incorporation date. To understand Kakira, one must distinguish family commercial lineage, ownership of productive assets, operating continuity and the identity of the legal company. Those distinctions matter more than an impressive anniversary number.

Rupture and return

Kakira's history includes the 1972 expropriation and a prolonged interruption of sugar production. The World Bank's contemporary project documentation describes the disruption and the subsequent rehabilitation effort. Kakira's own history recounts the family's return and eventual resumption of production. The exact sequence of management return, rehabilitation works and restored commercial output should be checked against contemporaneous records rather than compressed into a single “restart” date.

A new corporate vehicle

The World Bank appraisal describes the incorporation of Kakira Sugar Works (1985) Ltd on 15 May 1985 as part of a joint-venture restructuring. That is an institutional event, not a footnote. It is why this series records the 1914 group origin and the 1985 company incorporation separately. The 1985 ownership arrangements are historical and should not be presented as the current shareholder register. Read the World Bank appraisal.

Capital for reconstruction

The 1988 appraisal set out a proposed US$61.5 million rehabilitation financing plan. It included US$24.9 million in new IDA financing, US$7.4 million of existing IDA financing, US$8.7 million from the African Development Bank, US$9.4 million from the African Development Fund and US$11.1 million attributed to Kakira Sugar Works. These are appraisal financing estimates, not verified final disbursements. The distinction between sovereign concessional credit and terms on-lent to the operating company is equally important to any assessment of capital costs.

What the case demonstrates—and what it does not

The recovery suggests that enterprise continuity can depend on a combination of family commitment, state cooperation, development finance and technical rehabilitation. It does not, by itself, establish which element was decisive or whether the financing delivered its projected financial returns. Completion reports, audited accounts, output histories, ownership records and debt-service data are required to test those questions. This is the difference between an inspiring survival narrative and a rigorous institutional case study.

A question for African industrial policy

The relevant question is not merely how to establish industrial firms. It is how to preserve valuable operating capabilities through ownership disputes, political shocks and financial distress—and how to restart them without obscuring the cost of reconstruction. Kakira is a powerful case precisely because it is not a story of uninterrupted corporate existence. The public research directory records those qualifications.

Part of Africa's Enduring Enterprises. Research is provisional; documentary corrections welcome. Explore sources and methodology.

item.title: Why Africa's Enterprises Must Outlive Their Founders
item.description: A founding thesis about succession, governance and intergenerational enterprise survival.
item.content:encoded:
WRITING / AFRICA'S ENDURING ENTERPRISES

Why Africa’s Enterprises Must Outlive Their Founders

The question is not whether Africa can produce entrepreneurs. It is whether enterprise can become institution.

Kenneth S. Legesi · 19 October 2026 · Original editorial feature

A debate worth testing

A public conversation about whether an indigenous Ugandan business had survived for a century prompted a more important question: what does it take for a company to survive its founder? My response was simple: “Entrepreneurs start the businesses but never build the governance and institutions to ensure their longevity beyond the founder's vision.” The original exchange is here. The handwritten Uganda Business Longevity & Institution-Building Map developed that argument into a research agenda. A provocative social-media assertion is a hypothesis, not a census of historical enterprises.

The distinction between business and institution

A business can be commercially successful and still be organisationally fragile. Revenue, employment and even an impressive founder are insufficient tests of endurance. Institutions preserve decision rights, financial records, governance processes, managerial capability and access to capital when the individual who first assembled them is no longer in control. Longevity should therefore be measured not only in years but also through succession, ownership transfers, reinvestment and the capacity to survive shocks.

What the Uganda snapshot can and cannot tell us

The UBOS 2019/20 Census of Business Establishments provides a useful cross-sectional picture of enterprise structure. The handwritten map cites approximately 686,700 fixed-location establishments and a concentration of young, small and sole-proprietor businesses. These are starting points for checking the original census tables; they are not a longitudinal survival curve. In particular, the proportion of businesses currently older than fifty years cannot be interpreted as the probability that a newly established firm survives fifty years. Cohort data and business-register histories would be required for that claim.

Four different pathways

The cases in this series resist a single formula. Bugisu Co-operative Union raises questions about member governance and the continuity of a cooperative established in 1954. Banque Misr shows why founder departure and nationalisation must be analysed separately from institutional identity. Ethiopian Airlines invites scrutiny of long internal executive careers and state ownership. The Madhvani Group illustrates family-enterprise persistence through expropriation and the rehabilitation of industrial assets, even where operating-company continuity was broken. None of these examples establishes that a particular governance structure causes survival; each offers a testable proposition.

The agenda for institution-building

The practical agenda begins with separating founder and company assets, establishing reliable accounts and independent oversight, building a leadership bench, clarifying shareholder rights, and creating mechanisms for patient capital. It also requires legal enforcement, credible registries, functioning credit and equity markets, and the ability to reorganise distressed businesses without destroying productive capacity. The objective is not simply more start-ups. It is a larger stock of enterprises able to compound productive capital across generations.

How this series will work

Africa's Enduring Enterprises will maintain a public candidate directory, source register and documented case studies. We distinguish a founding story from legal incorporation, a family lineage from a company, and an announced financing package from actual disbursement. Corrections and new primary evidence are welcome. This first essay states the thesis; subsequent features examine the institutional mechanisms and the documentary record.

Part of Africa's Enduring Enterprises. Research is provisional; documentary corrections welcome. Explore sources and methodology.

item.title: Quickmart IPO: What Is a Share Really Worth at KES 7.50?
item.description: Independent assessment of Quickmart's IPO valuation, cash flows, lease economics and margin of safety.
item.content:encoded:
← All articles · Research overview · Home

Quickmart IPO: What Is a Share Really Worth at KES 7.50?

An independent investor's guide to earnings, cash flows, international comparisons and the margin of safety.

Kenneth S. Legesi, CFA | Legesi Investment Research | 12 October 2026

The investment case in five minutes

Quickmart's IPO offers exposure to an established Kenyan supermarket business. The offer price of KES 7.50 per share implies a KES 30bn equity valuation. The issue for investors is whether that price adequately compensates them for the risks and future cash flows they acquire.

The IPO documentation reports FY2025 revenue of approximately KES 50.43bn and profit after tax of KES 1.51bn. Management forecasts FY2026 net profit of approximately KES 2.10bn. The offer comprises 2bn existing shares, or 50% of the company's issued capital; Quickmart receives no new equity capital from the sale.

Our assessment remains WATCH / DEFER at KES 7.50, pending validation of the cash-flow model and lease economics. The revised DCF suggests potential upside, but the evidence does not yet establish a dependable margin of safety.

This is a free-access assessment. All methods and limitations below are part of the investment reasoning.

1. Is it a good business?

Quickmart's reported 72-store footprint provides scale in organised grocery retail. Its investment case depends on procurement, inventory discipline, occupancy costs, customer demand and location-level profitability.

Customers generally pay promptly while suppliers provide payment terms. That can support cash generation, but expansion requires fit-outs, equipment, inventory and time for new stores to mature.

Store growth creates shareholder value when incremental returns exceed the cost of capital. Investors should monitor same-store sales, margins, store payback, inventory turnover and returns on invested capital rather than relying on store counts alone.

2. Do profits translate into sustainable cash?

FY2025 reported operating cash flow after tax was approximately KES 4.83bn. It exceeded reported profit, but cash available to shareholders also depends on capital investment, lease payments, financing flows and working capital.

An illustrative subtotal is KES 4.83bn operating cash flow − KES 1.09bn PPE expenditure − KES 1.61bn lease principal = KES 2.13bn. This is not a fully reconciled FCFF or FCFE measure; the classification of interest and other financing flows still matters.

Dividends of approximately KES 1.65bn exceeded FY2025 reported earnings of KES 1.51bn. That is not automatically unsustainable because reserves and existing cash can support distributions. It makes the balance between growth, distributions and liquidity an important diligence question.

3. Is KES 7.50 a reasonable price?

Management's FY2026 forecast PAT is KES 2.103bn. Dividing by 4bn shares gives KES 0.52575 forecast EPS. The IPO price is therefore approximately 14.3x forecast reported earnings.

Our earlier earnings screen applied an illustrative 13x multiple, giving KES 6.83 per share, approximately 9% below the offer price. The multiple is a judgmental assumption, not an empirically derived fair-value adjustment.

| Applied forward P/E | Implied KES/share |
|---|---:|
| 10x | 5.26 |
| 12x | 6.31 |
| 13x | 6.83 |
| 14x | 7.36 |
| 16x | 8.41 |
| 17.7x | 9.31 |

International comparisons

Stanbic's September 2026 valuation parameters report a median FY2026E P/E of 17.7x and EV/EBITDA of 8.9x in an eleven-company grocery sample. The estimates are dated 21 September 2026, rather than live market valuations.

The universe spans Africa, Turkey and the Gulf. Business formats, scale, liquidity, country risk and lease accounting vary materially. Quickmart's 14.3x reported forward P/E is below the headline median, but that difference alone does not prove undervaluation.

Applying 17.7x directly gives KES 9.31 per share; applying an illustrative 20% discount gives KES 7.44. The discount is a sensitivity, not an independently established risk adjustment.

Source: Stanbic Bank Kenya/SBG Securities, printed page 3, Refinitiv estimates dated 21 September 2026. The illustration's side-panel calculations use rounded PAT of KES 2.10bn; this article uses KES 2.103bn.

4. What does the enterprise DCF suggest?

The revised working model starts with management's FY2027 forecast and extends analyst assumptions through FY2032. It uses a provisional 16% nominal KES WACC and 4% terminal growth. It is anchored to end-2026, not precisely the publication date.

| Component | KES bn |
|---|---:|
| PV FY2027–2032 cash flows | 19.02 |
| PV terminal value | 22.86 |
| **Enterprise value** | **41.88** |
| Less net financial obligations including leases | (7.27) |
| **Equity value** | **34.61** |
| Shares outstanding | 4.00bn |
| **Provisional value per share** | **KES 8.65** |

The arithmetic implies approximately 15.4% upside to the offer. It has been reproduced from the workbook's numeric inputs, but this does not validate the economic assumptions.

Approximately 55% of EV comes from terminal value. The discount rate lacks a completed market build, FY2027 working-capital outflow is a zero placeholder, and terminal reinvestment is not explicitly linked to sustainable ROIC.

The lease question

Lease liabilities are approximately KES 7.9bn in the model's source disclosures. Net obligations of KES 7.27bn differ from gross lease liabilities because debt and cash must also be considered.

The rental-based cross-check gives KES 6.75 per share, leaving a material KES 1.90 gap to the enterprise DCF. Its KES 2.05bn FY2027 rental input is unverified, and future lease additions, renewals and liabilities are not fully matched in either approach.

The rental result is not a validated lower valuation bound. The cash-flow conventions and capital structure need reconciliation before KES 8.65 can be treated as a price target.

5. Who receives the subscription proceeds?

Sokoni Retail Kenya Limited is selling 2bn existing shares. Full subscription at KES 7.50 implies KES 15bn gross proceeds for the selling shareholder. Quickmart receives no new equity capital.

A secondary sale can broaden ownership and create liquidity. Future expansion must nevertheless be financed by company cash generation or other funding sources, rather than IPO proceeds.

The disclosed two-year lock-up applies to 60% of the seller's retained shares, not the entire retained holding. Read the full offer restrictions and exemptions when assessing future selling pressure.

Investment conclusion

| Reference | KES/share | Status |
|---|---:|---|
| Earnings screen | 6.83 | Illustrative 13x FY2026 P/E |
| Offer price | 7.50 | Transaction term |
| Enterprise DCF | 8.65 | Provisional 16% / 4% model |
| Rental cross-check | 6.75 | Unreconciled proxy |

These indications should not be averaged into a target: their methods and evidential support differ.

WATCH / DEFER remains the assessment. Stronger evidence on sustainable cash generation, store-level returns, lease economics and capital allocation would support reconsideration. Weak new-store returns, stretched supplier credit, margin pressure or distributions that constrain investment would weaken the case.

This is not a prediction that the shares will fall after listing. It describes the evidence needed for a disciplined investment decision.

Which stock should we assess next?

Which listed company or upcoming IPO would you like assessed next? Share the company, ticker and exchange, together with the question you most want answered: valuation, dividends, financial strength, growth or governance.

Share this assessment with another investor and subscribe to Legesi for future research and Five-Finger Investor Guides.

Sources and methodology

See the official document links and page references, valuation methodology, limitations, and reproduction script. Historical information and management forecasts are distinct from analyst assumptions. Packaging reproduced model arithmetic; it did not complete a financial audit or market calibration.

For investor education and general information. Not personalised investment advice, an offer or solicitation, or a guarantee of performance. Read the full disclaimer.

Methods and source repository · Investment disclaimer

item.title: Dangote Petroleum Refinery IPO — Independent Buy-Side Research
item.description: Initial valuation, funding, governance and downside assessment of the proposed refinery IPO.
item.content:encoded:

Original underwriting conclusion — 17 September 2026

Historical view: this section preserves the original prospectus-based underwrite. The 18 October 2026 update above supersedes its valuation range, entry threshold and action framework.

DPRP is becoming a world-scale operating refinery; that does not make the IPO an attractive security at any price. At ₦525, investors pay approximately US$47.8bn for the equity and about US$47.7bn enterprise value after assumed deployment of net IPO cash. The price is equivalent to 9.2× mechanically annualised H1 2026 EBITDA and 13.1× annualised H1 earnings. US refiners trade around a 9.4× median LTM EV/EBITDA, but they offer longer operating histories, deeper liquidity, diversified assets, mature governance and lower-cost funding. DPRP therefore warrants a discount—not parity—on normalised earnings.

Action
PASS / WAIT FOR PROOF

Do not subscribe at ₦525. Revisit below ₦370 only after a facility-by-facility funding plan, sustained through-cycle margins and a fully diluted capitalisation are disclosed. A disciplined entry threshold is approximately ₦280, allowing a margin of safety to the constructive existing-operations value.

Decision hinge
Is US$6bn EBITDA sustainable?

The offer price effectively needs c.US$6.0bn of sustainable EBITDA at 8×, or substantial present value from unbuilt capacity. Audited history does not yet prove either.

What would change the view: audited quarterly evidence of sustainable utilisation above 85% and mid-cycle EBITDA above US$5bn; committed expansion financing without material dilution; a complete debt/security bridge; receivables normalisation; independent related-party oversight; and a share price below ₦370—with ₦280 preferred for an IPO margin of safety.
Second-edition conclusion: probability weighting produces c.₦333/share on present-value cases and c.₦508 of three-year expected terminal value. From ₦525, that three-year outcome is a negative c.1.1% annualised return before FX; from ₦280 it is c.21.9%. Peer, liquidity, hedge-cost, carbon and prospectus-deficiency work therefore reinforce the original entry discipline.

Investment thesis and variant perception

The asset is increasingly proven

US EIA data show 700 kb/d capacity after February maintenance; Nigeria shipped 561 kb/d of petroleum products in 2Q26, including 350 kb/d exports. Reuters/Kpler evidence indicates 565 kb/d Nigerian crude receipts in August and at least 520 kb/d October purchases. This materially reduces the “can it operate?” risk.

The earnings base is not yet proven

Gross margin moved from –9.5% in 2024 to 1.9% in 2025 and 17.9% in H1 2026. H1 contains only four months after management says stable full-capacity operations began. Product prices rose sharply and 2026 refining conditions benefited from global supply disruption.

The expansion is an option, not a completed asset

IPO cash funds just 10.85% of a US$14.269bn plan. Completion is variously stated as 2029 and 2030. Without committed funding, EPC protections, a crude-supply plan and project returns, assigning full multiple value to the second train transfers development risk to public investors.

Minority protections do not offset controller risk

The offer creates only 3.3% public ownership; beneficial control remains c.84.4%. Audit and Risk is chaired by a DIL executive, committees were newly constituted and untested, and several key policies were still being adopted.

Variant wedge: consensus enthusiasm is anchored on scarcity, scale and annualised H1 earnings. Our variant view is that the share price must be underwritten on post-working-capital, post-maintenance and post-expansion-financing returns. On that basis the current offer pays today for much of tomorrow’s execution.

Balance sheet and cash-quality points

  • At 30 June, debt was US$5.666bn, cash US$4.267bn and net debt US$1.398bn. The apparent improvement was capital-structure driven: US$4.0bn “project coreshift” proceeds and US$2.477bn share deposits accompanied repayment of the US$3.987bn DIL loan.
  • Receivables rose from ₦1.679tn to ₦4.029tn in six months; inventory rose 46% to ₦2.816tn. Post-period collection evidence is essential.
  • H1 reported capex was only US$37.9m, while the disclosed remaining-2026 plan is US$4.8bn. H1 “free cash flow” is therefore not distributable cash flow.
  • H1 earnings include a net FX gain and benefited from very large realised-price increases. Through-cycle gross refining margin, not annualised PAT, should anchor valuation.
  • Positive pre-operation CFO in 2021–23 came from contractor payables building despite zero revenue; it is not recurring cash-generation evidence.

Industry position: structural advantage, cyclical economics

Proven<130 kb/d

Nigeria seaborne imports in 2Q26, down from nearly 400 kb/d in 2023.

Export access350 kb/d

Nigeria product exports in 2Q26; 130 kb/d to Europe and nearly 120 kb/d to Africa.

Feedstock concentration35–38%

520–565 kb/d intake as a share of Nigeria’s 1.50m b/d August strict crude output.

DPRP’s moat is actual availability, scale, complexity, deep-water logistics and integrated evacuation—not simply nameplate capacity. Nigeria’s four state refineries have 445 kb/d combined nameplate capacity but have historically been offline or intermittent. Yet DPRP’s output is already too large for a purely domestic narrative: export markets are essential and expose shareholders to global cracks, freight and destination-market rules.

Cycle warning: the IEA projects global refined-product demand peaking in 2027 at 86.3m b/d. It expects 4.2m b/d of new capacity through 2030 against 1.6m b/d of closures—net supply growth above demand growth. 2026 disruption margins should not be terminalised.

Carbon transition and export-market exposure

DPRP may be physically competitive, but it cannot yet be placed reliably on a global carbon-cost curve. Its new asset base, Nelson Complexity Index of 11.5, broad crude flexibility, Euro-V product capability and 570MW captive plant support conversion and product-quality competitiveness. Conversely, coking, hydrocracking, RFCC, hydrotreating and hydrogen production are energy intensive. Complexity is not evidence of low emissions.

DCF / SOTP and WACC cross-check

A US-dollar DCF is appropriate because feedstock, product prices, debt and capex are predominantly dollar-linked. A reasonable operating-asset WACC is 14–16%: c.5% US risk-free rate, mature-market equity premium and refining beta, Nigeria country/equity risk and a company/governance premium, partly offset by debt. The 18–20% range remains appropriate for unfunded expansion cash flows. Approximately 12% is required for the existing cash-flow shape to approach ₦525—too low before operating, financing and governance risks are resolved.

Hard-currency return bridge and hedge feasibility

A foreign investor owns a naira-priced security even though DPRP’s operations are substantially dollar-linked. Company-level economic hedging does not remove shareholder translation, convertibility, repatriation, forward-basis or roll-cost risk.

Required bridge: naira equity return − realised NGN depreciation − hedge/roll cost − basis and slippage − repatriation friction = USD investor return.

Do not mistake 300–500bp for a verified full-hedge cost

The August 2026 364-day Nigerian T-bill stop rate was approximately 17.59%, versus a US two-year yield around 4.73% on 16 September. A covered-rate proxy implies roughly 12.3% annual forward discount before bid–ask, credit/collateral, tenor liquidity and basis. Executable bank/NDF quotes may differ materially.

IC requirement: obtain executable 1m/3m/6m/12m forward or NDF quotes for US$10m, US$25m and US$50m notionals, including collateral and unwind terms. Until then, describe 300–500bp only as a partial-hedge/portfolio-drag assumption—not the full hedge cost.

FX access has improved, with higher reserves and stronger capital inflows, but 85% of 2025 inflows were portfolio flows and only US$2.10bn went to equities. This remains rate-sensitive capital. Entry-price discipline should therefore be assessed in USD after explicit hedge and depreciation cases.

7Controller/RPT: value shifts through pricing, funding or services.MediumHighRPT balances rise; policy waivers; affiliate contracts.
8Policy/tax: price restraint, crude allocation or 2028 taxation lowers FCF.MediumMedium-highDomestic price intervention; higher effective tax.
9FX/repatriation: naira depreciation erodes hard-currency equity return.HighMediumFX liquidity tightens; e-CCI/repatriation delays.

24-month evidence calendar

Priority 1 before subscription: items 1–3, 7, 10–12 and 14. Until resolved, retain the higher WACC/governance discount, value expansion only as a probability-weighted option and do not underwrite dividends.
Formal issuer request: publish written corrections for the p.158 unit error and 2029/2030 timetable; provide debt/security and RPT roll-forwards; issue a fully diluted post-offer capitalisation/free-float schedule; and make the material operating, financing, site, EPC and governance documents available for diligence.

Priority questions for management and issuing houses

  1. Provide monthly throughput, utilisation, yields, unplanned downtime and realised GRM from January 2025 onward. This tests whether H1 2026 is repeatable.
  2. Bridge benchmark cracks to the stated US$24.2/bbl 2026 GRM. Show crude differentials, freight, yields, energy, hedging and inventory timing.
  3. Explain the H1 receivables increase to ₦4.029tn. Provide ageing, customer concentration, related-party content and post-period collection.
  4. Reconcile FY2025 US$6.243bn debt to H1 US$5.67bn all-secured debt. Identify facilities, security, maturity, covenants and uses.
  5. Provide the fully loaded expansion sources-and-uses plan. Identify contingency, interest, start-up losses and working capital.
  6. How much of the US$12.721bn gap is committed? State lenders, pricing, tenor, currency, security and draw conditions.
  7. Is further equity contemplated? State pre-emption rights and maximum fully diluted share count.
  8. Reconcile 2029 and 2030 completion dates. Separate mechanical completion, commissioning, testing and commercial operation for each plant.
  9. Provide EPC price/schedule guarantees and cost-overrun allocation. These determine project downside.
  10. Separate project returns for refining, polypropylene and LAB. Disclose EBITDA, ROIC, IRR and break-even margin.
  11. Provide sustaining capex and turnaround assumptions. H1 additions are not a steady-state proxy.
  12. Disclose NNPC and international crude-contract economics. Include formula, differentials, naira conversion, credit and duration.
  13. Confirm all related-party units on p.158 and publish a counterparty roll-forward. The prose/table appears inconsistent by 1,000×.
  14. Provide all material RPT contracts and independent pricing benchmarks. This supports the arm’s-length assertion.
  15. Why is Audit/Risk chaired by a DIL executive? State whether an independent chair/majority will be installed before listing.
  16. Which governance policies were fully effective at the prospectus date? Provide approval dates and compliance attestations.
  17. Provide the 50-year site sublease. Disclose rent, termination, renewal, improvements ownership and lender step-in.
  18. Provide the complete litigation schedule. Show claimant, amount, stage, provision, probability and insurance.
  19. Why are only two offer documents listed as material contracts? Supply the full operating, financing and technology contract register.
  20. State the board-approved dividend policy and covenant capacity. There is currently no underwritable payout path.

Source register, conflicts and assumptions

Material conflicts and limitations

  • Programme completion is 2029 in the summary and 2030 in the detailed use-of-proceeds section.

  • Related-party prose and tables on p.158 appear to differ by a factor of 1,000.
  • The move from unsecured DIL debt to an all-secured H1 capital structure is not fully bridged.
  • Current price, liquidity, index status and short interest do not exist pre-listing; the IPO price is not a traded market price.
  • No sell-side consensus exists in a sufficiently reliable form for use; estimates in this note are analyst assumptions.

See the standalone Prospectus Deficiency Memorandum for the formal 15-item schedule, materiality assessment and evidence requests.

item.title: Quickmart IPO: What Is a Share Really Worth at KES 7.50?
item.description: A good business is not necessarily a good investment at any price. Examining Quickmart’s earnings, cash flows, comparables and intrinsic value to assess if the IPO offers investors a margin of safety
item.content:encoded:
Home← All writingWorkRSS

WRITING / ARCHIVE

Quickmart IPO: What Is a Share Really Worth at KES 7.50?

Originally published on Substack: 2026-10-12 · Original publication ↗

Associated research repository ↗ (linkage to be verified against the article evidence)

By Kenneth S. Legesi, CFA | 12 October 2026

Kenya’s Quickmart IPO presents an interesting opportunity: a profitable supermarket operator with an established national footprint, growing revenues and ambitions to expand further.

The offer price is KES 7.50 per share, implying an equity market capitalisation of KES 30 billion.

At first glance, the numbers are attractive. Quickmart generated KES 50.4 billion in revenue and KES 1.51 billion in net profit in 2025. Management forecasts earnings growth in 2026 and 2027.

But the question for investors is not simply whether Quickmart is a good business.

The question is whether the price being asked adequately compensates investors for the risks of owning it.

I approach this through five questions: Is it a good business? Does it generate cash? Is the valuation reasonable? What exactly are investors buying? And what could go wrong?

The Quickmart IPO at a glance

Before assessing whether Quickmart’s IPO represents an attractive investment, it is important to understand the scale of the business, its financial performance and the terms on which shares are being offered. At KES 7.50 per share, the IPO values Quickmart at KES 30 billion, against FY2025 revenues of KES 50.43 billion and net profit of KES 1.51 billion. Management forecasts further earnings growth in 2026, but investors must distinguish the company’s operating performance from the price they are being asked to pay. The snapshot below summarises the key figures that provide the starting point for our investment assessment.

The last two figures are analytical estimates based on different methodologies, not independently validated price targets.

1. Is Quickmart a good business?

Quickmart has developed a substantial position in Kenya’s organised grocery retail market, operating approximately 72 stores at the time of the offer.

Supermarkets can be attractive businesses when they combine high inventory turnover, efficient procurement, disciplined operating costs and favourable supplier-payment terms.

Customers generally pay immediately, while suppliers may allow retailers time to settle invoices. This can support operating cash flow and enable growth without requiring equivalent increases in shareholder capital.

But supermarket retailing is also competitive and typically operates on relatively thin net margins.

Success depends on store location, product availability, pricing, customer loyalty, inventory management and logistics.

Quickmart’s expansion plans provide opportunities for growth. However, opening additional stores creates value only if the returns generated exceed the cost of the capital invested.

What matters is not simply the number of stores Quickmart opens, but how much economic value each new store creates.

The key operating indicators to monitor after listing include same-store sales growth, gross margins, store-level profitability, inventory turnover, new-store payback periods and return on invested capital.

2. Does Quickmart turn profits into cash?

Quickmart’s FY2025 results show a profitable business with substantial reported operating cash generation.

FY2025 financial performance, KES billion

  • Revenue, 50.43

  • Reported EBITDA, 5.08

  • Adjusted EBITDA, 5.36

  • Profit after tax, 1.51

  • Operating cash flow after tax, 4.83

  • Property and equipment expenditure, 1.09

  • Lease principal repayments, 1.61

  • Dividends paid, 1.65

Operating cash flow exceeded reported net profit by a considerable margin.

That is encouraging, but investors should avoid treating all operating cash flow as freely distributable cash.

Quickmart must maintain existing stores, finance expansion, manage inventory, settle contractual lease obligations and preserve adequate liquidity.

A simplified calculation illustrates the distinction:

KES 4.83bn operating cash flow − KES 1.09bn capital expenditure − KES 1.61bn lease principal = approximately KES 2.13bn.

This is an illustrative cash subtotal, not a fully reconciled measure of free cash flow. It does not by itself establish the cash available to shareholders.

The company also paid approximately KES 1.65 billion in dividends during 2025, compared with net profit of KES 1.51 billion.

Distributing more than one year’s profit is not inherently problematic. A company may have accumulated reserves and sufficient cash resources.

However, a growing retailer must balance dividends against capital expenditure, working-capital needs and financial obligations.

The investment question is whether Quickmart can simultaneously expand, meet its obligations and sustain shareholder distributions without weakening its financial position.

3. Is KES 7.50 a reasonable price?

Valuation is where a good business becomes either an attractive or unattractive investment.

At the IPO offer price, Quickmart is valued at approximately KES 30 billion.

Management forecasts FY2026 profit after tax of approximately KES 2.103 billion.

With 4 billion shares outstanding, forecast earnings per share are:

KES 2.103bn ÷ 4bn = KES 0.526 per share.

At KES 7.50, investors are paying approximately 14.3 times forecast FY2026 reported earnings.

Is that expensive or cheap?

One approach is to compare Quickmart with listed grocery retailers elsewhere. Another is to estimate the present value of the cash the business could generate.

Neither method should be used without considering its limitations.

The earnings-multiple approach

Applying an illustrative 13x forward P/E multiple gives:

KES 0.526 × 13 = KES 6.83 per share.

This is approximately 9% below the IPO offer price.

The 13x multiple is a screening assumption. It reflects a judgmental discount to international peers for differences in market risk, company scale, liquidity and operating characteristics. It is not a statistically validated fair-value multiple.

The valuation changes materially with the multiple selected:

This illustrates an important principle: a valuation multiple is an expression of expectations and risk, not a universal rule.

What do international grocery retailers trade at?

Stanbic Bank Kenya/SBG Securities’ September 2026 valuation parameters include 11 listed grocery retailers across South Africa, Morocco, Egypt, Turkey and Gulf markets.

The sample’s median FY2026 forecast P/E is approximately 17.7x, with a median EV/EBITDA of 8.9x.

Quickmart’s 14.3x forward reported P/E is below that international median.

That may suggest an attractive entry price, but the comparison needs interpretation.

Retailers in different countries face different financing costs, inflation, currency risks, consumer purchasing power and stock-market liquidity.

They may also have different store formats, margins, growth expectations and accounting policies.

A direct application of the 17.7x peer median would imply approximately KES 9.31 per Quickmart share. But that does not mean Quickmart necessarily deserves that valuation.

A 20% discount to the median, for example, would imply approximately KES 7.45 per share, close to the IPO price.

That discount is illustrative, not an independently established adjustment.

The conclusion from comparables is that Quickmart is priced below the international peer median, but whether the discount is sufficient remains an open question.

4. What does a discounted cash-flow valuation suggest?

An earnings multiple tells us how the market values comparable profits.

A discounted cash-flow model attempts to answer a different question: What is the present value of the cash Quickmart could generate in the future?

An enterprise DCF begins with management’s FY2027 forecasts and extends independent assumptions through FY2032.

It uses a provisional nominal Kenyan-shilling weighted average cost of capital of 16% and a perpetual terminal growth rate of 4%.

The resulting valuation bridge is:

The provisional DCF therefore indicates approximately 15.4% potential upside to the KES 7.50 offer price.

However, this result requires several qualifications.

First, approximately 55% of enterprise value comes from terminal value—the value attributed to cash flows beyond the explicit forecast period.

Second, the 16% WACC and 4% perpetual growth rate are analytical assumptions that still require complete market calibration.

Third, future cash flows depend on management delivering its forecasts, maintaining margins and generating appropriate returns on reinvestment.

Fourth, the treatment of lease obligations requires further reconciliation.

Why the lease treatment matters

Quickmart has substantial contractual lease commitments associated with its store network.

Under IFRS 16, many lease obligations are recognised on the balance sheet, while their costs affect the financial statements differently from conventional operating rental expenses.

An alternative rental-based valuation cross-check indicates approximately KES 6.75 per share, compared with KES 8.65 from the revised enterprise DCF.

The difference of approximately KES 1.90 per share is material.

The rental-based cross-check uses assumptions that have not yet been fully reconciled to contractual lease schedules. It is therefore not a validated lower valuation bound.

A complete valuation should consistently account for lease payments, renewals, interest, new-store leases and the financial obligations deducted from enterprise value.

The cost of capital also needs to be supported by market-observed long-term Kenyan interest rates, an appropriate equity risk premium, comparable-company risk and actual financing costs.

The KES 8.65 DCF result is therefore an indicative scenario—not a definitive intrinsic-value target.

5. What exactly are investors buying?

The IPO structure is particularly important.

Quickmart is offering 2 billion existing shares, representing 50% of its issued share capital, through a secondary sale by Sokoni Retail Kenya Limited.

At KES 7.50 per share, a fully subscribed offer would generate approximately KES 15 billion in gross proceeds for the selling shareholder.

Quickmart itself receives no new equity capital from the IPO.

This does not automatically make the transaction unattractive.

Secondary offerings can create liquidity for existing shareholders, broaden ownership and establish a publicly traded market for the company.

But the distinction matters for investors evaluating future growth.

If Quickmart intends to expand its store network, it must finance that expansion through internally generated cash, borrowing, supplier financing or other sources—not through the proceeds of this IPO.

Investors should therefore consider the company’s dividend policy, capital allocation priorities, debt and lease obligations, related-party transactions and the incentives of its continuing shareholders.

A listing also creates expectations around governance, transparency and financial reporting.

These factors can materially influence long-term investment returns.

So, should investors buy Quickmart at KES 7.50?

The analysis produces three principal valuation reference points:

The separate rental-based cross-check indicates KES 6.75, but remains unreconciled.

These estimates should not be averaged into a single price target. They are based on different methods and do not yet have equivalent evidential support.

Quickmart appears to be an established, profitable and growing supermarket operator. Its commercial proposition is credible, and its earnings forecasts indicate potential for further expansion.

But at KES 7.50, the investment case is not conclusively attractive on the information currently validated.

The revised DCF suggests upside, while the more conservative earnings approach indicates downside. The outstanding lease reconciliation and discount-rate calibration are material to the conclusion.

My assessment: WATCH / DEFER

I would want stronger evidence on sustainable cash generation, lease economics, capital allocation and returns from new stores before concluding that the IPO offers a sufficient margin of safety.

That is not a prediction that the shares will fall after listing. Market prices can diverge substantially from analytical estimates, particularly around an IPO.

It is a statement about the evidence needed to make a disciplined investment decision.

A good business is not necessarily a good investment at any price. What matters is the relationship between price, future cash flows and risk.

Which stock should we analyse next?

The purpose of this article is to make investment analysis more accessible, rigorous and practical—particularly for investors assessing African capital markets.

Which listed company or upcoming IPO would you like me to assess next?

Share the company name, ticker and exchange in the comments, along with the question you most want answered: valuation, dividends, financial strength, growth prospects, governance or risks.

Your suggestions will help shape future independent company assessments.

If you found this Quickmart analysis useful, share it with another investor and subscribe for more related content.

Sources and methodology

This analysis draws on the following principal documents:

  1. Quickmart PLC — IPO Information Memorandum, October 2026.

  2. Quickmart PLC — FY2025 Audited Financial Statements.

  3. EY — Reporting Accountant’s Report, September 2026.

  4. Stanbic Bank Kenya/SBG Securities — Quick Mart PLC Offer Price Valuation Parameters, 22 September 2026, incorporating Refinitiv estimates as at 21 September 2026.

Historical financial information and management forecasts are distinguished from independent valuation assumptions. The earnings-multiple screening and DCF are illustrative analytical estimates.

The DCF remains provisional pending full reconciliation of lease obligations, working-capital assumptions, terminal reinvestment and market calibration of the discount rate.

Disclaimer: This publication is for educational and general informational purposes only. It is not personalised investment advice, a recommendation to subscribe for shares or a guarantee of future performance. Investors should consult the official offer documents and assess their own investment objectives and risk tolerance.

Historical edition. Original date preserved; subsequent updates, if any, are recorded separately. View original publication.

item.title: The Gem Inside the Rump
item.description: Why some public companies secretly behave like venture capital funds
item.content:encoded:
Home← All writingWorkRSS

WRITING / ARCHIVE

The Gem Inside the Rump

Originally published on Substack: 2026-08-26 · Original publication ↗

Associated research repository ↗ (linkage to be verified against the article evidence)

In 2019, if you had asked any analyst covering East African equities to describe Car and General Kenya, they would have told you the same thing: a Nairobi-listed motor vehicle distributor with colonial-era roots, modest margins, thin coverage, and a share price that had drifted sideways for most of the decade.

They would have been right. And they would have missed everything.

Because inside Car and General, something was being built that had almost nothing to do with selling motorbikes. A motorcycle financing startup called Watu Credit was quietly rewriting the rules of asset-backed lending across the continent — not through venture capital, not through a Silicon Valley pitch deck, but through Car and General’s commercial infrastructure, its dealer networks, and its deep East African market knowledge. And then out through six countries and half a billion dollars in disbursements.

Car and General’s share price never got the memo.

The Architecture of a Mispricing

Markets are precise about some things and systematically wrong about others. They are precise about cash flows they can model. They are systematically wrong about value that is hidden, structural, or requires a different mental model than the one the market applies to the visible business.

Car and General trades as a motor vehicle distributor because that is what it has always been. That label determines which analysts cover it, which comparable companies they use, and what multiple it receives. The label is not wrong. It is incomplete.

Watu Credit is not a motor vehicle story. It is a fintech story. It uses proprietary credit scoring models trained on asset behavior and mobile money repayment history — data no bank in East Africa possesses at this scale. It finances motorcycles, three-wheelers, and smartphones on lease-to-own terms for borrowers who have never held a formal bank account. It has disbursed more than USD 500 million across Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Ivory Coast, and beyond. A pure-play fintech with Watu Credit’s characteristics would not trade at a distribution-company multiple. In a world where African fintech comparables trade at 4–8× revenue, Watu Credit’s standalone value is not zero. But that is approximately what Car and General’s share price implies.

This gap — between what a company appears to be and what it actually contains — is the Embedded Call Option.

The Vocabulary

The series introduction established why this framework needed naming. Here is the vocabulary that makes it operational.

The Rump is the mature core business. It is what analysts model. It is what most investors are paying for. It generates cash, employs most of the staff, and dominates the income statement. It is real and valuable — but it is, in the relevant sense, already priced.

The Gem is the embedded asset. It is what the market is not pricing — or pricing badly. It may be a fintech subsidiary, a digital platform, an AI application, a data business, or a minority stake in something growing at 40% per year. The Gem is undervalued for structural reasons: too small to move the parent’s valuation metrics, obscured by the Rump’s accounting, or below the scale at which analysts begin to model it seriously.

The Embedded Call Option is the asymmetric payoff structure that results. The investor acquires the Rump at its market-implied value and receives the Gem at a fraction of what it would trade at if listed independently. If the Gem unlocks — through a spin-off, an IPO, a strategic sale, or a re-rating — the payoff is non-linear. If it never unlocks, the investor still holds the Rump at a reasonable price. The downside is bounded by the Rump. The upside is determined by the Gem.

The Telecom Hiding a Bank

MTN Uganda has operated in Uganda since 1998. It sells airtime, data bundles, and postpaid contracts. It competes with Airtel. Its peers are other African telcos. The market prices it accordingly.

But MTN Uganda also owns MTN MoMo — Mobile Money — which processes transactions worth more than Uganda’s entire formal banking system’s annual throughput. MoMo has over 18 million registered users in Uganda alone. Across the MTN Group’s 19 markets, the MoMo platform has approximately 72 million active users. It is a payment processor, a savings wallet, a lending platform, an insurance distribution channel, and — for millions of Ugandans who have never held a formal bank account — a financial identity system.

A pure-play digital financial services company with MoMo’s scale and growth rate would attract a 15–25× revenue multiple in any rational comparable set. MTN Uganda trades at a blended telecom-fintech multiple that applies telecom pricing to the entire enterprise. MoMo — the Gem — is included at whatever residual the market assigns after pricing the telecom. In practice, that residual is a fraction of standalone value.

“The market prices the label. The investor with a different lens prices the architecture.”

Why This Is Structural, Not Accidental

Analysts cover sectors, not structures. A telecom analyst benchmarks MTN Uganda against Airtel Uganda and Safaricom. The fintech business does not appear in the comparable set. The fintech analyst, conversely, does not cover listed telcos. The Gem falls between coverage silos by design.

Standard valuation frameworks are backward-looking. They discount what is known. A business with venture-like upside embedded inside a conglomerate discount has a payoff profile that spreadsheets systematically understate. And if MoMo generates 25% of group revenue but is growing at 45%, it still cannot move consolidated EPS meaningfully when the telecom business is four times its size. The analyst who covers EPS does not have a reason to update the model for a subsidiary too small to change the bottom line.

The result is systematic. Persistent. And exploitable by investors willing to read the architecture rather than the label.

The Payoff Structure

The asymmetry is in the first two rows. The bear case requires genuine deterioration of the core business, not merely the Gem failing to unlock. An investor who correctly prices the Rump at or below fair value has bounded the bear case at a manageable level.

“Sometimes the most valuable part of a company is the part investors don’t yet recognize.”

SOTP Valuation Walkthrough: MTN Uganda

Expected return: potentially mid-to-high teens annually, including dividends, if MoMo value is progressively unlocked. The telecom business provides the cash-flow foundation; MoMo provides upside optionality.

Next in the Series, Article 2: Africa's Hidden Fintechs. The continent's largest embedded optionality opportunities are not in venture capital portfolios or private markets, they are sitting inside listed companies priced as if the fintech revolution never happened, and why nearly a trillion dollars in mobile money flows is the Gem the market has decided to label as a telecom. See an overview for the series and why I wrote this series here.
