item.title: Why Freedom, Not Peace, Prices Returns in Africa
item.description: A Machiavellian framework for distinguishing geopolitical agitation from institutional absorption, with a historical 2023 Africa Investability Index.
item.content:encoded:
Home← All writingAfrica Investability IndexRSS

RESEARCH / AFRICA INVESTABILITY INDEX

Why Freedom, Not Peace, Prices Returns in Africa

Rethinking risk in Africa: from headlines to institutions

Kenneth Legesi · 16 January 2026 · Originally published on Impala Market

Author republication. Text reproduced from the original edition; original charts and tables are linked rather than embedded. The formula is preserved as published and remains subject to methodological reconciliation.

Africa is not uniformly risky; it is unevenly investable. What markets often price as danger is frequently just noise. The real determinant of returns is not how often countries are tested, but how well their institutions absorb stress when it arrives. By separating agitation from institutional strength, the Investability framework shows why some of Africa’s noisiest markets may be among its most investable, while some of its calmest hide significant tail risks.

For investors, the implication is clear: stop allocating to Africa by headlines and start allocating by institutional resilience.

“A little bit of agitation gives resources to souls and what makes the species prosper isn’t peace, but freedom.” — Jean-Jacques Rousseau, The Social Contract (1762)

Over the past 12–18 months, Africa’s investment story has again been written by headlines: contested elections, coups, currency devaluations, and sovereign debt restructurings. From FX adjustments in Nigeria and Egypt, to political transitions across West and Southern Africa, to the long shadow of debt workouts in Ghana and Zambia, the message reaching global markets has been familiar: instability equals risk.

For many allocators, this seems to confirm a simple conclusion that Africa is, once again, “high risk.” But that conclusion rests on a basic mistake. It treats visible stress as a proxy for danger to capital. It collapses political contestation, macro adjustment, and institutional weakness into a single narrative of risk—and in doing so, misses the only question that really matters to investors: not how often systems are tested, but how they respond when pressure arrives.

That distinction between noise and resilience is where Africa continues to be most mispriced.

What investors routinely misunderstand is not Africa’s volatility, but its meaning. Noise is treated as danger; calm as safety. Yet across Africa, as in all frontier markets, the link between political agitation and investment outcomes is shaped less by the presence of conflict than by the strength of institutions that absorb it.

Drawing on Machiavelli’s argument in Discourses on Livy that political conflict, when institutionalised, strengthens republics rather than weakens them, this framework distinguishes between volatility that can be priced and risk that cannot. Machiavelli was explicit that social and political tension is not a pathology of free systems, but a source of their resilience, provided it is channelled through laws and institutions rather than suppressed by force.

“Those who condemn the quarrels between the nobles and the plebs seem to me to censure the very things that were the first cause of Rome’s keeping itself free.” — Niccolò Machiavelli, Discourses on Livy, Book I, Chapter 4
“For in every republic there are two diverse humors, that of the people and that of the great, and all the laws made in favor of liberty arise from their disunion.” — Niccolò Machiavelli, Discourses on Livy, Book I, Chapter 4

For investors, the translation is precise. Conflict processed through institutions produces volatility that markets can price. Conflict that overwhelms institutions produces tail risk that markets cannot. The distinction Machiavelli drew about political freedom is the same distinction modern finance must draw about capital safety.

Risk, measured properly

A persistent error in African investing is the conflation of geopolitical risk with investment risk. While the two are often bundled together in headlines, they describe fundamentally different dimensions of capital safety.

Geopolitical risk captures exposure to macro-shocks: regime survival, armed conflict, diplomatic realignment, and social unrest. It is typically proxied by high-frequency datasets such as the ACLED Conflict Index, geopolitical risk sentiment indicators, or composite measures like the Fragile States Index (FSI). This is the weather of a nation—loud, episodic and highly visible.

Because it dominates news flow, it is often overweighted by global allocators, even when its transmission to commercial outcomes is indirect.

Investment risk, by contrast, is narrower and more operational. It concerns commercial legibility: whether contracts are enforced, policies evolve predictably, capital can exit, and disputes are resolved through rules rather than discretion.

These dynamics are better captured by structural governance measures such as the World Bank’s Worldwide Governance Indicators (WGI) or the Ibrahim Index of African Governance, which illuminate the plumbing of the economy rather than its headlines.

The distinction matters because the two risks do not always move together.

Africa offers repeated examples of divergence. Some countries are politically noisy yet commercially legible—where contestation is channelled through courts, regulators, and markets. Others appear tranquil on the surface while quietly accumulating tail risk, as discretion replaces rules and exit optionality erodes.

Original article visual references: “Table 1: Noise is visible. Absorption drives returns” and “Table 2: Quiet isn’t safe. Institutions are.” Refer to the original Impala Market edition for these figures.

The distinction hinges on a single question: where does pressure go when it emerges?

From philosophy to measurement

To move beyond anecdote, Machiavelli’s observation is translated into a quantitative framework. The analysis maps African countries across two dimensions that determine whether stress becomes a source of renewal or a source of rupture for capital.

Agitation is defined as the intensity of political, social, and economic stress that tests a state’s institutional capacity—capturing the frequency and severity of shocks rather than their outcomes. We proxy this dimension using the Fragile States Index (FSI) total score, which reflects pressures across security, legitimacy, and social cohesion.

The FSI score is rescaled to a 0–100 Agitation Score (AGS), providing a consistent measure of the stress environment in which institutions must operate and capital must be protected.

Institutional absorption is defined as the capacity of a state to absorb political and economic stress through rules rather than discretion, thus preserving contract enforcement, policy continuity, and credible dispute resolution when pressure rises. We proxy this capacity using the World Bank’s Worldwide Governance Indicators (WGI), combining three dimensions most directly linked to commercial legibility—Rule of Law, Government Effectiveness, and Regulatory Quality.

These scores are averaged and rescaled to a 0–100 Institutional Absorption Score (IAS), providing a transparent measure of a country’s ability to protect capital under stress rather than merely in calm conditions.

Four African investment regimes

To operationalise the distinction between geopolitical noise and investment resilience, we map African countries on a two-dimensional matrix that combines agitation (measured by the Fragile States Index) with institutional absorption (measured by the Worldwide Governance Indicators). The chart plots each country against these two forces and draws quadrant lines at the median levels of stress and institutional capacity.

The result is not a league table of “safe” and “unsafe” markets, but a regime map revealing four distinct environments in which risk behaves differently and capital requires different instruments. These regimes define the strategic logic for equity, duration, and optionality across Africa.

Original visualisations: “Machiavellian Investment Matrix for Africa (Part 1)” and “Machiavellian Investment Matrix for Africa (Part 2).” The original article specifies median agitation 62.8 and median absorption 42.0. View the original Impala Market publication for the plots.

1) Productive turbulence

High agitation, high institutional absorption. These are Africa’s most misunderstood markets. Political contestation is visible and frequent, but it is channelled through courts, regulators, elections, and public debate.

Countries in this category, per 2023 data, include Kenya, Ivory Coast and Equatorial Guinea. For investors, volatility raises pricing error rather than confiscation risk. Capital markets function; exits exist. These environments support public equities, financial infrastructure, scalable platforms, and infrastructure with arbitration frameworks. Duration tolerance is highest here. Risk is not eliminated but it is compensated.

2) Quiet accumulation

Low agitation, high institutional absorption. This quadrant is defined by administrative competence and limited contestation. Decision-making is centralised; execution is efficient.

Countries in this category, per 2023 data, include Mauritius, Botswana and Ghana. These markets favour manufacturing, logistics, export platforms, and policy-aligned real assets. Medium-duration capital performs well. The principal risk is political transition: succession events can reprice assets abruptly precisely because volatility has been suppressed rather than expressed.

3) Stagnant stability

Low agitation, low institutional absorption. Here, apparent calm conceals weak adaptive capacity. Institutions are slow-moving; discretion substitutes for contestation.

Countries in this category, per 2023 data, include Gabon, Sierra Leone and Madagascar, reward caution. Regulatory drift and informal risk favour short-duration exposure. Private credit, trade finance, and yield-backed assets dominate. Long-duration equity quietly underperforms, not through crisis but through erosion.

4) Destructive turbulence

High agitation, low institutional absorption. This is where conflict overwhelms institutions. Rules are suspended rather than tested.

Countries in this category, per 2023 data, include Sudan, South Sudan and Somalia, and parts of the Sahel cluster here. Investment is possible only through risk transfer: sovereign guarantees, development-finance overlays, or option-like exposure. Balance-sheet capital is structurally misaligned.

Ranking Africa: investability, not optimism

Using the combined FSI–WGI framework, countries can be ranked by a simple but powerful investability score that captures not how often systems are stressed, but how well they absorb that stress when it arrives. The score integrates two forces that investors routinely conflate: agitation, measured by the Fragile States Index, and institutional absorption, measured by the Worldwide Governance Indicators.

In practical terms, this means countries with strong institutions retain high investability even in noisy environments, while those with weak institutions see investability collapse as agitation rises.

By penalising fragility while rewarding rule-based capacity, the resulting ranking distinguishes markets where volatility is merely noisy from those where it becomes destructive to capital. In effect, the investability score does not ask which countries are calmest; it asks which countries remain commercially legible under pressure—and therefore which can sustain equity exposure, duration risk, and long-term capital with confidence.

Investability Index = 100 × (IAS/100) × (1 − AGS)

High IAS lifts investability. High AGS reduces investability. Countries can remain investable even with agitation if absorption is high.

The Investability Index reveals a distribution across African markets in 2023. The median score of 15.59 forms a natural dividing line between countries where institutions still provide a baseline of capital protection and those where fragility overwhelms absorption capacity. Above the median sit markets where volatility is visible but rules continue to hold; below it lie systems where surface calm can conceal deep structural tail risk.

Crucially, the highest-ranked countries are not those with the least noise, but those whose institutions remain strongest relative to the stress they face. This pattern shows that Africa does not face a single “risk problem,” but a deep divide in investability, and it is this divide, not headlines, that should guide long-term capital allocation.

The Africa mispricing

Africa’s capital markets are not uniformly risky. They are unevenly understood.

Global investors too often mistake quiet for safety and noise for danger. Yet history shows the opposite is often true. Systems grow stronger not by suppressing conflict, but by absorbing it through institutions.

For investors, the lesson is direct. Returns accrue where rules hold under pressure: where markets can fail, adjust and recover without breaking.

Across Africa, the most investable markets are rarely the calmest. They are the ones where stress strengthens institutions instead of exposing their absence.

That is why, in Africa more than most places, risk, measured properly, is not a hazard. It is a privilege.

Sources

IMF (2024), Regional Economic Outlook: Sub-Saharan Africa; World Bank (2024), Africa’s Pulse; Fund for Peace (2023), Fragile States Index; World Bank (2023), Worldwide Governance Indicators; African Development Bank (2024), African Economic Outlook; Financial Times and Reuters coverage (2023–2024) on African elections, coups, FX adjustments, and sovereign debt restructurings; Acemoglu & Robinson (2012), Why Nations Fail; North, Wallis & Weingast (2009), Violence and Social Orders.

View the original article and visualisations on Impala Market.

Explore the Africa Investability Index research programme.

item.title: How I Turned Macro Outlooks into ETF Portfolios and How They Performed by Year-End 2025
item.description: Originally published on Substack.
item.content:encoded:
Home← All writingWorkRSS

WRITING / ARCHIVE

How I Turned Macro Outlooks into ETF Portfolios and How They Performed by Year-End 2025

Originally published on Substack: 2026-01-03 · Original publication ↗

TL;DR

At the start of 2025, I translated macro outlooks from Bloomberg, JP Morgan, HSBC, Trump Executive Orders and Guidance from the All-in Podcast (Besties) into real ETF portfolios using ChatGPT and tracked them through the year. By December 29, 2025, all portfolios delivered double-digit returns, with the most diversified strategies matching or slightly outperforming global benchmarks on a risk-adjusted basis. The key takeaway wasn’t superior prediction, but better portfolio structure: balanced, macro-aware portfolios produced smoother returns than thematic or speculative bets. For African investors in particular, the experiment reinforces a simple idea — thinking globally and diversifying across assets matters more than chasing headlines.

Background

At the start of 2025, I read the global macro and investment outlooks published by leading institutions such as Bloomberg, JP Morgan, and HSBC. These reports are widely read, frequently quoted, and often shape how institutional capital is positioned. But as an individual investor, especially one investing from Africa, I kept coming back to the same question: how do you actually implement these views in practice?

Rather than treat the outlooks as high-level commentary, I used ChatGPT to translate each institution’s macro narrative into a concrete, investable ETF portfolio. Each portfolio effectively became a custom index, reflecting how that institution expected the year to unfold. I then invested in those portfolios in January 2025 and tracked their performance through the year without changing allocations.

To see the exact portfolios, see in the article here.

What the Portfolios Were Trying to Do

Bloomberg’s outlook leaned toward balance. It expected slower but positive growth, resilience in US technology, continued infrastructure spending, and a role for bonds in cushioning volatility. The resulting portfolio blended equities, infrastructure, emerging markets, and credit.

JP Morgan’s outlook centred on a “soft landing” scenario. Growth was expected to slow without tipping into recession, inflation to cool gradually, and markets to reward quality assets. Its portfolio reflected this with diversified global equities, bonds, and real estate exposure.

HSBC took a more growth-oriented stance. It was more constructive on emerging markets, infrastructure, and innovation, accepting higher volatility in exchange for higher potential upside.

I also included a more speculative portfolio — the Trump Opportunities Fund — built around themes such as defence spending, energy security, and crypto-related exposure. This was deliberately more concentrated and risk-on.

Year-End Performance: The Numbers

By the end of December 2025, all portfolios finished the year in positive territory and delivered double-digit USD returns.

The Bloomberg 2025 portfolio led the group, finishing up about 18.9% for the year. JP Morgan 2025 followed at roughly 16.2%, while HSBC Growth 2025 delivered around 15.4%. The Trump Opportunities Fund ended the year up about 12.1%, recovering meaningfully from mid-year volatility but still lagging the more diversified strategies.

For context, the S&P 500 and FTSE All-Share also finished the year strongly, both in the high-teens.

At face value, this suggests that the macro-aligned portfolios broadly kept pace with global benchmarks. But the more important story sits beneath the headline returns.

Risk-Adjusted Performance: Why the Journey Matters

When viewed through the lens of Sharpe ratios, the differences between portfolios become clearer.

The Bloomberg portfolio recorded the strongest risk-adjusted performance, with a Sharpe ratio close to 0.9. This reflected not just high returns, but relatively smooth performance through the year. JP Morgan’s portfolio followed closely, with a Sharpe ratio in the 0.75–0.8 range, reinforcing its reputation as a steady, balanced strategy.

HSBC Growth finished with a lower Sharpe ratio, around 0.6, despite strong returns. This was expected. Emerging markets and innovation exposure introduced more volatility, and investors had to tolerate larger swings to earn those gains.

The Trump Opportunities Fund had the lowest Sharpe ratio of the group, around 0.4. Although it ended the year positive, it required significantly more risk to get there. This neatly illustrates why headline returns alone can be misleading.

Interestingly, both the S&P 500 and FTSE All-Share posted Sharpe ratios below the Bloomberg and JP Morgan portfolios. Broad markets performed well in 2025, but diversified macro-aware portfolios achieved similar outcomes with less volatility.

What 2025 Confirmed About Macro-Driven Investing

Looking back, none of the institutions predicted the year perfectly. Inflation moderated but didn’t disappear. Interest rates stayed restrictive longer than expected. Emerging markets contributed later than anticipated. Innovation worked, but selectively.

Yet the portfolios still worked because they were built for uncertainty, not precision. Diversification across assets, regions, and risk types mattered more than getting any single call exactly right.

This is also where ChatGPT proved useful. Not as a forecasting tool, but as a translator. It helped convert abstract macro language into investable structures. Human judgment still mattered, particularly around sizing risk and staying invested, but the distance between theory and execution was meaningfully shortened.

Is This Better Than Buying a Global Index?

Not necessarily, and that’s an important point.

For many investors, simply buying a global equity index and holding it remains a very strong strategy. It is low-cost, simple and historically difficult to beat over long horizons.

Where this approach adds value is in risk management and intentional tilting. Macro-aligned portfolios allow investors to adjust exposure consciously, manage volatility, and understand why portfolios behave the way they do. The most sensible conclusion is not replacement, but layering: a global index as the core, with macro or thematic allocations as overlays.

What This Means for African Investors

For investors in Uganda and across Africa, this experiment reinforces the case for thinking globally. Local markets are often concentrated illiquid, and exposed to currency risk. Global ETFs offer diversification that is difficult to achieve domestically.

Execution is no longer the barrier it once was. With USD funding channels, international brokerage access, and increasingly flexible financial infrastructure, global investing is becoming practical rather than aspirational.

Closing Reflection

The 2025 experiment wasn’t about beating the market. It was about testing whether macro views could be translated into real portfolios and held through a full cycle.

The answer clearly is yes, but only when structure and discipline come first.

For me, the most valuable outcome was not the return number, but the clarity it brought to process. In an uncertain world, portfolios don’t need perfect forecasts. They need to be built to survive being partly wrong.

Disclaimer: This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute investment advice. Please consult your financial advisor before making any investment decisions.

Professional overthinker. Occasional optimist. Building a platform for #InvestinAfrica - driving impact through capital, innovation, and technology.

item.title: The AI Bubble: Why Manias Never Really Die (Part 2)
item.description: How disciplined investors survive the world’s most expensive optimism.
item.content:encoded:
Home← All writingWorkRSS

WRITING / ARCHIVE

The AI Bubble: Why Manias Never Really Die (Part 2)

Originally published on Substack: 2025-12-30 · Original publication ↗

The Real Question Isn’t If It’s a Bubble. It’s How to Live Through One

Every generation finds its obsession, a narrative so potent that logic simply cannot compete with imagination.

For our parents, it was the fiber-optic cables and dot-coms of the 90s. For us, it is Artificial Intelligence.

The debate is no longer about whether AI will change the world; that consensus is already settled. The real challenge for the investor is surviving the “In-Between.” This is the feverish phase where capital outpaces proof, where supply cannot track demand and where the future is priced in decades before it arrives.

This is the final, data-backed revision of your target section. The figures have been updated to reflect the extraordinary scale of the late-2025 capital cycle, with specific footnotes for institutional-grade referencing.

The Eye of the Storm: A Capital Cycle Without Precedent

We are currently in the eye of the most powerful capital formation cycle since the birth of the internet. This isn’t just a software boom; it is a physical rebuilding of the global economy’s engine. The signals are no longer anecdotal—they are measurable in hundreds of billions of dollars.

  • Nvidia’s $500 Billion Bottleneck: The transition to the Blackwell Ultra (B300) architecture has created a “supply-constrained” environment that defies standard cyclicality. As of December 2025, Nvidia holds a staggering $500 billion backlog for the 2025–2026 period, with next-generation units effectively sold out through the next four quarters [1][2].

  • ASML and the Lithography Ceiling: The bottleneck of the entire revolution sits in Veldhoven. ASML’s order backlog remains near record highs at €36–38 billion [3]. With production of High-NA EUV machines limited to roughly 20 units annually, the queue for 2nm-ready hardware now extends into 2027 [4].

  • The $400 Billion Arms Race: The “Big Four”—Microsoft, Amazon, Google, and Meta—have unveiled 2025 capital budgets that eclipse the GDP of most nations. Combined annual Capex is projected to hit $405 billion this year, a 31% increase over already record-breaking 2024 levels [5][6].

  • The Physical Bedrock: The boom has moved from chips to “plumbing.” Data center capital expenditures surged 59% year-over-year in late 2025, driven by a massive pivot toward liquid cooling and grid-scale power distribution [7]. For every dollar spent on silicon, hyperscalers are now committing nearly 75 cents to the surrounding infrastructure of power and cooling [8].

The infrastructure build-out is real. The excitement is justified. But even revolutions have price tags, and right now, those tags are stretched to the edge of euphoria.

What the Data and History Tell Us

When you zoom out, manias follow a distinct, historical rhythm. They are not chaotic; they are mathematical.

The cycle always moves through four distinct acts: Discovery, where technology expands imagination; Acceleration, as capital floods the zone; Euphoria, when valuations decouple from earnings; and finally, the Reset, which wipes out the speculators to reward the patient.

AI today sits in the precarious gap between acceleration and euphoria.

The fundamentals are undeniably robust. Demand for compute power and model training has physically outpaced global electricity capacity. The supply chain—from high-end GPUs to industrial power transformers—is operating at maximum utilization. However, while the story remains perfect, the numbers are starting to blink red.

The Warning Lights in the Data:

  • Valuation Extremes: The top 10 AI stocks now trade at 50 times forward earnings, while the median software company trades at 22 times. This spread is now more than two standard deviations above the long-term average (10-year mean).

Key Insights

  1. The +2 sigma Breach: The historical average spread between large-cap tech and the median software company is approximately 12 points. At a 28-point spread in late 2025, the market is currently 2.3 standard deviations (>2 sigma) above the 10-year mean.

  2. The “Efficiency” Ceiling: While Top 10 AI stocks (Nvidia, Microsoft, Meta, etc.) are seeing valuations cool slightly from mid-2024 peaks (from 54 times to 50 times), the Median Software multiple is pinned at 22 times. This suggests that while “AI leaders” are being given the benefit of the doubt on growth, the rest of the SaaS world is being valued on current cash flow.

  3. Historical Context: At the peak of the dot-com bubble (March 2000), the top four tech names traded at nearly 70 times 2-year forward earnings. In comparison, today’s Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta) trade at a more “reasonable” 26 times expected two-year-ahead earnings, while the hardware-heavy “Top 10” stay closer to the 50 times mark due to cyclical chip demand.

  • Collapsing Breadth: Market participation has narrowed significantly. Fewer than half of the stocks in the Nasdaq are rising, even as the index hits nominal highs, a classic sign of internal exhaustion.

The Gravity of Yields: Real yields have risen 120 basis points from their 2023 lows. In financial physics, higher real yields act as gravity, eventually pulling down inflated valuation multiples.

This is how every mania matures: the fundamentals remain intact, but the prices simply outrun the profits. It is 1998, not 2000. The technology is real, but the market is assuming perfection in an execution-heavy world.

The “Prove It” Phase: The ROIC Gap

Unlike the 2000 bubble, the “Generals” of this era such as Microsoft, Meta, Alphabet are remarkably profitable. The risk today isn’t bankruptcy; it is the Return on Invested Capital (ROIC) Gap.

In 2025, the market’s curiosity has shifted. It is no longer asking, “How many GPUs did you buy?” but rather, “How much revenue did those GPUs generate?” When Capex grows at 30% while AI-attributed revenue grows at 10%, the valuation multiple must eventually contract to meet reality. We have officially entered the “Prove It” phase of the cycle.

How to Navigate the Mania Without Getting Burned

If the first rule of investing in a mania is don’t fight it, the second is don’t drown in it.

The goal isn’t to time the top—that is a fool’s errand—but to build a portfolio capable of surviving the drawdown when the tide inevitably recedes. To do that, we must move from emotional reaction to structural discipline.

1. Separate the “AI Core” from the “AI Hopes”

Every mania has truth at its center and storytelling at its edges. The art of survival is knowing which is which. In 2025, the market has begun to bifurcate, and your allocation must reflect that reality.

The AI Core: The “Railway Engineers”

The Core consists of entities that own the physical and functional necessity of the era. They sit on hard earnings, massive cash flows, and visible backlogs that stretch into 2027. They are the modern equivalents of the 19th-century steel makers—the ones who own the engine, the fuel, and the rails.

  • Key Players: Nvidia (NVDA) and TSMC (TSM) provide the architecture and the forge. Google (GOOGL) and Microsoft (MSFT) own the full vertical stack—from custom silicon and subsea fiber to the model interfaces. Eaton (ETN) and Vertiv (VRT) provide the power and cooling “plumbing” without which the digital brain cannot function.

  • Exposure: Large-cap equity or VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) / iShares AI Infrastructure ETF (EXI).

The AI Hopes: The “Speculative Frontier”

The Hopes consist of companies living on promise, narrative, and momentum. They represent the “optionality” in your portfolio—the high-beta satellites that may become the giants of 2030, but are currently navigating the perilous “Prove It” phase of 2026.

  • Key Players: Vertical SaaS leaders like Palantir (PLTR) and C3.ai (AI); robotics innovators such as Symbotic (SYM); and speculative hardware like IonQ (IONQ). These firms deserve a seat at the table for exposure, but never for dependence.

  • Exposure: High-growth satellite positions or Global X Robotics & AI ETF (BOTZ) / ARK Autonomous Tech & Robotics ETF (ARKQ).

The Golden Rule of Sizing: If AI is the revolution of our time, the aim isn’t to avoid it but rather to size it. If a 40% sector drawdown would blow up your long-term financial plan, your allocation is too big. A healthy portfolio finances its “hopes” from the realized profits of its “core,” not from new risk.

2. Replace Conviction with Process

P/E ratios are largely useless during revolutions; they measure historical performance in an environment defined by velocity. To survive 2025, you must replace “gut feelings” with emotional automation.

Instead of traditional multiples, use metrics that track how rapidly growth converts into actual liquidity:

  • $EV /Forward Gross Profit

  • $EV /Next-12-Month Free Cash Flow (FCF)

A disciplined process requires pre-set “Guardrails” to override your own greed and fear:

  1. The Exit Trigger: When a stock trades two standard deviations (+2 sigma) above its own 3-year valuation band, you must trim. Not because the company is bad, but because the price has outrun the math.

  2. The Entry Trigger: When a “Core” leader is down 25–30% from its peak, but earnings revisions remain positive, you add.

Structure turns volatility into strategy. By capping “Hopes” at 15%, you maintain upside without risking insolvency.

Discipline beats bravado. You don’t need to know when the music stops; you just need a rule for what to do when it skips a beat.

3. Watch the Five Early Warning Lights.

Manias rarely crash without warning. They start whispering first.
The trick is to listen, not to the headlines, but to the quiet, structural tells in the data.

Across every speculative cycle — from the South Sea Bubble to dot-coms — the market has announced its turning points in roughly the same five ways.
We’re seeing all of them now, to varying degrees.

a) Breadth Narrows (The “Concentration” Trap)

This is the oldest warning sign in the book: when the index rises, but fewer stocks participate in the rally. As of late 2025, the top 10 stocks account for over 40% of the S&P 500’s total market cap—an all-time high. It’s classic late-cycle behavior: the leadership has become dangerously thin.

b) Issuance Spikes (The “Supply” Shock)

Late in every mania, sellers come out to feed the demand. Companies rush to IPO, and retail traders pile into short-dated call options. With single-stock call volumes reaching historic highs of 40 million contracts per day, the market is effectively “selling” its future volatility for present-day hype.

c) Real Yields Rise (The “Oxygen” Drain)

Rising real yields—the inflation-adjusted cost of money—are the oxygen drain that ends speculative surges. At 1.8%, the “cost of capital” has effectively doubled from its lows. For long-duration growth stocks like AI, this is a silent killer of valuation multiples.

d) Earnings Revisions Flatten (The “Expectation” Wall)

A mania is sustainable as long as earnings outpace expectations. But according to the latest data, S&P 500 earnings estimates have essentially stalled. When analysts stop raising forecasts but prices keep soaring, the marginal dollar is being driven by sentiment, not substance.

e) Volatility Vanishes (The “Complacency” Signal)

When the VIX—Wall Street’s “fear gauge”—sits in the low teens, it means investors have stopped pricing in risk. Every major market correction of the last decade began from a similar level of false calm.

The Survival Directive: When three or more of these lights flash Red, history says it’s time to shift from offense to defense. This doesn’t mean you run for the exits; it means you trim your winners, build your T-bill ladder, and stop assuming the next quarter’s return will look like the last.

Manias always sound rational at their peak. But the data never lies—you just have to listen.

4. Energy: The New Silicon

In 2023, the bottleneck was H100 chips. In 2025, the bottleneck is Grid Capacity.

You cannot disrupt physics with code. While software scales at zero marginal cost, the electrical grid requires copper, transformers, and years of permitting. The most resilient “shovels” in this mania are no longer just the chip designers—they are the companies solving the physical constraints of intelligence.

  • The Grid: Vertiv, Eaton, and Schneider Electric. These are the “plumbing” providers of the data center, turning raw high-voltage power into the stabilized current a GPU requires.

  • The Cooling: As power density increases, air cooling is failing. Liquid cooling providers are now the gatekeepers of next-gen server clusters.

  • The Landlords: Data Center REITs (like Equinix or Digital Realty) own the “digital dirt.” In a world of infinite software, specialized physical space is the ultimate scarcity.

The Insight: As margins eventually compress for chipmakers due to competition, profits migrate down the chain to the infrastructure that cannot be easily replicated.

5. Size for Survival

Conviction is a virtue, but concentration is a risk. Here is the uncomfortable math of 2025: If your AI exposure dropped 50%, and your total portfolio fell by more than 10–12%, you are not “invested”—you are overexposed.

A sustainable allocation framework for the “In-Between” phase looks like this:

This mix ensures you stay invested in the future while remaining liquid enough to buy the assets of those forced to sell when the cycle turns.

6. Hedging as Insurance, Not Speculation

Sophisticated investors do not hedge because they are “bears”; they hedge so they can afford to remain “bulls.” Think of a hedge as a seatbelt: you don’t wear it because you plan to crash; you wear it so you can drive fast with confidence.

  • The 2% Rule: Allocate 1–2% of your portfolio’s annual value to “portfolio insurance”—typically 3–6 month index or sector puts. This is a sunk cost, like a premium, that protects against a “black swan” event.

  • The “Trim & Tuck” Strategy: When a core holding hits a “Euphoria” level (trading at +2 sigma above its 3-year mean valuation), trim 10% of the position. “Tuck” that capital into a 5% yielding T-bill ladder.

This process provides the liquidity needed to buy the dip when the speculative “Hopes” sector inevitably corrects. You aren’t betting against AI; you are betting on your own ability to stay in the game.

7. Benchmark Your Progress

You cannot manage what you do not measure. In the AI era, comparing your performance solely to the S&P 500 is misleading because the index itself is now an AI-heavy proxy.

A sensible benchmark for a modern AI-tilted allocation blends three elements:

  1. Nasdaq-100 (QQQ): For software and large-cap tech.

  2. Semiconductor Index (SOX): For the hardware cycle.

  3. MSCI ACWI: For global equity context.

If your portfolio beats this mix with smaller drawdowns, you are practicing disciplined investing. If you are only winning because you are taking more risk, you haven’t found a strategy—you’ve just found a temporary tailwind.

AI in the Total Portfolio

Avoid the “Concentration Trap” by treating AI as a high-performance engine, not the entire vessel. Use a Core-Satellite Framework to maintain equilibrium:

  • The Global Core (60–70%): Broad, low-cost index exposure (MSCI ACWI / S&P 500). This captures the Productivity Dividend—adoption by non-tech firms—without the “Hype Premium.”

  • The AI Tactical Sleeve (15–20%): Your alpha engine of “Shovels” and profitable “Generals.” This is the only sleeve subject to the +2 sigma Trim Rule.

  • Liquid Ballast (15–20%): Cash, T-bills, and Gold. With real yields at 1.8%, this is Optionality—the dry powder needed to buy the reset when the “music skips.”

In a market “reset,” AI stocks, Bitcoin, and the Nasdaq-100 move in lockstep. Owning five different chipmakers isn’t diversification; it’s concentration in different wrappers. True balance requires assets that “hate” what AI “loves.” If AI thrives on high liquidity, your ballast must thrive on volatility.

When a parabolic run pushes your AI sleeve from 15% to 25%, harvest. Rebalance those gains into your Core or Ballast. This isn’t a lack of conviction—it is the mechanical conversion of speculative momentum into permanent structural wealth.

The Long Game: Surviving the Engine of Progress

We often treat market manias as collective delusions—moments where humanity loses its grip on math. But history suggests a different perspective: Manias are not mistakes; they are the high-octane fuel of progress.

They are the mechanism by which society “over-invests” in the future, funding the infrastructure of a new world at a speed that rational capital would never allow.

  • The Railway Mania of the 1840s left thousands of investors penniless, but it gifted Britain the physical backbone of an industrial empire.

  • The Dot-com Crash of 2000 wiped out trillions in “paper wealth,” but it laid the fiber-optic cables that made the modern, hyper-connected economy possible.

  • The AI Mania is currently doing the same. It is funding a planetary-scale build-out of compute, energy, and connectivity that will serve as the foundation for the next century of intelligence.

The Darwinism of the Drawdown

The technology will survive. The infrastructure will remain. But not every investor will make it to the other side.

The difference between a “speculator” and a “survivor” isn’t their ability to predict the future—it’s their ability to endure it. The market eventually punishes those who confuse a great story with a great price, but it rewards those who use discipline as their anchor.

We are living through one of the most significant capital formation events in human history. To be here is a privilege; to stay here requires a process.

“The future doesn’t belong to the loudest voice in the room or the boldest bet on the board. It belongs to the investor who builds, hedges, and rebalances—the one who understands that in a revolution, staying solvent is the ultimate act of defiance.”

Manias don’t die. They simply mature, quietly compounding in the portfolios of those who were prepared for the music to skip a beat.

Sources & References

[^1]: Evercore ISI / Bloomberg (Dec 2025): Nvidia’s $500B Multi-Year Backlog: Analyzing the Blackwell-Rubin Transition.

[^2]: Nvidia Q3 Fiscal 2026 Earnings Report (Nov 19, 2025): Data Center Revenue Reaches $51.2B; Blackwell Units Sold Out Through Mid-2026.

[^3]: ASML Holding N.V. Q3 2025 Financial Results: Backlog Analysis and EUV Shipment Forecasts.

[^4]: Zacks Investment Research (Aug 2025): ASML Sees 30% EUV Growth: The High-NA Production Bottleneck.

[^5]: Statista / Houlihan Lokey Report (Dec 2025): Tech’s AI-Fueled Spending Surge: Combined Capex of Meta, Alphabet, Amazon, and Microsoft.

[^6]: IG Market Wrap-Up (Dec 19, 2025): 2025 Year in Review: Big Tech’s $405 Billion AI Infrastructure Bet.

[^7]: Dell’Oro Group (Dec 18, 2025): Data Center Capex Quarterly Report: AI Investment Cycle Broadens Beyond Early Training.

[^8]: CreditSights / FinancialContent (Dec 2025): Infrastructure Economics: Why 75% of Hyperscaler Spend is Now AI-Specific.

item.title: When every man builds his own ark, civilization drowns
item.description: The Tragedy of the Commons
item.content:encoded:
Home← All writingWorkRSS

WRITING / ARCHIVE

When every man builds his own ark, civilization drowns

Originally published on Substack: 2025-11-03 · Original publication ↗

Disclaimer: This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute investment advice. Please consult your financial advisor before making any investment decisions.

Last week, a post by Ian Gumisiriza, better known as @T_E_F_L_O_N, stirred heated debate on X (formerly Twitter).
He wrote:

“VERY UNPOPULAR OPINION: Kampala was flooding long before Ham started any works on Nakivubo Channel.”

The post did what storms of rain often do to Kampala: it exposed what lay beneath the surface.

Replies poured in.
Some blamed the construction works for blocking drainage and worsening the floods.
Others argued the floods had been inevitable - that the real culprits were decades of poor planning, encroached wetlands and absent accountability.
But hidden beneath the noise was a deeper truth: Kampala was not flooded by rain alone. It was flooded by rational decisions made in a broken system.

The city didn’t flood because of Ham. It flooded because the system that enabled him behaves exactly as designed.

This article explores the idea, The tragedy of the commons, seen through the lens of a city drowning in its own logic. Every trader, builder and official acts rationally. Yet together, their actions create the perfect storm.

What Are We Really Seeing?

Before we go further, it helps to remember where the idea of the “Tragedy of the Commons” came from.

The term was coined by the ecologist Garrett Hardin in a 1968 essay in Science.
He imagined a shared pasture, a commons, where each herder acts rationally by adding more cattle, because the private benefit goes entirely to them while the cost of overgrazing is shared by everyone. Over time, the pasture collapses under the weight of self-interest. The insight was not new. In 1833, economist William Forster Lloyd had described the same logic in his lectures on overgrazing in England’s communal lands. But Hardin’s version gave the metaphor its modern life.

When resources are shared but responsibility is not, rational behavior becomes destructive.

Today the commons are no longer fields; they are wetlands, drainage channels, city budgets, and public trust.

Kampala’s floods are simply a modern version of the same story, flooding is the surface symptom of something deeper, a social equilibrium where every participant acts rationally within a broken system.

The trader rents a cheaper stall in the valley because that’s what they can afford.

The developer builds there because land at higher ground costs more.

The official approves it because fees and favors are quicker than enforcement.

And the taxpayer buys a piece of land on higher ground wherever they can, fences off their house, buys a generator and hires private security because “that’s how the country works.”

Each decision makes sense in isolation. Together, they create the tragedy of the commons: individually rational behavior producing collective ruin.

The commons are a fragile network of trust. When that trust is monetized, privatized, or abandoned, the network collapses. What we call a “natural disaster” is often just the bill for years of deferred responsibility.

Where did the System break?

Our problem is not ignorance. It is misaligned incentives. The people in charge know the blueprints, the cost estimates, the hydrological data, the case studies and benchmarks - I too explored these themes in my post on X.

What the people in charge lack is the motivation to act when accountability carries no personal price.

Citizens, meanwhile, have stopped believing. They pay taxes but expect nothing back. Corruption, like erosion, starts small and becomes a landscape. Soon, distrust becomes policy: everyone protects themselves first, because nobody expects protection from the system.

“Corruption” here means a system that has worn down - where honesty, accountability and public duty fade away, until people are forced to look out for themselves instead of the community - see more under Notes and References at the end of this article.

Consequently, risk ends up sorting people by what they can afford.

Those with resources relocate uphill, insure their assets, or leave the country altogether. Those without resources rebuild in the same place, hoping next time the water will be kinder. The same flood, two realities.

In Kampala, this stratification is visible from the air: wealth on the ridges, vulnerability in the valleys. When resilience becomes a private luxury, the commons dies quietly.

How do we escaping this Collective Trap?

The temptation is to demand better government. But governance is only as strong as the culture that sustains it. No policy can substitute for a people who have abdicated their shared responsibility. To rebuild the commons, we must invert the model: from dependence to participation, from hierarchy to agency.

1. Radical Transparency as Default

Corruption survives in shadows. Transparency is not a website or a dashboard; it’s a social norm. Citizens must expect to see what is collected, what is spent, and what was promised. When people can trace cause to effect - tax to drain, levy to culvert - the invisible hand of accountability reappears.

2. Local Stewardship Over Distant Authority

Centralized control breeds distance and apathy. But when management shifts to the smallest effective unit for example the neighborhood, the parish, the street committee - people act because they see the consequences.

Collective maintenance, not municipal miracles, keeps drains clear and waste out. Responsibility must be as local as the water itself.

3. Shared Data, Shared Decisions

The next civic revolution is informational. When rainfall, blockage, and flood alerts are open to all, citizens coordinate faster than bureaucracy. Knowledge, once distributed, becomes self-correcting. If everyone sees the same truth, manipulation loses its edge.

4. Adaptive Insurance - Not Financial, but Social

Insurance is the pooling of risk among people who trust each other. It need not be sold by companies; it can be built through community savings groups, rotating funds, and local pacts. The principle is simple, those who stand together absorb shocks better than those who stand alone. When disaster hits, recovery should feel like reciprocity, not charity.

5. Skin in the Game at Every Level

The surest way to fix a system is to make the decision-makers live inside its consequences. Let the regulators who approve drainage projects commute through the same channels. Let the officials who sign off wetland developments reside where they license construction. Exposure breeds diligence; immunity breeds decay.

Without personal stakes, governance turns into performance art.

As Charlie Munger liked to remind us, “Show me the incentive and I’ll show you the outcome.” When leaders bear no cost for failure, the system quietly optimizes for appearances instead of results. Meetings multiply, reports thicken, and nothing real changes.

From Dependency to Decentralization

The flood is not merely water; it is information. It tells us where we have outsourced too much, trusted too little and acted too late.

A healthy society decentralizes by instinct, not by technology. It doesn’t wait for permission to cooperate. It builds redundant systems of care and accountability so that failure in one node doesn’t collapse the whole network - when the official drain fails, the community trench still works, when the contractor absconds, the neighborhood fixes what it can - such distributed responsibility is messy but antifragile. It learns faster than it breaks.

Dependence on central authority breeds fragility; distributed stewardship breeds resilience. Freedom, at its core, is the ability to correct mistakes locally before they become disasters nationally.

The Hill and the Valley

Every flood redraws the map of responsibility. It tells us who can escape and who must endure. Yet, even those on the hills are not safe; they merely postpone the reckoning. A city divided by altitude cannot survive indefinitely.

The water is impartial. It flows toward the path of least resistance, and right now, that path is moral, not physical. Until citizens rediscover the commons as an extension of themselves, the rain will keep teaching the same lesson.

In the end, resilience is not an engineering project. It is a collective decision to care, before the water arrives.

Professional overthinker. Occasional optimist. Building a platform for #InvestinAfrica - driving impact through capital, innovation, and technology.

Appendix: Notes & References

  1. Garrett Hardin, “The Tragedy of the Commons,” Science, Vol. 162, No. 3859 (Dec. 13, 1968), pp. 1243–1248.

  2. Office of the Auditor General (Uganda), Annual Reports 2018–2023: Recurrent findings on procurement irregularities, cost overruns, and weak supervision in Kampala Capital City Authority (KCCA) drainage and infrastructure projects. Example: “Rehabilitation of Nakivubo Channel experienced unaccounted advances and delayed completion.”

  3. Inspectorate of Government (IGG), Annual Integrity Surveys (2019–2023) — Cites corruption risks in land administration and urban planning, including issuance of wetland titles and informal payments for development permits.

  4. World Bank (2020) Resilient Urban Infrastructure for Inclusive Cities: Uganda Country Report - Identifies “institutional fragmentation, procurement inefficiency, and corruption risks” as barriers to effective drainage and waste-management systems.

  5. UN-Habitat & Makerere University (2019–2022): Studies on Urban Governance and Wetland Protection - Document elite capture and political interference as leading causes of wetland loss and non-enforcement of zoning regulations in Kampala.

  6. Ministry of Water & Environment, Wetlands Department (2022) - Reports approximately 70 % loss of Kampala’s wetlands since the 1990s, much of it involving officially sanctioned developments or titled land, indicating regulatory failure.

  7. Kampala Capital City Authority (KCCA) Budget Framework Papers 2015–2023: Drainage expenditure more than doubled over the period, while channel coverage and maintenance expansion lagged significantly, suggesting inefficiency and governance gaps.

item.title: The AI Bubble: Why Manias Never Really Die (Part 1)
item.description: From the railway boom to the AI revolution; how markets finance progress, lose their minds and find their footing again.
item.content:encoded:
Home← All writingWorkRSS

WRITING / ARCHIVE

The AI Bubble: Why Manias Never Really Die (Part 1)

Originally published on Substack: 2025-10-12 · Original publication ↗

Disclaimer: This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute investment advice. Please consult your financial advisor before making any investment decisions.

The Spark Before the Storm

I am currently reading The Nature of Technology: What It Is and How It Evolves by W. Brian Arthur, it is a slow but enjoyable read. I agree that it is one of the most insightful books ever written on how technologies emerge, combine, and transform economies and how those domains in turn reshape the economy.

One section that particularly caught my attention is the interplay between technology and finance: how every technological breakthrough needs its financial counterpart to scale, how capital markets act as midwives of innovation, and how enthusiasm can spill into speculation. This concept is expounded on further by Carlota Perez as described in her 2003 book, Technological Revolutions and Financial Capital: The Dynamics of Bubbles and Golden Ages.

That reflection naturally led me to AI, the technology du jour shaping both our imagination and our investments. It made me wonder: if every past technological leap, from railways to the internet, has sparked both transformation and mania, can those lessons guide us through the present moment?

This week’s markets offered a hint. The Nasdaq slipped roughly 2%, AI leaders swung 10% intraday, and yet conversations still orbit one word, AI. In the markets, the excitement is palpable; so is the unease. Everyone wants exposure, but no one wants risk.

It’s been that way for the past few years. Since late 2022, when the first generation of large language models captured public attention, AI-linked equities have dominated returns. The semiconductor index has more than tripled, the major AI platform stocks have risen five- to ten-fold, and a handful of names now account for over 30% of the S&P 500’s total market value1. Yet beneath those headlines lies sharp volatility: 10% daily swings, 30–40% corrections in single names, and repeated rotations as investors question whether earnings can keep pace with expectations.

See from The Kobeitsi Letter2 commentary on the performance of the Semiconductors Index, relative to the S&P 500 equal-weighted index which reached 0.86, the highest since the 2000 Dot-Com Bubble.

Even outside the technology sector, markets have been pulled into AI’s gravitational field: utilities rallying on data-centre power demand, industrials on cooling and grid equipment, and real estate on hyperscale land. Every portfolio seems to carry a trace of the theme.

“Every generation thinks it has invented a new way to make money fast. It hasn’t.”
Niall Ferguson, The Ascent of Money

History tells us that moments like these, when optimism meets over-extension, often feel euphoric right before they turn instructive. The challenge for investors isn’t spotting the excitement; it’s distinguishing durable transformation from temporary mania.

How do we tell when genuine innovation crosses into mania and what does a wise investor do about it?

The Anatomy of a Mania

1. The Pattern That Never Changes

History doesn’t repeat, but it often rhymes, especially where money meets invention.
Every great wave of technology has begun with a spark of discovery, grown into a blaze of optimism, and ended in the ashes of overreach. Yet each left behind a stronger, more connected, more capable world.

The Railway Mania (1840s)

The first great industrial mania began with steam. Britain’s railway revolution promised to collapse distances and fuel commerce. Between 1843 and 1847, the number of miles of track approved by Parliament tripled. Investors rushed in — shopkeepers, farmers, aristocrats — everyone owned “railway scrip.”

Railway scrip was a tradable promise of participation in the railway revolution—an early, paper-based version of speculative tech equity. It fueled the dreams (and disasters) of the 1840s boom, much like startup shares and AI tokens do in our own age.

When profits failed to match expectations, credit tightened, and the bubble burst. Shares fell as much as 85%, fortunes vanished, and projects were abandoned mid-construction. Yet, within a decade, the same tracks underpinned Victorian industrial dominance. The frenzy, though ruinous to many investors, had financed the very arteries of modern trade.

The Roaring Twenties (1920s)

The 1920s combined electricity, cars, and mass production: the technological trinity that defined modern life. The U.S. economy surged, and the Dow Jones rose sixfold in less than a decade. Ordinary citizens bought stocks on margin, convinced that a “new era” of permanent prosperity had begun.

But behind the exuberance lay fragile foundations: slowing productivity, speculative credit, and a market decoupled from earnings. The 1929 crash erased nearly 90% of the Dow’s value and ushered in the Great Depression. Yet the electrification and manufacturing capacity built in that decade became the backbone of mid-century prosperity.

The Internet Boom (1990s)

The dot-com era was the next great act of optimism. Between 1995 and 2000, the Nasdaq soared eightfold as investors imagined a limitless digital economy. Companies with no profits, sometimes no products, achieved billion-dollar valuations on the promise of “eyeballs” and “clicks.”
When reality intruded, the market collapsed by 78%. But the infrastructure survived: the fiber-optic cables, servers, and networking protocols financed during the boom made cloud computing, e-commerce, and digital payments possible. The wreckage of the mania became the foundation of the modern internet economy.

Crypto and Electric Vehicles (2017–2021)

The cycle repeated with digital assets and clean energy. Bitcoin rose twentyfold in a single year; new tokens appeared daily; valuations detached from utility. Electric-vehicle makers enjoyed trillion-dollar market caps before achieving consistent profits.
When rates rose and liquidity drained, speculative tokens vanished and EV shares fell 60–80%. Yet blockchain technology continues to evolve quietly in payments and supply chains, while electric mobility is reshaping transport and energy. The crash again purified excess and redirected capital toward real progress.

The other manias are included in the table below, including the run-up in prices, table created with Chamuka Drawit.

Economic historian Carlota Perez argues that every major technological revolution follows a recognizable four-part rhythm. From the Industrial Revolution to the Internet Age, the same sequence repeats — only the names and tools change.

Stage 1: Irruption - The Breakthrough (2017 - 2020)

Every revolution starts quietly, with a technical leap that seems academic at first.

For AI, this began with the Transformer architecture introduced by Google in 2017, the foundation for models like GPT, Claude, Gemini and others. Suddenly, machines could handle not just data but language, reasoning and creativity.

These breakthroughs built on decades of progress in neural networks, cheap cloud computing and open-source collaboration. In Perez’s terms, this was the irruption phase - the spark that revealed a new technological frontier.

At this stage, adoption was limited to research labs and specialized developers. Yet the groundwork was being laid: cloud infrastructure from Amazon, Microsoft and Google; GPUs from Nvidia; and vast datasets that would fuel machine intelligence.

Stage 2: Frenzy - The Capital Rush (2023 - 2025)

The frenzy phase is when finance meets imagination. Speculative capital floods in, convinced it has found the future, and for once, it’s not entirely wrong.

We entered this phase in 2023. ChatGPT’s viral adoption triggered a gold rush. Nvidia became a trillion-dollar company; OpenAI secured a record-breaking $40 billion funding round3, Anthropic is aiming for up to $10 billion in new capital4 and corporate AI investment globally has already exceeded $250 billion annually5.

This year, data center construction has exploded. Microsoft, Amazon and Google each announced $80–100 billion capex plans, while countries from Japan to the UAE declared national AI missions. Venture funding in AI startups is at record highs, and even non-tech firms now label themselves “AI-powered” to capture investor attention.

But as with every frenzy before such as railways, radio and internet, valuations have detached from fundamentals. GPU shortages, model training costs and power constraints are surfacing as the limits of optimism6.

This is where manias begin to rhyme. Perez calls this “the turning of the tide,” when excess money builds the roads for future prosperity, even as it sets up the eventual correction.

Stage 3: Turning Point - The Correction (2026 - 2027?)

In every cycle, the frenzy outruns reality. Markets reach a point where the marginal dollar of investment produces less excitement and more scrutiny789, for example:

  • According to Bloomberg Intelligence AI Infrastructure Report 2025, hyperscaler capex has grown ~50% YoY, yet projected AI revenue contribution for 2025–26 has risen by less than 20% - this implies a declining marginal return per invested dollar.

  • Per Goldman Sachs Research – AI Economics Deep Dive 2025, Analysts estimate the AI infrastructure payback horizon has extended to 5–7 years, up from 3–4 years expected in 2023

For AI, this inflection may arrive when infrastructure growth outpaces near-term monetization, when data centers are built faster than they can be filled with profitable workloads. Costs will collide with competition, open-source models will undercut proprietary ones, margins will compress and investors will suddenly rediscover valuation discipline.

The turning point isn’t necessarily catastrophic; it is the system’s reset. Many early players will fail or consolidate, while survivors with genuine advantages in areas such as chips, cloud scale, power access, and proprietary data will emerge stronger.

If Perez’s framework holds, 2026 to 2027 could resemble the 2001 to 2003 period that followed the dot-com boom, a painful but ultimately productive reset. Then, as now, the world had overbuilt infrastructure ahead of demand: too many websites, too much fiber-optic capacity, and too little profit to justify valuations. The crash cleared the field for durable businesses like Amazon and Google to emerge and for broadband and cloud computing to take hold.

In the same way, a future AI correction may feel severe in the moment with funding drying up, valuations compressing and speculative projects fading. Yet, it would also set the stage for a decade of genuine deployment and productivity gains as AI becomes embedded across industries.

Stage 4: Synergy - The Integration (Late 2020s and Beyond)

After the storm comes the synthesis. AI will stop being a separate story and become part of everything: industry, finance, healthcare, logistics, education.

This is when productivity gains materialize. Think of AI copilots built into office software, autonomous manufacturing systems, or energy grids optimized by predictive models. AI won’t feel like “AI” anymore; it will simply be how things work.

This synergy phase is quieter but far more valuable. The internet had its own version after 2003: e-commerce, cloud computing and digital payments flourished long after the dot-com crash.

The Deeper Truth

Manias, Perez reminds us, aren’t random explosions of greed. They are the financing mechanism of progress — the messy but necessary overreaction that builds the infrastructure the world later depends on.

The 1840s railway mania financed the tracks that powered 19th-century trade. The 1920s electrification bubble wired the modern home. The 1990s dot-com boom paid for the fiber-optic cables that made cloud computing possible.

Today’s AI boom is doing the same — building the data centers, chips, and energy systems that will form the nervous system of the next economy.

Investors may pay the price upfront, but society reaps the benefit over decades.

Speculative excess is not an accident but the mechanism through which technological revolutions finance the infrastructure of the future. Each cycle ends with over-investment, but that over-investment lays the tracks — literal or digital — for the next age.

2. Historical Echoes

We now stand amid another frenzy. The rise of generative AI through large language models, image synthesis and machine reasoning has triggered a global race to compute, connect and capitalize.
AI’s rally began with the release of transformer-based models in 2017, but true ignition came in late 2022 when chatbots and copilots entered the mainstream. Since then, the semiconductor index has more than tripled; the largest AI platform stocks have multiplied five- to tenfold; and a handful of companies now represent more than a quarter of major indices.

The scale of investment is staggering. Big Tech’s combined AI capital expenditure exceeds $350 billion a year10.

  • Microsoft plans to spend roughly $80 billion on AI data centers.

  • Amazon and Google are in the $100 billion range.

  • Meta is targeting $66–72 billion, with similar spending projected for 2026.

  • TSMC, the world’s largest chip foundry, expects $38–42 billion in annual capex.

  • Equinix and Digital Realty, the “landlords of the internet,” each invest over $3 billion a year to expand data-center capacity.

  • Even governments, from Japan to the UAE, are launching sovereign AI infrastructure funds.

This isn’t vaporware. It’s real money building a new physical internet: high-voltage substations, cooling towers, silicon fabs, and server farms. But markets being markets, optimism has already raced ahead of earnings. AI start-ups command multi-billion valuations on speculative revenue and secondary markets trade equity in companies that have yet to turn a profit.

Just as in previous cycles, the best technologies may still host the worst investments when price outruns profit. The market may be financing the future, but it’s doing so with borrowed time and leveraged expectations.

3. The Mania Mindset

At the heart of every boom is a recurring pattern of psychology that technology merely amplifies.

  • Overconfidence Bias: “This time it’s different.” Investors believe they are smarter, data is richer, and the market has evolved beyond the old rules.

  • FOMO: “I can’t afford to miss it.” Social proof becomes a trading signal and every headline confirms the narrative.

  • Narrative Fallacy: “If it’s a great story, it must be a great investment.” Investors conflate technological possibility with financial inevitability.

  • Liquidity and Leverage: Easy money acts as fuel. Inexpensive credit and abundant venture funding magnify every impulse.

Today’s AI boom is showing the same warning signs that have marked the final stages of every major market frenzy. Venture investors are pouring record sums into a few headline AI startups, driving valuations far beyond what these companies currently earn. In early 2025 alone, AI firms raised more than $70 billion, nearly 60% of all global venture funding11. At the same time, many tech companies are rebranding their products as “AI-powered” to attract attention and fresh capital12. Meanwhile, just a handful of giants; Microsoft, Apple, Amazon, Google, Nvidia, Meta, and Tesla now make up about 30% of the S&P 500’s total value, meaning most of the market’s gains come from a very small group of stocks.

In short, money, hype, and excitement are all crowding into the same few names, a familiar pattern seen before in every great boom from railways to dot-coms.

At a fundamental level, we are witnessing a capital-intensive transformation — data centers, chips, and power infrastructure are the railroads of our age. Each generation of investors finances the next generation of progress, whether it’s steel and steam or silicon and syntax.

But history offers a warning: when enthusiasm becomes uniform and expectations become exponential, even transformative technologies can experience brutal corrections.

Where might we be in the cycle?

Looking across the data, market behavior and capital flows, the evidence suggests that AI has moved firmly into the late-frenzy phase of Carlota Perez’s technological cycle: the period when excitement and capital peak, reality begins to intrude and the seeds of the next reset are sown.

  1. The Build-Out is Real, and Extraordinary

The numbers speak for themselves. Global AI infrastructure spending has entered an unprecedented phase of acceleration:

  • Microsoft is guiding roughly $80 billion in AI and data-center investment this fiscal year.

  • Amazon and Google are each expected to spend around $100 billion in 2025, while Meta plans $66–72 billion.

  • TSMC’s foundry capex remains near record highs at $38–42 billion, and data-center landlords such as Equinix and Digital Realty are each investing more than $3 billion annually.

  • Global electricity demand is rising faster than forecast as AI data centers compete with households and industry for power.

This is the installation stage in full force, capital spending that lays the physical groundwork for a future economy of intelligent machines. It is real, tangible and transformative. Yet, as in every previous technological boom, the market has begun discounting years of future cash flows today.

  1. Market Behaviour Shows Late-Cycle Traits

Valuations have expanded faster than earnings. The semiconductor index has tripled since 2022 and a small cluster of mega-cap AI leaders now contributes over 30 percent of total S&P 500 market capitalization. Equal-weighted stock indexes are falling behind the main market averages, which means that only a few big companies are driving most of the gains. This kind of narrow leadership is a classic sign that the market is in the late, overheated stage of a boom.

Daily volatility in AI names exceeds 8–10 percent, even as the overall volatility index (VIX) drifts in the mid-teens — a sign of complacency at the index level despite turbulence underneath. Investors are still confident, but positioning is crowded, and expectations are stretched.

  1. Strains are Emerging beneath the Surface

Every mania runs into its own limits. The cracks beneath the AI boom are becoming visible in four key areas — supply, power, talent, and investor sentiment.

  • Supply bottlenecks: Nvidia’s H100 and H200 chips remain on allocation with 6–9 month wait times, and high-bandwidth memory suppliers like SK Hynix and Samsung are sold out through 2025, despite ramping output 60 %. Even ASML, the Dutch company that makes the world’s most advanced chipmaking machines, has a record order backlog of more than €39 billion. These EUV (extreme ultraviolet) systems are essential for producing the high-performance chips that power AI, and demand for them far exceeds supply. In short, the world can’t build new compute capacity fast enough to keep up with the pace of AI expansion.

  • Power constraints: Global data-center electricity use is projected to double from 460 TWh in 2022 to more than 1,000 TWh by 2026. In Virginia’s “Data-Center Alley,” grid-connection requests have surged 250 % since 2022, with five- to seven-year wait times. Ireland and Singapore have paused new permits to protect strained grids.

  • Human capital: Demand for AI talent grew 40 % YoY in 2024 while supply rose only 14 %. U.S. senior ML engineers now command $450 k+ total pay, up 30–40 % since 2022, as firms like OpenAI and Meta bid millions to retain scarce expertise.

  • Investor fatigue: The semiconductor index has tripled since 2022, while sector earnings are up only 60 %. The “Magnificent 7” make up about 30 % of S&P 500 value, yet equal-weighted returns are flat. Even Nvidia’s 20 % earnings beat in August 2025 saw its stock fall 7 %.

Together, these numbers tell the story of an industry running hot, real progress colliding with physical, human and financial limits. These are not fatal flaws. They are the natural growing pains that mark the transition from pure optimism to practical execution.

  1. Why “Late-Frenzy”?

The metrics suggest that the market that has overshot fundamentals but not yet broken down, the precise inflection where enthusiasm meets friction.

  1. Interpreting the Moment

If Perez’s framework holds, 2026–2027 could mirror the 2001–2003 post–dot-com adjustment, a painful but necessary reset. Then, as now, over-investment built the digital plumbing such as fiber-optic cables and server farms that enabled a decade of real productivity growth.

A similar process is unfolding today. The world is building the computational, power and connectivity backbone for an AI-driven economy. Some capital will be misallocated; some companies will fail. Yet the infrastructure, and the eventual productivity gains, will endure.

In short, we’re between excitement and fatigue. Investors still believe in the promise of AI, but we’re starting to see the limits - where high prices will soon need real profits to back them up. The progress is real, the money flowing in is huge, yet the early signs of pressure are starting to show.

Final Thoughts

We have reached the point in the cycle where excitement must give way to execution. This is when investors, policymakers and builders need to shift from announcing the future to quietly building it profitably. The AI mania isn’t ending — it’s evolving, moving from euphoria to endurance.

In Part 2: Navigating the Mania, I will explore how investors can keep their footing through the turbulence, how to stay confident but cautious, identify the true long-term winners and use market swings as opportunities rather than threats.

Because while manias may fuel progress, it’s discipline, not hype, that decides who lasts.
