item.title: Goat Farming or Goat Ponzi?
item.description: Investors Should Always Ask the Herd Questions
item.content:encoded:
Home← All writingWorkRSS

WRITING / ARCHIVE

Goat Farming or Goat Ponzi?

Originally published on Substack: 2025-10-12 · Original publication ↗

In Uganda’s bustling investment landscape, goat farming has become an unexpected headline act. Across WhatsApp groups, community meetings, and glossy brochures, a model marketed by Youth Progressive Agriculture (YPA) has gained traction: buy goats, hand them over to YPA, and in three years walk away with a healthy profit.

At first glance, it looks like a clever blend of agriculture and cooperative finance. However, beneath the surface, the model raises some red flags that seasoned investors associate with Ponzi schemes.

How the YPA Model Works

The mechanics are laid out simply:

  • A farmer buys between 1 and 1,500 goats at UGX 750,000 each.

  • The contract runs for three years.

  • YPA promises an increment of at least one goat per year per goat purchased.

  • At the end of three years, YPA keeps the initial goats “as payment,” and the farmer walks away with the surplus — either cash or goats.

  • Farmers must also recruit at least one new farmer each year and pay annual fees for membership, administration, and farm visits.

On paper, this suggests a doubling of your herd value in three years. A 100-goat investor, for instance, puts in UGX 75 million upfront, pays about UGX 1 million in fees, and supposedly exits with 200 goats worth UGX 150 million. That looks like a near-100% return over three years — far more than any bank deposit, Treasury bond, or even private credit deal in Uganda.

The Problem: Biology Doesn’t Work That Way

In real farming, goats are living, breathing, and often dying creatures. A closer look at goat biology reveals why the YPA promises strain credibility:

  • A doe typically produces 1.3 to 1.8 kids per year, but mortality can cut that by 20–40%.

  • Adult losses (from disease, culling, or accidents) average 10–18% annually.

  • Market prices fluctuate; flooding the market with thousands of goats depresses margins.

Under typical Ugandan farm conditions, you might expect 0.8–0.9 saleable kids per doe per year — short of YPA’s guaranteed “+1.”

In optimistic conditions — high survival, strong vet care, stable feed — the numbers can approach 1.0. But a system that guarantees this output across thousands of investor goats without factoring in drought, parasites, or market risk is less agriculture and more financial fiction.

The Red Flags

Beyond the biology, the structure of YPA’s contract itself raises alarms:

  1. Mandatory recruitment of new farmers. Any scheme requiring participants to bring in others is structurally dependent on fresh inflows — a classic Ponzi marker.

  2. Confiscation of initial assets. At contract end, YPA keeps the goats you paid for. In traditional agribusiness partnerships, the farmer retains the breeding base; the manager earns through service fees or revenue share.

  3. Guaranteed returns without risk disclosure. Farming is inherently risky. Weather, disease, and market volatility make it impossible to guarantee steady increments.

  4. Opaque fee model. Membership, administration, farm visits, “goat increments” — it is unclear how fees align with actual operating costs.

In short: investors face asymmetric risk. You provide the capital, YPA controls the animals, and you only ever see what they tell you at the end of three years.

A More Sustainable Alternative

Livestock can be a powerful investment. But the structure matters. A safer model looks more like a managed cooperative account than a pyramid scheme.

  • Investor retains ownership. The goats are tagged and remain the investor’s property.

  • Transparent management fees. A fixed fee per goat per year (say UGX 60,000–100,000) covers vet care, labor, and feed.

  • Performance-based incentives. Managers may take 10–15% of net profits from goat sales — aligning incentives with outcomes.

  • Choice of payout. Investors can receive cash each year from sold kids or compound returns by retaining offspring to grow the herd.

  • Exit flexibility. At any time, investors can liquidate their herd or physically reclaim their goats.

Under this approach, a 100-goat investor might gross UGX 63 million per year from sales, netting UGX 45–50 million after fees. That’s a 40–45% annual return under normal conditions — attractive, but not unrealistic, and crucially, it comes from goats actually being bred, raised, and sold.

The Bigger Lesson: Always Do Your Own Research

The YPA model may yet be well-intentioned. Perhaps it has created employment, built herds, and supported communities. But the red flags — forced recruitment, confiscated assets, guaranteed returns — mirror the playbook of schemes that collapse as soon as growth slows.

For investors, the moral is simple:

  • Ask the hard questions. How exactly are returns generated? Who owns the base asset? What happens if disease wipes out 20% of the herd?

  • Look for transparency. Returns should be linked to actual sales and performance, not promises.

  • Prefer aligned incentives. Managers should earn when herds thrive, not when they confiscate your goats.

Agriculture in Africa is full of opportunity. But opportunity without structure quickly turns into disappointment. Before you write a cheque, remember: if the numbers look too good to be true, they usually are.

📌 Bottom Line: Goat farming can be profitable, but only with realistic assumptions, transparent contracts, and aligned incentives. Investors should resist the allure of “guaranteed” returns and instead demand models that stand up to biology, economics, and common sense.

item.title: I Hope This Helps Someone Today: How to Safely Hold Your Bitcoin
item.description: Originally published on Substack.
item.content:encoded:
Home← All writingWorkRSS

WRITING / ARCHIVE

I Hope This Helps Someone Today: How to Safely Hold Your Bitcoin

Originally published on Substack: 2025-10-10 · Original publication ↗

The future is decentralised. The future is now. The future is you.

Visual designed with https://drawit.chamuka.ai/, an excellent tool for creating smart visuals and publishing layouts

Every so often, someone asks me:

“Kenneth, I just bought some Bitcoin. Which wallet should I use?”

And every time, I smile — because that question says something powerful:
we’re finally moving toward a world where people are taking ownership of their own value.
The future is decentralised, and the future is now.

But here’s the truth no one tells you: where you keep your crypto matters as much as what you buy.

🔐 If You Hold the Keys, You Hold the Power

If you’ve got an appreciable amount of crypt (I set this threshold at $5,000 or more) and you’re planning to buy and hold BTC or other crypto for the long term, your safest path is self-custody — owning your keys, not trusting anyone else to hold them.

That means using a hardware (cold) wallet like Trezor or Ledger.
These devices keep your Bitcoin offline — untouched by hackers, government bans, or exchange shutdowns.

It’s the purest form of financial freedom.
But it comes with a responsibility: if you lose your secret phrase or private keys, no one can help you recover it.
No password reset. No “Forgot your PIN?”.

That’s the price — and privilege — of sovereignty.

When Convenience Matters: Hot Wallets

If you want quick access on your phone or browser, but still want control, go for a non-custodial hot wallet.

My go-tos:

  • Trust Wallet — easy, popular, multi-chain

  • Cake Wallet — private, supports BTC & Monero

You still own your keys, so no one can freeze your funds.
But remember: if you lose your recovery phrase, that’s it. There’s no helpline.

If You Prefer Simplicity (and a Safety Net)

If self-custody feels daunting, or you just want a password-reset option, use a reputable centralised exchange like:

  • Binance

  • Coinbase

  • Kraken

They’ll hold your BTC for you, manage backups, and let you recover your account if something goes wrong.

The catch?
You don’t actually own the coins — they do.
And if something happens (a hack, insolvency, or regulatory freeze), your funds might be locked.

It’s the old crypto truth:

“Not your keys, not your coins.”

For Quick Local Use

If you just want to buy and move small amounts quickly — maybe to test the waters — you can use regional apps like Chipper Cash.

They’re convenient and integrate with mobile money, but they don’t publish proof of reserves or independent audits.
So, I wouldn’t hold large amounts there long-term.

Bitcoin-Only Simplicity

If you want a wallet that’s purely for Bitcoin, nothing else, check out the community list on Bitcoin.org.
It’s a good place to start if you’re minimalist or security-focused.

My Takeaway

Why This Matters

In a world of collapsing currencies and financial intermediaries, decentralisation isn’t just a trend — it’s a mindset.
It’s about trust without permission.
About ownership without dependence.
About risk as a doorway to freedom.

So if you’re buying Bitcoin today, don’t just think about how much you have — think about where and how you hold it.

Self-custody isn’t for everyone. It’s not meant to be.
But for those ready to take that step, it’s one of the most liberating moves you’ll ever make.

item.title: Why Your Brain Is Your Worst Investment Enemy
item.description: How psychological biases sabotage your portfolio, and what to do about it
item.content:encoded:
Home← All writingWorkRSS

WRITING / ARCHIVE

Why Your Brain Is Your Worst Investment Enemy

Originally published on Substack: 2025-09-23 · Original publication ↗

If you've ever held onto a Stanbic Bank Uganda stock hoping it would "come back" to your purchase price, or panic-sold during a market dip on the Uganda Securities Exchange only to watch prices recover days later, you're not alone. Whether you're investing in USE-listed companies, trading commodities (coffee, maize, beans, etc.) or participating in a SACCO investment scheme, you've experienced what psychologists call cognitive dissonance, the mental discomfort that occurs when your beliefs clash with reality.

In investing, this psychological phenomenon is your portfolio's worst enemy. Here's why your brain works against you and how to fight back.

The Psychology Behind Bad Investment Decisions

Your Brain's Survival Instincts Are Outdated

Our brains evolved to help us survive on ancient savannas, not navigate modern financial markets. The same mental shortcuts that kept our ancestors alive now sabotage our investment returns.

Loss aversion makes losses feel twice as painful as equivalent gains feel good. This is why you'll agonize over a $1,000 loss while barely celebrating a $1,000 gain. In practical terms, this leads to:

  • Holding losing stocks too long, hoping to "break even"

  • Selling winners too quickly to "lock in gains"

  • Making fear-based decisions during market downturns

The Confirmation Bias Trap

Once you buy a stock, your brain becomes a detective, but only for evidence that proves you were right. You'll eagerly read positive analyst reports while dismissing negative news as "market overreaction" or "temporary setbacks."

This selective attention creates dangerous blind spots. For example the investors who held onto tech stocks through 2022's brutal selloff, convinced that "innovation always wins in the long run"? Many ignored clear warning signs about valuations and rising interest rates.

How Dissonance Shows Up in Your Portfolio

The "This Time Is Different" Syndrome

Every bubble feels rational from the inside. In 2021, retail investors poured money into meme stocks and SPACs, convinced they'd discovered a new form of investing. When reality hit, the cognitive dissonance was painful, leading many to double down instead of cutting losses.

Anchoring to Irrelevant Numbers

Your brain loves reference points, even meaningless ones. You might refuse to sell a share at $40 because you paid $50 ignoring that the company's fundamentals have deteriorated. The original price is history what matters is future potential.

The Sunk Cost Spiral

"I've already lost so much, I can't sell now" is perhaps the most expensive sentence in investing. Whether it's a individual stock, cryptocurrency, or even a struggling portfolio manager, throwing good money after bad is a classic dissonance response.

Real-World Examples from Recent Markets

AI Stock Mania (2023-2024): Many investors rode AI stocks up, then held through significant corrections, convinced their original thesis remained intact despite changing valuations and competitive dynamics.

Interest Rate Reality (2022-2025): Bond investors who loaded up on long-term bonds in 2021's low-rate environment often held losing positions far too long, unable to accept that the era of near-zero rates was ending.

Your Anti-Dissonance Investment Strategy

1. Create Decision Rules Before You Need Them

When emotions are calm, establish clear criteria for buying and selling. Examples:

  • "I'll sell if a stock drops 20% below my purchase price"

  • "I'll take profits when a position grows to more than 10% of my portfolio"

  • "I'll rebalance every six months, regardless of recent performance"

2. Schedule Regular "Brutally Honest" Reviews

Monthly portfolio check-ins with a simple question: "If I had this amount of cash today, would I buy these exact investments?" If the answer is no, you know what to do.

3. Embrace the Power of "I Don't Know"

The strongest investors admit uncertainty. Instead of crafting elaborate justifications for underperforming investments, sometimes the honest answer is: "This isn't working out as expected."

4. Diversify to Reduce Emotional Attachment

When you own 30 stocks instead of 3, no single position can devastate your portfolio or your psyche. Index funds and ETFs automatically provide this emotional buffer.

5. Use Dollar-Cost Averaging

Regular, predetermined investments remove timing decisions and reduce the psychological weight of any single purchase. Whether markets are up or down, you stick to the plan.

The Bottom Line

Your brain's psychological quirks served our species well for millennia, but they're poorly suited for modern investing. Recognizing these biases won't eliminate them, but it will help you build systems to work around them.

The most successful investors aren't the ones who eliminate emotions; they're the ones who plan for them. By acknowledging your psychological limitations and creating structures to counteract them, you can stop being your own worst investment enemy.

Remember: The market will test your psychology repeatedly. Having a plan for when that happens isn't just smart - it's essential for long-term investment success.

item.title: Macro-Themed Portfolios with ChatGPT: 2025 ETF Performance (as at Aug 8, 2025)
item.description: Originally published on Substack.
item.content:encoded:
Home← All writingWorkRSS

WRITING / ARCHIVE

Macro-Themed Portfolios with ChatGPT: 2025 ETF Performance (as at Aug 8, 2025)

Originally published on Substack: 2025-09-05 · Original publication ↗

TLDR
At the start of 2025, I reviewed macro outlooks from major investment houses and used ChatGPT to turn their ideas into ETF-based portfolios - custom indexes reflecting each firm’s view. This article tracks how those portfolios have performed up to August 8, 2025, compares them to the S&P 500 and FTSE All-Share, highlights the key drivers of returns, and considers what adjustments may be needed for the rest of the year.

Goal: Build Investment Portfolios Using Global Insights and AI

Like many investors in Uganda or across Africa, I’ve often wondered: how do I invest beyond my local market? And more importantly, how do I make sense of all the information out there such as macroeconomics, market trends and forecasts?

So at the start of 2025, I set a goal: build global investment portfolios using real-world economic insights and tools, from Uganda.

To frame and guide the investing decision, I read the macro outlooks from the leaders in the field of investing and economics such as Bloomberg, JP Morgan, HSBC and summarised the outlook and implied themes for the year, translated these into investable ETF allocations. I used ChatGPT to do this.

Target: Convert Macro Ideas Into Real Portfolios

At the start of 2025, here’s what the different players were saying:

Bloomberg Outlook (Jan 2025)

  • Expected US growth to slow modestly but remain positive.

  • Saw opportunities in infrastructure spending, supported by US fiscal programs.

  • Anticipated tech resilience, particularly in AI, cloud computing and semiconductors.

  • Viewed China as a selective opportunity, especially in tech, if policy stimulus materialized.

  • Recommended a balanced allocation between growth sectors and investment-grade credit.

JP Morgan Outlook (Jan 2025)

  • Predicted a “soft landing” for the US economy.

  • Favored quality stocks globally, with a tilt toward developed markets.

  • Expected yields to stay elevated in the first half of the year, benefiting short-duration bonds.

  • Believed global real estate could see a modest recovery.

  • Recommended diversified portfolios combining equities, fixed income, and alternatives.

HSBC Outlook (Jan 2025)

  • Saw strong potential in emerging markets, supported by lower US dollar strength.

  • Expected infrastructure and renewable energy to lead growth.

  • Anticipated that China would stabilize but remain volatile.

  • Suggested overweight positions in innovation sectors like clean tech and biotech.

  • Favored a higher equity allocation versus bonds.

Trump Opportunities Fund (TOF) – Thematic Strategy

(Not a bank outlook, but a strategy I created from more speculative themes)

  • Heavy allocations to US defense contractors, oil and gas, and blockchain/crypto.

  • Expected defense spending to grow in response to geopolitical tensions.

  • Saw crypto as a hedge against monetary policy unpredictability.

Story: The Portfolios in Action

Step 1: Building the Portfolios

Using ChatGPT, I matched each outlook to ETFs that reflected those strategies to arrive at weights or percentages to allocate to each ETF for a given risk appetite (used a moderate risk investor across all strategies).

The prompt: “Here is the 2025 global macroeconomic/investment outlook from [Bloomberg/JP Morgan/HSBC/etc.]. Based on the themes in this outlook, suggest a diversified ETF portfolio that reflects their asset allocation view. Include equity, fixed income and thematic ETFs where relevant. Please provide ETF tickers, approximate weights, and a short explanation for each choice.”

For the Trump Opportunities Fund (TOF), the prompt was: “What are the relevant ETFs to go long (buy) and short (sell) based on the executive orders signed by President Trump”

  • Bloomberg 2025:

    • QQQ – Invesco QQQ Trust (Nasdaq-100)

    • VTI – Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF

    • EEM – iShares MSCI Emerging Markets ETF

    • KWEB – KraneShares CSI China Internet ETF

    • PAVE – Global X US Infrastructure Development ETF

    • LQD – iShares iBoxx $ Investment Grade Corporate Bond ETF

    • HYG – iShares iBoxx $ High Yield Corporate Bond ETF

    • SHV – iShares Short Treasury Bond ETF.

  • JP Morgan 2025:

    • VTI – Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF

    • IEFA – iShares Core MSCI EAFE ETF

    • BND – Vanguard Total Bond Market ETF

    • HYG – iShares iBoxx $ High Yield Corporate Bond ETF

    • VNQ – Vanguard Real Estate ETF

  • HSBC Growth 2025:

    • VWO – Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF

    • ARKK – ARK Innovation ETF

    • PAVE – Global X US Infrastructure Development ETF

    • EEM – iShares MSCI Emerging Markets ETF

    • QQQ – Invesco QQQ Trust

  • TOF:

    • IHI – iShares US Medical Devices ETF

    • XLE – Energy Select Sector SPDR Fund

    • ITA – iShares US Aerospace & Defense ETF

    • BLOK – Amplify Transformational Data Sharing ETF (Blockchain)

    • BITO – ProShares Bitcoin Strategy ETF

The allocations are as show below, this was applied to a hypothetical $10,000 portfolio for each strategy, assuming a moderate risk investor:

Step 2: YTD Performance (Jan 10 – Aug 8)

As at 08 August 2025, this is the Portfolio YTD Return for each strategy

Quick Take:

  • Bloomberg leads, benefiting from tech resilience and infrastructure.

  • JP Morgan steady, with bond allocations cushioning volatility.

  • HSBC still lagging, hurt by uneven EM and China performance.

  • TOF volatile but slightly better than earlier in the year due to oil rebound.

Step 3: Risk-Adjusted Performance (Sharpe Ratio)

To assess the excess return per unit of risk, also defined as the Sharpe Ratio*

*Sharpe Ratio = return minus risk-free rate, divided by volatility.

By August 8, 2025, the Sharpe Ratios tell a clearer story than raw returns alone:

  • Bloomberg 2025 (Sharpe Ratio, 0.172) maintains the strongest risk-adjusted performance. Its steady exposure to US tech and infrastructure has delivered returns without excessive volatility.

  • JP Morgan 2025 (Sharpe Ratio, 0.115) sits in second place. Its balanced equity and bond mix has kept volatility in check, though upside is modest.

  • HSBC Growth 2025 (Sharpe Ratio, -0.020) has slipped into negative Sharpe territory. Emerging market and innovation themes have not compensated for the higher volatility so far.

  • TOF (Trump Opportunities Fund) (Sharpe Ratio, -0.210) remains highly volatile, and the Sharpe Ratio shows that the extra risk has not translated into meaningful returns.

  • S&P 500 (Sharpe Ratio, -0.150) surprisingly posts a negative Sharpe Ratio, reflecting subdued returns against relatively high volatility.

  • FTSE All-Share (Sharpe Ratio, 0.025) is just above break-even, showing modest risk-adjusted gains thanks to steadier performance from energy and financials.

Overall, this reinforces the value of diversified strategies like Bloomberg and JP Morgan versus concentrated or speculative approaches. Risk-adjusted measures show not just who is winning, but who is winning wisely.

Can You Do This from Uganda or Africa?

Absolutely, here is how:

  • Use brokers that give global exposure. I personally have experience with Interactive Brokers but others like Saxo, Bamboo, or Hisa also claim exposure to global securities for African users. The biggest hurdle is the AML/KYC especially showing proof of address (African problems).

  • Fund with USD (bank wire, forex, or even stablecoins).

  • Buy ETFs on US or UK stock exchanges.

You don’t need millions to start. A few hundred dollars, good strategy, and discipline go a long way.

So What is the Outlook for the Rest of 2025?

Bloomberg

  • Still positive on US tech and infrastructure.

  • More cautious on China given policy uncertainty.

  • Suggests maintaining investment-grade bonds as rates could fall in late 2025.

JP Morgan

  • Still sees a soft landing scenario ie the US economy would slow down but stay positive, markets could perform steadily.

  • Prefers high-quality equities and short-duration bonds.

  • Cautious on adding to Emerging Markets (EM) exposure until clearer signs of global growth.

HSBC

  • Keeps faith in EM and infrastructure themes.

  • Sees potential for China to rebound if fiscal stimulus increases.

  • Suggests trimming innovation-heavy allocations if volatility remains high - AI, Biotech and cleantech anyone?

TOF

  • Defense stocks still expected to outperform if geopolitical tensions rise.

  • Oil likely to remain volatile; energy allocation may need active rebalancing.

  • Crypto exposure remains speculative higher upside, higher risk.

What I’ve Learned

  • Bank and Investment team outlooks give a starting point.

  • ChatGPT is a powerful translator of macro theory into actionable portfolios - macro reports are complex and you need to digest them simply, allows comparison of the different outlooks easily. However, this does not replace the need for own due diligence or the need to update your portfolio as market conditions and context changes.

  • ETFs make execution simple from almost anywhere - easy access, flexible entry size for positions, instant diversification, transparency and liquidity as you invest.

  • African investors can and should think globally - why? relying only on local markets exposes them to concentrated risks like currency depreciation, political uncertainty, and sector dominance (often banks). Global investing through ETFs provides diversification across regions and industries, access to high-growth themes such as AI, clean tech, and semiconductors that aren’t available locally, and a hedge against weakening local currencies. With today’s tools—USD accounts, mobile FX apps, and international brokers—it’s easier than ever for African investors to preserve wealth and participate in the same opportunities that drive returns in global markets.

Join the Journey

I’ll keep tracking these portfolios and updating as the year goes on.

If you’re interested in building your own macro-smart portfolio, whether with $100 or $100,000, join the conversation and share your experiences.

item.title: Why MTN Uganda Is a Free Call Option on Fintech’s Future
item.description: Originally published on Substack.
item.content:encoded:

WRITING / ARCHIVE

Why MTN Uganda Is a Free Call Option on Fintech’s Future

Originally published on Substack: 2025-07-26 · Original publication ↗

Associated research repository ↗ (linkage to be verified against the article evidence)

Disclaimer: This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute investment advice. Please consult your financial advisor before making any investment decisions. Do your own research.

I wrote this when MTN was initially scheduled to complete the EGM for a vote on a structural separation of the Telcom business from the mobile money business on July 2. The analysis still applies in my view.

This week MTN Uganda shareholders voted on the structural separation of the Telcom business (MTN) from the mobile money business (MTN MoMo).

My thoughts:

1/ Most investors still see MTN Uganda as a mature telco play.
But buried inside it is a high-margin, fast-growing fintech - MTN MoMo - that the market barely values.

Even after the price rally to UGX 261/share, MoMo is still almost free.

And that’s where the real upside lives. I discussed this here.

2/ As of June 30, MTN trades at UGX 261/share, MTN trades at ~UGX 5.85 Trillion market cap.
But the telecom segment alone, using 6.0x EBITDA (a method of valuing businesses using similar comparable companies e.g. Airtel, Safaricom), is worth UGX 9.39 Trillion, implying a value of UGX 418/share (undervalued vs the current share price of UGX 261/share, undervalued by ~UGX 3.54 Trillion).

So MoMo, by implication, which contributes 36% of profits, is valued at just UGX 0.00 to UGX 1.00 Trillion. Reverse calculation shows MoMo is being valued at zero - or possibly negative value due to market uncertainty, discounting, or structural complexity.

3/ Yet MoMo posted, 31 December 2024:
📈 UGX 394B EBITDA
💰 UGX 250B Net Profit
📊 36% of group earnings

MTN MoMo is still being massively discounted. Fair value could be UGX 5 Trillion. based on peer fintech multiple (Wave, Airtel Money) trading at 12.5x EBITDA, sometimes as high as 18x (MTN Group valued its fintech arm at 18x EBITDA in 2024 – implying UGX 7,100B for MoMo).

4/ MTN Uganda = a live, liquid, dividend-paying call option on MoMo.

  • No expiry

  • No premium

  • No time value decay - Do not expire. Do not lose value simply because time passes. Pay dividends while you wait. Can be held indefinitely

  • Just pure embedded upside

5/ And the unlock is live:
📅 July 2 EGM → Vote on MoMo separation
🎯 Minority holders get 24% of FinCo via a trust
📈 FinCo to list from 2028 (I hope it can be earlier)

More details can be found in the EGM Circular.

6/ Upside Potential:

Based on a Sum of the Parts (SOTP) valuation:

I think this value can be unlocked faster. I discussed this here.

7/ You don’t get many trades like this:

  • Defined catalysts

  • Real floor value

  • Fintech upside

  • Embedded call with real cash flows

item.title: Optionality and the Investor’s Mindset: Part 2, What's Umeme's Probability of Winning the Arbitration?
item.description: Originally published on Substack.
item.content:encoded:
Home← All writingWorkRSS

WRITING / ARCHIVE

Optionality and the Investor’s Mindset: Part 2, What's Umeme's Probability of Winning the Arbitration?

Originally published on Substack: 2025-07-01 · Original publication ↗

Associated research repository ↗ (linkage to be verified against the article evidence)

Disclaimer: This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute investment advice. Please consult your financial advisor before making any investment decisions.

Recap

In my previous article, "Optionality and the Investor's Mindset: Lessons from Umeme" I explored how the concept of optionality helps investors think clearly about risk and reward. Options offer limited downside with potentially significant upside, allowing investors to strategically navigate uncertainty.

Umeme Limited’s current situation provides a vivid, real-world illustration of this concept. As recently reported by New Vision, Umeme announced a substantial interim dividend of UGX 222 per share, payable by July 31, 2025. This dividend is being paid from the USD 118 million already received from the Government of Uganda following the end of its electricity concession in March 2025.

Where Are We Now?

As it stands, Umeme is no longer an operational company; rather, it has become a legal and financial entity holding a significant claim against the Government of Uganda. Umeme contends it is still owed USD 174 million more than it received, and it has initiated arbitration proceedings in London to recover this amount.

The recent dividend announcement underscores the unique structure of this situation: investors now hold a guaranteed cash distribution alongside a highly uncertain legal claim—effectively transforming Umeme shares into an "option-like" investment.

Decoding the Current Share Price

Currently trading at about UGX 415 per share, Umeme’s valuation consists of three distinct elements:

  1. Confirmed Dividend: UGX 222 per share, payable shortly.

  2. Residual Cash Buffer: An additional estimated UGX 54 per share remaining from funds already received.

  3. Disputed Arbitration Claim: The remaining market-implied UGX 139 per share is a reflection of investor beliefs about Umeme’s chances in arbitration.

Residual Cash Buffer: UGX 54 per share (estimated), Of the USD 118 million:

  • ~USD 95 million covers the dividend (UGX 222 × 1.62B shares)

  • ~USD 6–10 million assumed for legal/admin costs

  • Leaves ~USD 10–15 million = UGX 54–82/share

  • We conservatively value this at UGX 54.

What does this UGX 139 mean? The full USD 174 million arbitration claim would be worth about UGX 407 per share. By pricing it at UGX 139, the market implicitly estimates Umeme’s chance of recovery at about 34%. Investors, therefore, seem cautious—expecting some payout but significantly less than the full claim.

What Does This Mean for Investors?

This setup beautifully illustrates optionality at work. Investors face a capped downside, UGX 276 per share from the dividend and residual cash. If Umeme’s arbitration fails completely, investors still hold real cash. Yet the upside, if Umeme succeeds fully or partially in arbitration, is significant, potentially pushing share value up to UGX 683 at full recovery, which would represent a substantial gain.

Linking Back to Optionality

Reflecting on the earlier article Optionality and the Investor’s Mindset: Lessons from Umeme, this case highlights exactly how investors can use optionality to manage uncertainty effectively:

  • Limited Downside: Investors receive guaranteed cash distributions now.

  • Asymmetric Upside: Potential gains from arbitration far exceed any additional losses, offering attractive risk-reward.

  • Market Insight: The share price reveals precisely how investors collectively value uncertainty.

The key investor decision now is simple yet profound, do you believe the arbitration will succeed beyond the market’s implied 34% recovery expectation? Your answer determines whether Umeme shares are undervalued or overpriced at UGX 415.

Final Thoughts

Umeme's current situation is more than a fascinating case study, it's a practical demonstration of optionality. Investors with a clear understanding of this concept are well-positioned to evaluate and potentially benefit from such unique opportunities.

item.title: Optionality and the Investor’s Mindset: Part 1, Lessons from Umeme
item.description: Lessons in risk reward and why small decisions today can shape outsized outcomes tomorrow
item.content:encoded:
Home← All writingWorkRSS

WRITING / ARCHIVE

Optionality and the Investor’s Mindset: Part 1, Lessons from Umeme

Originally published on Substack: 2025-06-19 · Original publication ↗

Associated research repository ↗ (linkage to be verified against the article evidence)

Disclaimer: This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute investment advice. Please consult your financial advisor before making any investment decisions.

What if you could make a bet on the future, one that preserved your downside, but kept the upside open-ended? That’s the quiet appeal of an option, a financial instrument often misunderstood as speculative but, at its core, is a structured way to navigate uncertainty.

Right now, a curious example of this is playing out in Uganda. Umeme, the country’s former electricity distributor, no longer runs any power lines, no longer maintains the grid. And yet, its stock has resumed trading. Investors aren’t buying kilowatts or infrastructure. They are buying the possibility of a payout, tied to a pending legal claim. In other words, they’re buying optionality.

This article is about more than markets, it is about how we price future outcomes, how we live with uncertainty and how the structure of options, financial or otherwise, can help us make smarter bets in life.

What’s an Option?

An option gives you the right, but not the obligation, to benefit from a possible future outcome.

There are two basic types:

Call Option - The Right to Upside

Imagine putting down a deposit to hold a plot of land for one to purchase at a given price for a given period. If the land becomes valuable, you follow through and buy it. If it doesn’t, you walk away, losing only the deposit. This is a land option.

Call options are about keeping access to a favorable future while limiting downside exposure.

This is the nature of Umeme stock today. Its shareholders are not betting on earnings or dividends, they are holding a claim on a legal process, with a capped downside and an uncertain but meaningful upside.

Put Option - The Right to Protection

Now consider the opposite scenario. You already own something say, that same land, and you are unsure about the future value (war, fake title, flooding, land rezoning). You buy a guarantee that lets you sell it back at a pre-agreed price if the value falls.

That is a put option, a hedge against loss. It protects you when things go wrong, even if you hope they won’t.

In everyday life, a put might look like:

  • Travel insurance, life insurance

  • An emergency fund

  • A probationary period on a job

  • A short-term lease before buying property

Both types of options are about navigating risk, one opens a path to reward, the other cushions potential loss.

The Umeme Case: A Real-World Option

In March 2025, Umeme’s 20-year electricity concession ended. The government paid USD 118 million as part of the agreed buyout. But Umeme insists that the total owed is closer to USD 292 million, an additional payment of USD 174 million, and has decided to take the matter to international arbitration.

Umeme Limited was first incorporated in Uganda as a private limited company on May 6, 2004, and later converted into a public company on June 28, 2012 under the Companies Act. Umeme is a subsidiary of Umeme Holdings, which is itself a subsidiary of Actis Infrastructure 2 LP, an investment fund under the management of Actis, through a holding company in Mauritius, Actis Infrastructure Umeme Limited. Umeme took over the distribution system for the distribution and supply of electricity in Uganda from Uganda Electricity Distribution Company Ltd (UEDCL) under the concession for a period of 20 years commencing March 1, 2005.

So what do shareholders really own?

Not a utility, but a legal claim. A financial interest in the outcome of a binding arbitration process. This is what gives the shares value.

At the time of writing this article, Umeme is trading at UGX 415 per share. We shall take the view of an investor who purchased Umeme at UGX 275 per share. This coincides with the share price about the time GOU announced it would not renew Umeme’s concession in around December 2022 (see figure below):

To understand options, I will define some of the related terms using Umeme as an analogy of a call option.

  1. Call Option: A call option gives you the right to buy something at a fixed price in the future.

Umeme analogy: As a shareholder, you’ve paid UGX 275 per share to gain exposure to a much bigger payoff - if the arbitration succeeds.

  1. Strike Price: This is the price you must pay to exercise the option - in the land option example above this is the price at which you can buy the land versus its current market price.

Umeme analogy: The strike price is the UGX 275 you paid per share to hold the stock. That’s your upfront cost for the “right” to benefit from the arbitration.

  1. Premium: This is the cost of the option, what you paid for the opportunity - in the land option example above this is the deposit you pay for the right to buy the land at the Strike Price.

Umeme analogy: The premium is also UGX 275 per share, the amount you invested to “lock in” the chance at a big payout from the legal win.

  1. Expiration: The date by which the option must be resolved (or becomes worthless).

Umeme analogy: There’s no exact expiry date, but the arbitration ruling will eventually resolve the claim, likely in 1–2 years. That’s your real-world “expiration.”

  1. Intrinsic Value: This is the value the option has right now, based on current facts.

Umeme analogy: Even if nothing else is paid, Umeme already received USD 118 million, which supports a per-share value of UGX 272. That’s your intrinsic value.

  1. Time Value: The value of the uncertain future payout, how much potential remains as time goes on.

Umeme analogy: The hope of winning USD 174M is the time value. The longer the claim remains alive, the more potential upside you hold.

  1. In the Money: An option is “in the money” if it would already pay off if resolved today.

Umeme analogy: At UGX 275 per share, and with UGX 272 backed by the paid USD 118M, if the legal claim pays out an additional amount say USD 174 million which translates into an additional UGX 401.5 per share you are in the money.

  1. Out of the Money: An option is “out of the money” if it’s not currently worth anything, but could be if conditions change.

Umeme analogy: If you bought at the current price of UGX 415, hoping for a legal win, you’re out of the money today but could win if the full claim is paid.

Options Show Up in Life, Too

This framework isn’t just confined to financial markets. In life, we regularly make choices that resemble options:

  • Enrolling in school is an option on future career paths.

  • Saving and investing early is an option on future freedom.

  • Learning a language or acquiring a skill is an option on geographic or professional flexibility.

  • A mentorship is an option on future perspective and access.

  • Relocating, dating, starting a side project - all these can behave like options.

They often cost something upfront such as time, energy, money but leave room for upside later.

Optionality is the discipline of saying “I don’t need this to pay off now. But I want to keep the chance alive.”

Aligning options with life goals begins with intentionality. Rather than trying to predict the future, focus on positioning yourself to benefit from it. Ask yourself, what outcomes do I value over the next 5, 10, or 20 years? What actions today preserve my ability to pursue those outcomes later even if I’m not ready or certain now? And just as important, where might I already hold valuable options in life: skills, relationships, experiences that I’ve overlooked or underutilized? Like financial options, the key is to protect your downside while keeping the door open to future upside.

Final Thought

Umeme’s story is unusual. But it’s also illustrative. The stock has shifted from a utility play to a legal option. Most investors missed the transition. Some might miss the value. But the lesson runs deeper than that:

The best bets in life aren’t always about being right. Sometimes, they’re about not losing much if you're wrong, and gaining a lot if you're right.

You don’t need to predict the future. But you can position yourself to benefit from it.

Professional overthinker. Occasional optimist. Building a platform for #InvestinAfrica - driving impact through capital, innovation, and technology.

item.title: The Illusion of Ownership: What MTN Uganda’s MoMo Restructure Means for Investors
item.description: A Case Study in Risk, Rights, and Shareholder Value in Africa’s Capital Markets
item.content:encoded:
Home← All writingWorkRSS

WRITING / ARCHIVE

The Illusion of Ownership: What MTN Uganda’s MoMo Restructure Means for Investors

Originally published on Substack: 2025-06-16 · Original publication ↗

Associated research repository ↗ (linkage to be verified against the article evidence)

In a previous article, The Untold Story Behind Africa’s Most Valuable Fintech Spinout, I explored how MTN has built one of Africa’s most powerful digital finance businesses and why its value often goes unnoticed by everyday investors.

This follow-up discusses a related and expected development: MTN Uganda’s proposal to separate its Mobile Money business (MoMo) into a new company.

This article unpacks what’s at stake, especially for MTN Uganda’s minority shareholders, and why this decision could shape how future fintech (or high growth assets) value is shared, or not, across Africa’s public markets. It also raises an important question, the kind that matters for anyone investing in African markets:

Do investors really own what they think they own?

What MTN Uganda Is Proposing

For context, MTN Uganda has called an Extraordinary General Meeting (EGM) on July 2, 2025 to approve a major structural separation of its mobile money arm (MTN MoMo).

As has been shared in the Shareholder Circular, ahead of the EGM, the crux of the vote:

  • MTN MoMo (U) Ltd will be merged into a new entity, MTN New FinCo, which is licensed by BoU.

  • Ownership of New FinCo will be:

    • 76.015% MTN Group Fintech Holdings B.V.

    • 23.985% via a Trust for MTN Uganda minority shareholders

  • Dividends from MTN New FinCo will flow through the Trust to minority shareholders.

  • The Trust is temporary, with a 3–5 year horizon, after which MTN New FinCo may be listed.

At a glance, this looks clean and compliant.

But the deeper issue? The shareholder disappears.

This is a pivotal corporate event, not just for MTN Uganda, but for how African capital markets handle the ownership of high-growth assets like fintech. It’s a real-time case study of a question:

How can investors in African (frontier) markets extract the most return per unit of risk and actually retain control of the value they help create?

Too often, the answer is: they can’t. Because while they may appear to own a stake, the underlying structure tells a different story one where control, transparency, and access to upside quietly slip away.

The Disappearing Shareholder

The proposed structure effectively sidelines MTN Uganda’s minority shareholders.

First, it replaces direct ownership with indirect exposure. Investors no longer own a piece of the mobile money business itself, instead, they hold a claim via a trust, with no voting rights, no board representation, and no control over key decisions.

Second, there is no guaranteed liquidity. While there is mention of a future listing for MTN New FinCo, there is no fixed timeline, no legal commitment, and no mechanism ensuring that trust units will be converted into listed equity. Investors are being asked to wait indefinitely without clarity on when or how they can access the value they’re promised.

Third, the structure offers no assurance of performance transparency. If the FinCo remains unlisted for years, there is no obligation to publish detailed financials. Yet this business will likely be one of the most valuable and fastest-growing component of the MTN ecosystem in Uganda.

This isn’t true ownership. It’s synthetic exposure, a placeholder asset governed by someone else’s discretion. It’s the capital markets equivalent of being invited to the party, but locked in the lobby while the real celebration happens behind closed doors.

We have seen this before

This is the illusion many retail and institutional investors in frontier markets live under. We have seen it before in Tigo Tanzania’s unfulfilled IPO, Jumia’s offshore listing in New York, Ethiopia’s exclusion of bank investors, Dangote Cement’s opaque related-party dynamics and Zambia’s ZCCM-IH’s role as a policy vehicle, not a value driver.

The pattern is clear, exposure without control is not ownership. And without ownership, risk becomes a one-way street. You may be promised returns, but if you can’t vote, can’t see the books, and can’t exit then you don’t truly own the asset. You are exposed to the downside but locked out of the upside. That’s not investing. That’s carrying risk without any control over how it is managed or shared.

The examples from Nigeria, Ethiopia, Tanzania, and Zambia reveal a recurring pattern in frontier markets, retail and institutional investors are often given the illusion of ownership without meaningful rights. Whether through offshore listings, opaque trust structures, or related-party governance, these models systematically separate investors from the true engines of value creation. The result is limited control, poor transparency, and restricted access to liquidity or influence. These cases underscore a crucial lesson: capital formation is not just about access to returns, but about trust, visibility, and alignment. For markets like Uganda, how minority shareholders are treated today will shape the depth, credibility, and inclusiveness of public markets tomorrow.

True ownership means having a say, having transparency, and having a choice. Without those, you're not a shareholder you're just a bystander.

Why This Matters

1. For Uganda’s Capital Markets
If Uganda aspires to build deeper, more inclusive capital markets, we must embrace a simple principle, risk must be paired with rights. Investors who commit capital should be rewarded not just with potential returns, but with the tools to protect and grow their stake namely, visibility, voice, and exit. When structures obscure ownership or delay access to value, they erode trust and reduce the incentives for long-term participation.

2. For Africa’s Fintech Future
MTN MoMo is arguably Africa’s most scaled and systemically important fintech platform. Its growth has been driven not just by technology, but by infrastructure, user adoption, and regulatory goodwill across markets like Uganda. Yet under the proposed structure, most of that value accrues to MTN Group, while local investors are locked out of both governance and future upside. If this becomes the norm, where local markets host the risk but not the reward, it sets a dangerous precedent for how African fintech is financed and owned.

A Better Way Forward

There is an alternative that balances regulatory compliance with shareholder rights and delivers fairness, transparency, and long-term market integrity.

MTN Uganda could directly allocate shares in FinCo to existing shareholders, held in escrow if necessary. The new entity should commit to a USE listing within a defined timeframe, publish quarterly financial disclosures, and embed strong governance safeguards, including pre-emptive rights for existing shareholders on any future equity issuances or exits.

This approach would still satisfy Bank of Uganda’s regulatory ring-fencing requirements while preserving the trust and participation of investors.

Final Thought

If this proposal moves forward as-is, MTN Uganda’s minority shareholders will be left with exposure without control, income without voice, and value without a vote. That’s not real investing, that’s waiting in the dark while someone else decides your outcome.

This moment is bigger than one company or one EGM. It’s about how African markets choose to handle the value created by their most promising sectors. And for investors, especially in fintech and other high-growth sectors, it is a reminder that structure matters as much as strategy.

You shouldn’t just ask, “Is there upside?” You should ask:

  • Can I exit?

  • Can I see the numbers?

  • Can I influence what happens next?

Because without transparency, governance, and optionality, all you’re left with is risk without agency.

Disclaimer: This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute investment advice. Please consult your financial advisor before making any investment decisions.

item.title: Unlocking Climate Finance for East Africa
item.description: Bridging the Gap Between Policy and Action
item.content:encoded:
Home← All writingWorkRSS

WRITING / ARCHIVE

Unlocking Climate Finance for East Africa

Originally published on Substack: 2025-05-28 · Original publication ↗

🔁 This article is part of a 10-part series on Carbon Markets in East Africa - a deep dive into climate finance, opportunity, and action across the region. To read the introduction to the series and the full article lineup, see here. In Article 1 I explored how carbon markets are rising across the region. This article looks at the broader climate finance ecosystem and the urgent need to move from ambition to execution.

The Scale and Urgency of the Climate Finance Gap

In Article 1, we saw how East Africa is being positioned as a major supplier of high-quality carbon credits. But the bigger question remains:

How will East Africa finance the full range of climate actions it has committed to under the Paris Agreement?

The cost of implementing Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) across the East African Community (EAC) is massive, and heavily reliant on external support.

While each country has made commitments to reduce emissions and enhance resilience, most lack the domestic fiscal space to finance their NDCs independently. In nearly all cases, more than 70% of NDC financing needs are conditional on international support through grants, concessional loans, and climate market instruments.

Source: UNFCCC NDC Registry, Country Submissions (2023)

Yet Africa receives just ~3% of global climate finance flows, and less than a third goes to adaptation, which is critical for East Africa’s resilience.

This underscores the urgent need to unlock climate finance flows into East Africa through coordinated strategies, catalytic mechanisms, and institutional readiness.

The Levers to Unlock Finance at Scale

To build on the foundation explored in Article 1 (carbon markets), EAC countries need to leverage three catalytic mechanisms:

1. Carbon Finance as a Catalyst, Not a Panacea

As explored in Part 1, carbon markets can do more than reduce emissions. They can unlock new sources of capital for clean energy, forestry, agriculture, and resilient infrastructure.

But their catalytic power depends on how well they are integrated into national finance strategies and development plans.

Without alignment with NDCs, community priorities, and credible verification, carbon markets risk becoming disconnected from local impact.

Despite rising interest, East Africa remains underrepresented in the global carbon credit market.

As shown above:

  • Kenya leads the region with 35 Verra-registered projects

  • Uganda (23), Tanzania (11), and Rwanda (8) follow

  • Burundi, DRC, and South Sudan remain largely absent

  • The entire EAC accounts for a small fraction of the over 500 Verra-registered projects in Africa

This gap reflects the absence of enabling infrastructure: registries, MRV systems, accredited entities, and investor-ready pipelines.

To fully leverage carbon markets, EAC countries must go beyond project-by-project registration. They need:

  • National registries aligned with Article 6 of the Paris Agreement

  • Clear rules on benefit-sharing and community safeguards

  • Investment platforms that link verified carbon assets to global buyers

Carbon finance can be a gamechanger - but only when built into a coordinated climate finance ecosystem.

2. Blended Finance: De-Risking the Pipeline

Private investors are often hesitant to finance climate projects in East Africa due to high perceived risks - from political uncertainty and currency volatility to limited project track records.

Blended finance addresses this challenge by strategically combining concessional capital (from donors, climate funds, or development banks) with commercial capital (from private investors). The concessional portion helps absorb early-stage risk or offer guarantees, making projects more attractive and viable for private participation.

Examples from the region:

Uganda’s Building Resilient Communities, Wetland Ecosystems and Associated Catchments project is an example of blended climate finance in action.

  • Lead Funder: Green Climate Fund – $24.1M grant

  • Co-funders: Government of Uganda (in-kind), UNDP (implementer)

  • Target: Restore 60,000 ha of wetlands in 24 districts (including Limoto Wetland, Pallisa District, Eastern Uganda)

  • Beneficiaries: ~800,000 people

  • Focus: Nature-based adaptation, climate-resilient livelihoods, and local capacity building

The project uses grant capital to de-risk restoration and community livelihood activities (e.g., fish farming, eco-tourism, rice irrigation), while strengthening institutional climate planning. A model for EAC countries leveraging concessional capital to unlock ecosystem-based adaptation and rural resilience.

The Global Energy Alliance for People and Planet (GEAPP) is supporting the rollout of solar mini-grids across Nigeria, rural Kenya and Rwanda through a blended finance model designed to accelerate clean energy access.

  • Funders: GEAPP, Rockefeller Foundation, IKEA Foundation, Bezos Earth Fund

  • Model: Concessional capital blended with private investment

  • Focus: Off-grid solar systems for rural households, SMEs, and public facilities

  • Technology: Solar PV + batteries + smart meters

  • Implementation Period: 2021–2025

  • Notable Investment: $10M GEAPP anchor investment in Nigeria’s Energy Transition & Access Facility for Africa (ETAFA) facility catalyzed $50M total - a model extendable to East Africa

A scalable model combining donor de-risking, private sector delivery, and public sector support. Mini-grids are powering last-mile communities and proving investable with the right capital stack.

3. National Climate Finance Institutions: The Anchor Missing in Most EAC Countries

While carbon markets and blended finance can catalyze climate action, they depend on strong national institutions to access, manage, and scale climate finance.

Across the EAC, this is the least developed link in the climate finance chain.

Of all EAC countries, only Rwanda has established a robust national climate finance institution - FONERWA, the Rwanda Green Fund.

Why National Climate Finance Institutions Matter

These institutions serve as:

  • Access points to international climate funds like the Green Climate Fund (GCF), Adaptation Fund (AF), and Climate Investment Funds (CIF)

  • Coordinators across ministries, local governments, and development partners

  • Deployers of capital to vetted, bankable, and inclusive projects

  • Trackers of climate finance impact and reporting obligations under the Paris Agreement

Without them, countries rely on external intermediaries, face disjointed project flows, and struggle to link climate finance with national development planning.

Case Study: FONERWA

FONERWA (Rwanda Green Fund) is widely recognized as the most effective national climate finance platform in the East African region.

  • Strong governance and fiduciary systems

  • Robust project pipeline development, aligned with national priorities

  • Trusted by donors and multilaterals as a direct access entity

Results:

  • Over $250 million mobilized from partners like GCF, UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), and African Development Bank (AfDB)

  • More than 40 projects funded, spanning adaptation, mitigation, and resilience

FONERWA offers a replicable model for other EAC countries seeking to scale climate finance through domestic institutions.

What EAC Countries Should Do

To strengthen climate finance readiness, governments should:

  • Establish dedicated national climate finance institutions (either new or embedded within existing development banks)

  • Pursue GCF accreditation or partner with accredited entities on a pathway to independence

  • Develop a national climate investment plan to align projects with funding windows

  • Build capacity for MRV, fiduciary standards, and project selection

Without institutional readiness, even the best carbon market or finance mechanism remains untapped potential.

From Readiness to Results

Individually, carbon markets, blended finance, and national climate institutions offer powerful tools. But without a supporting ecosystem to activate them, these mechanisms risk remaining underutilized.

The current reality is clear, most East African countries are not yet ready to fully absorb or scale climate finance. Despite updated NDCs and growing interest from global investors, the enabling systems are still underdeveloped.

Common barriers include:

  • Lack of national climate finance strategies to prioritize and coordinate action

  • Weak project pipelines, especially outside energy and forestry

  • Underdeveloped MRV systems and absence of digital carbon registries

  • Limited institutional capacity to design, fund, and monitor projects

Summary by country

  • Rwanda is the clear regional leader, with a dedicated climate finance institution (FONERWA), strong MRV systems, a maturing carbon registry, and a structured project pipeline.

  • Kenya has a published strategy and functioning MRV systems. It is piloting a national registry and has an active project pipeline - especially in energy and agriculture.

  • Uganda is in a transitional phase. It has engaged with the Green Climate Fund and developed project pilots (e.g. wetlands restoration), but lacks a formal finance strategy or registry.

  • Tanzania, Burundi, South Sudan, and DRC are still in early stages. These countries have yet to establish foundational systems such as national climate strategies, MRV frameworks, or formal project pipelines.

Only Kenya and Rwanda have made meaningful progress toward linking their NDCs with national financing strategies and investment pipelines. Others remain stuck at the planning stage.

What is needed now is not just more funding but a deliberate shift from fragmented efforts to a structured, country-owned climate finance architecture.

Steps to Accelerate Results

  1. Integrate Climate Finance into National Development Planning
    Embed climate finance priorities into national budgets, economic blueprints, and sector investment strategies - not just environmental policy.

  2. Establish or Strengthen National Climate Finance Institutions
    Set up dedicated funds or empower development banks to act as central nodes for climate finance aggregation, deployment, and coordination.

  3. Operationalize Carbon Market Readiness
    Build national registries, set up Article 6 policy frameworks, and align carbon project pipelines with NDC targets and benefit-sharing rules.

  4. Use Blended Finance as a System, Not an Exception
    Scale concessional instruments to unlock private investment in key sectors: energy access, water security, nature-based solutions, and resilient agriculture.

  5. Invest in Capacity and Data Infrastructure
    Develop MRV systems, build local expertise in climate finance structuring, and digitize project tracking and reporting tools.

Quick Reference: Bridging the Climate Finance Gap

To translate climate ambition into investable action, EAC countries should:

  • Enact national carbon market frameworks (registries, Article 6 rules, benefit-sharing policies)

  • Develop coordinated project pipelines and matchmaking platforms

  • Invest in MRV systems and digital traceability tools

  • Build capacity across Ministries of Finance, development banks, and project originators

  • Engage the African Carbon Markets Initiative (ACMI) and participate in early Article 6 transactions

The transition from climate ambition to investable action requires not just more capital, but better systems.

Conclusion

East Africa has the ambition and the raw potential. What it now needs is speed, systems, and structure.

Carbon markets may be the ignition, but the engine of transformation is a regional climate finance ecosystem built on institutions, transparency and bankable projects.

References

  1. UNFCCC NDC Registry. (2023). Nationally Determined Contributions. Retrieved from: https://www4.unfccc.int/sites/NDCStaging

  2. Climate Policy Initiative. (2022). Global Landscape of Climate Finance.

  3. McKinsey & Company. (2022). Africa’s Green Opportunity: Scaling Carbon Markets.

  4. World Bank. (2023). Country Climate and Development Reports (CCDRs) – Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda.

  5. Verra Registry. (2023). Carbon Project Database. Retrieved from: https://registry.verra.org

  6. FONERWA. (Rwanda Green Fund). Retrieved from: https://fonerwa.org

  7. African Carbon Markets Initiative (ACMI). (2022). Launch Report – COP27.

item.title: Risk is Personal, but Also a Privilege
item.description: The Real Cost of Chasing Returns
item.content:encoded:
Home← All writingWorkRSS

WRITING / ARCHIVE

Risk is Personal, but Also a Privilege

Originally published on Substack: 2025-05-19 · Original publication ↗

Everyone wants higher returns. But not everyone should take the same risks.

Some investors dive headfirst into crypto, startups, or stocks. Others hold land, treasury bonds, or savings accounts. What drives these differences? It’s more than knowledge or product access.

Risk is personal. But it is also a privilege.

We often confuse our willingness to take risk with our ability to absorb loss. In Uganda and across much of Africa, this misalignment is why many portfolios underperform, why panic selling happens, and why seemingly bold investors often stall.

This article translates the thesis and purpose for this substack Risk is a Privilege into a practical framework for understanding risk tolerance, rooted in both psychology and real-life constraints.

Understanding Risk Tolerance

Willingness to Take Risk

This is your emotional comfort level with volatility or losing money. It's how you feel when your portfolio or an investment drops 20%.

Ability to Take Risk

This is your actual financial capacity to take losses without derailing your life. It depends on income stability, assets, liabilities, and time horizon.

You might feel bold. But can your life actually absorb the impact?

That’s where the danger lies. Many of us are taught to chase returns before building resilience.

What the Numbers Show

I recently asked some of you to complete a Risk Return Profiler to determine how you assess your own investing risk, both in terms of how you feel about taking risk, and how well your financial situation supports it. The results provided a revealing snapshot of how emotions and reality often diverge in personal finance, particularly across different professions, income levels, and life stages.

Distribution of Risk Profiles

  • 79% of respondents identified as "Aggressive."

  • None of the respondents viewed themselves as “Conservative”

  • Yet many of these same investors want to withdraw funds in 1–3 years or have limited buffers.

People feel aggressive, but may not be positioned to survive aggressive risk.

Time Horizon vs Risk Profile

  • Many Aggressive investors have short time horizons.

  • A visual misalignment between expected withdrawal timing and declared risk appetite.

Age vs Risk Profile

In general, research shows that risk tolerance tends to decrease with age. This is largely due to a shorter investment horizon and a growing need for capital preservation over capital growth. Younger investors are typically more risk-tolerant, often favoring growth-oriented assets like equities and alternative investments. Older investors, especially those approaching retirement, tend to shift toward more conservative portfolios to protect their accumulated wealth.

However, as the data shows, this trend isn't always followed in practice. I observed a significant number of older respondents identifying as "Aggressive" investors, this underscores the importance of regularly reassessing one’s risk profile - not just by age, but also by current financial goals, responsibilities, and context.

Preferred Asset Classes

As a primer and for an appreciation and understanding of the different asset classes, I have previously written an article on Unit Trusts, NSSF, Bonds, Equities, and Alternatives: Where Should Ugandan Investors Put Their Money.

The data showed that:

  • Savings and bonds still dominate preference lists.

  • Despite high-risk attitudes, few investors choose alternative assets.

Preferred Asset Classes by Risk Profile

A deeper analysis shows that:

  • Aggressive investors favor Equities and Alternative Assets far more than Moderates.

  • Moderate investors consistently ranked Savings and Bonds as top choices.

  • Unit Trusts fall in the middle ground, suggesting suitability for both types of investors.

  • Alternative Assets, even among Aggressives, are not top-ranked, perhaps due to lack of access or understanding.

  • Across all profiles, Savings remain one of the most preferred, reflecting a cultural emphasis on liquidity and capital protection.

These findings underscore a mismatch that’s both common and dangerous in personal finance:

We often want more return than our lives can safely handle.

This mismatch, is seen across real-life situations: boda boda riders and informal traders risking savings in forex or crypto schemes; young professionals investing in volatile markets without emergency funds; communities losing SACCO savings to speculative ventures; retirees shifting pensions into risky investments; and individuals over-leveraging to buy land or property. In all cases, the emotional drive to grow wealth outpaces financial readiness, exposing people to loss they can’t absorb.

A Better Way to Think About Risk

To bridge this gap, I use a Risk Tolerance Matrix that plots Willingness vs. Ability to Take Risk

Using the data from the profiler, this matrix reveals how real individuals across professions relate to risk. The upper red zone highlights those whose willingness to take risk exceeds their financial readiness - often gig workers or students. The lower orange zone shows the overcautious - individuals with capacity but lacking confidence, like civil servants or older professionals. The green line is the ideal: those with emotional and financial alignment. Use this figure to reflect on where you are—and where you need to be.

You can only take risk sustainably when your willingness and ability align, below an example investor positioning by ability willingness to take risk:

The top-right quadrant represents aligned, confident investors like Jamal the Entrepreneur. Bottom-left reflects conservative, low-capacity individuals like Moses the Farmer. The figure illustrates the importance of matching financial capacity with emotional readiness.

Why This Matters in Uganda & Africa

In most African markets:

  • Income is volatile and unemployment is high (gig work, informal sector) - characterized by irregular income and limited job security.

  • Inflation is real - diminishing the real returns on low-risk investments like savings accounts and government bonds, erode purchasing power which can deter long-term savings.

  • Safety nets are weak (no unemployment benefits, weak health insurance) - In most cases, these benefits are restricted to formal sector workers, leaving the majority without a financial safety net during periods of unemployment or illness.

  • Investment Products are limited (few accessible diversified options) - Uganda’s limited investment landscape offers few options beyond land, SACCOs, and government bonds. With ETFs, REITs, and private equity largely inaccessible, and financial literacy still low, many investors face inflation risk, lack diversification, and are vulnerable to scams posing as legitimate opportunities (D9 Club, TelexFree, OneCoin and Mirror Trading International).

So when someone says they are ready to take on high risk, I now ask: “If this investment went to zero, would your life be fine?” If the answer is no, you’re not ready, regardless of your mindset.

How to Align Your Risk

So, if you’ve realized your risk appetite doesn’t quite match your financial footing, here’s how to bring the two into alignment, one step at a time.

  1. Check your cushions: Emergency fund, health insurance, life insurance, stable income? That is your “ability.”

  2. Understand your timeline: for example, don’t invest in volatile assets if you need the cash next year.

  3. Start slow, build confidence: Use treasury bonds, unit trusts, and SACCOs to grow into risk.

  4. Let your investments mature with you: You don’t need to go from 0 to crypto overnight. Mental note to write about crypto another day!

Final Thought

Risk is not something we “have.” It’s something we earn the right to take through preparation, structure, and experience. When we ignore this, we confuse bravery with recklessness. But, when we embrace it, we realize that true financial freedom is not the ability to take risk. It’s the ability to survive it.

So if you feel aggressive, ask yourself, Can I afford to be? And if you're afraid, remember you can build up to it, one wise choice at a time.

Want to Know Your Risk Profile?

Complete the profiler here. You will get a personalized risk profile with actionable suggestions to guide your investment decisions.

Disclaimer: This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute financial advice. Please consult your financial advisor before making any investment decisions.
