item.title: The Untold Story behind Africa’s Most Valuable Fintech Spinout
item.description: Inside Africa’s quiet $5.2 Billion fintech opportunity and the mispricing that frontier markets can’t see
item.content:encoded:
Home← All writingWorkRSS

WRITING / ARCHIVE

The Untold Story behind Africa’s Most Valuable Fintech Spinout

Originally published on Substack: 2025-05-07 · Original publication ↗

🧭 TLDR

MTN has created one of Africa’s most valuable fintech assets, valued at $5.2 billion by Mastercard. Yet investors in the listed MTN subsidiary OpCos are largely pricing these OpCos as traditional dividend telcos. Ownership of mobile money (MoMo) operations remains within these listed subsidiaries, but the market may not fully recognise the digital optionality hidden in these stocks.

Mispricing in Frontier Markets: The Opportunity and the Frustration

In mature markets, when companies unlock new high-growth divisions, valuations respond swiftly.

Stripe, for example, despite a downround, recently touched a ~20x revenue multiple due to its digital payments growth. Adyen in Europe, and Block (formerly Square) in the US, have seen reratings as investors priced in platform scalability.

"A rerating happens when the market assigns a higher value to a company’s earnings or revenues—not because profits have suddenly grown, but because perceptions have shifted. Reratings reflect changing investor expectations around growth, risk, or strategic clarity. In frontier markets like Africa, reratings can be powerful, but also delayed, as liquidity, narratives, and structural reforms often lag behind fundamentals. Recognizing when a business deserves a higher multiple—and positioning early—can be one of the most rewarding strategies in investing."

However, in frontier markets, even when real value is created, it may not be priced fairly - or timely. This was alluded to by Mr. Japheth Katto in his comment on my article on Stanbic, regarding what I am seeing as a shareholder. I have repeated the comment below.

“…Question for you: what is your view on the share price of Stanbic at the USE given all the positives in your article? May be this is an article for another day, not only on the Stanbic share price but other listed companies of your choice. Thank you for keeping us enlightened.”

I shall return to Stanbic another day but I thought I would explore this topic through the lens of MTN Group vs the MTN Country Operating Companies (OpCos).

Markets rarely reward fundamentals alone. For a rerating to happen, investors usually need a catalyst:

  • strategic clarity

  • cleaner disclosures

  • stronger capital discipline

  • or a visible monetization event like an IPO

In frontier markets, the gap between fundamentals and valuations can persist until such catalysts make the hidden value undeniable. This is the crux of this article.

To set the scene, and to explain why I’ve been invoking names like Stripe, Adyen, and Block, even though they are not African companies, we first need to understand MTN and how markets may reward or fail to reward frontier market growth stories.

MTN from telecom giant to fintech powerhouse, 1994 - 2024

MTN’s roots stretch back to 1994, when it launched operations in South Africa as a state-licensed mobile operator serving a handful of thousand early adopters. Over the next two decades, MTN expanded aggressively across the continent, building a pan-African voice and data network that now connects over 290 million telecom subscribers across 19 countries.

But around 2014–2015, a deeper shift began. Recognizing the limits of traditional voice and data growth, MTN started laying the groundwork for mobile financial services. Initially basic money transfers, then later expanded into merchant payments, remittances, savings, and microcredit. By 2018, MTN Mobile Money (MoMo) had crossed 30 million users. By 2020, despite economic lockdowns across Africa, MoMo registered transaction volumes surged to over 9 billion transactions worth $152 billion, representing a sharp acceleration.

As of FY2024, MTN’s mobile money ecosystem now serves more than 69 million active MoMo users, with annual transaction values exceeding $260 billion across its markets. Importantly, MoMo revenue has grown from a side business into a significant earnings contributor: accounting for approximately 25–35% of service revenues in markets like Uganda and Ghana. Meanwhile, the number of telco subscribers continues to expand, reaching nearly 290 million across the footprint. However, it is the growth of MoMo that has become the real catalyst for future earnings and valuation upside.

This evolution did not happen by accident. MTN undertook a deliberate restructuring by licensing standalone MoMo entities like MobileMoney Ltd in Ghana (2022) and MTN Mobile Money Uganda Ltd (2021), preparing for regulatory independence and future financial innovation. Operational carve-outs, separate boards, improved disclosures, and technological investments followed. More on this below.

Finally, in 2023, external validation arrived, Mastercard, one of the world’s leading digital payments companies, agreed to invest $200 million for a minority stake in MTN Group Fintech at a $5.2 billion valuation.

Yet despite this extraordinary journey, from a basic mobile operator to a sophisticated digital financial platform, market perceptions have not fully caught up. Investors, continue to price the listed MTN OpCos largely as mature, dividend-yielding telecom stocks. They fail to reflect the fintech optionality, the scale network effects, or the new revenue diversification emerging inside the company.

The $5.2 Billion Question and the Value mismatch

On 14 August 2023, the Financial Times and other media reported that Mastercard was investing $200 million into MTN Group Fintech, acquiring a minority stake.

This investment, values the MTN Fintech Group business at $5.2 billion on a cash and debt free basis and introduces Mastercard as both a strategic investor and operational partner. The transaction with Mastercard brings key enablers in fraud prevention, KYC/fraud management, digital identity, and cross-border and global payment interoperability.

When a company is valued 'on a cash and debt free basis,' it is essentially being valued on its Enterprise Value (EV). Enterprise Value reflects the worth of a company’s core operating assets, independent of how those assets are financed. It excludes cash (which reduces risk) and debt (which adds risk), focusing purely on the business’s ability to generate profits and growth. In the MTN Fintech deal, Mastercard’s $5.2 billion valuation represents what the business would be worth to any buyer, before accounting for financing structure or balance sheet strength.

What is the value of MTN Fintech Business?

Mastercard’s $200 million investment which values MTN Group Fintech at $5.2 billion, implies an enterprise value (EV)/revenue multiple of ~5.2x based on FY2023 MTN fintech revenue of ~$1.0 billion.

See a comparison to other regional and global fintech valuations:

This suggests MTN Fintech may be priced conservatively relative to peers (e.g. Airtel).

How does this translate into the MTN OpCos?

To assess what this means, for example for MTN Uganda, one would need to:

  1. Analyze MTN Uganda’s market capitalisation and enterprise value.

  2. Estimate MoMo's contribution to MTN Uganda’s revenue and EBITDA.

  3. Compare against standalone fintech and telecom peers.

  4. Implications for MTN OpCo share price

Analysing MTN Uganda’s market cap and enterprise value:

As of April 25, 2025, MTN Uganda Limited (ticker: MTNU) has a market capitalization of approximately UGX 6.05 trillion and an enterprise value of approximately UGX 7.28 trillion (Source: Uganda Securities Exchange (USE) market data and MTN Uganda’s 2024 audited financials, as compiled and analyzed as of April 25, 2025.)

Estimating MoMo contribution to MTN Uganda’s revenue and EBITDA:

In FY2024, MoMo contributed UGX 982 Billion towards MTN Uganda revenue, representing 30% of MTN Uganda revenue, UGX 3.27 Trillion.

Compare against standalone fintech and telecom peers:

Value of fintech business in MTN Uganda, using peers or Mastercard deal = 5.2 x 982 Billion = UGX 4.91 Trillion

Below we show the current valuation for the respective telecom companies are trading at relative to peers.

Value of telecom in MTN Uganda, using peers below, say 1.85x = 1.85 x 2,291 Billion = UGX 4.24 Trillion

Based on the analysis above on an EV/Revenue comparables basis, the Total Enterprise Value (UGX Trillion) = 4.91 + 4.24 = UGX 9.15 Trillion.

This suggests an upto 25% upside on the current enterprise value of UGX 7.28 Trillion.

A sensitivity analysis against different EV/Revenue multiples for the telecom and fintech businesses is shown below and what it means for Enterprise Value of MTN Uganda (UGX Billions).

The corresponding upside/downside for Enterprise Value versus the current Enterprise Value is as shown below.

The Link between Enterprise Value, Equity Value and therefore share price

Enterprise Value is linked to Equity value through a formula:

Market value of equity + Market value of debt - Cash = Enterprise Value

Applying this to MTN Uganda, given a Market Capitalisation of UGX 6.05 trillion and an enterprise value of approximately UGX 7.28 trillion, implies [Market value of debt - Cash] = UGX 1.23 trillion.

Market Value of Equity = Enterprise Value - [Market Value of Debt - Cash]

Market Value of Equity = UGX 9.15 trillion - UGX 1.23 trillion = UGX 7.92 trillion, into 22.45 billion shares which implies a share price of UGX 352.7, versus the current trading price of UGX 270 as of 30 April 2025.

This suggests an upto 30% upside on the current share price of UGX 270.

A similar analysis may be completed for the other MTN OpCos.

But who really owns the fintech (MoMo) value?

Currently, MTN Group’s strategic direction involves transitioning its mobile money operations into a fintech-focused structure under "MTN Group Fintech." The MTN Group Fintech consolidates mobile financial services across Africa, including. An evolution of MTN Fintech Group over the past four (4) years towards this is shown below.

In preparation for the Mastercard deal and in response to regulatory requirements, each country has operationally carved out MoMo as standalone legal entities.

These MoMo entities may eventually be consolidated under MTN Group Fintech Holdings B.V., a private limited company incorporated in the Netherlands in 2013 (Co. No. 57916667). While this holding structure is currently dormant from a public reporting perspective, it reflects MTN’s intent to centralize ownership for strategic investment participation and future monetization.

However, while this transformation is underway, the legal and financial structures remain varied across key markets:

  • Uganda: MTN Mobile Money Uganda Ltd remains a wholly owned subsidiary of MTN Uganda Ltd, providing direct exposure to fintech revenues and earnings.

  • Ghana: MTN Ghana owns MobileMoney Ltd outright, and financial performance is fully consolidated within Scancom PLC.

  • Nigeria: MoMo PSB is a wholly owned subsidiary of MTN Nigeria Communications Plc, following the 2024 acquisition of the remaining 20% stake. The entity is fully consolidated in MTN Nigeria’s results.

While the ultimate vision may be to consolidate MoMo entities under a future MTN Fintech Group holding structure, this is not yet the current legal reality in any of the three core markets.

None of the reviewed annual reports for Uganda, Ghana, or Nigeria provide explicit strategic guidance on whether MoMo earnings will remain within the listed telecom entities or eventually be redirected to a group-level fintech structure. All three listed entities currently retain their MoMo earnings, which are fully consolidated.

Without that clarity, investors may find it difficult to assess the sustainability of current earnings and dividend flows derived from MoMo operations.

As operations scale, and with enhanced disclosures and investor engagement, the market could begin to more accurately value the embedded fintech businesses. However, the timing of this is not clear or certain.

Questions That Remain

As the valuation debate around MTN's fintech business at each OpCo unfolds, some critical questions remain unanswered. It is incumbent upon MTN to provide clear guidance to its shareholders. First, clarity is needed on whether future dividends from the MoMo business will be retained within MTN OpCo for the benefit of local shareholders, or whether they will be upstreamed to MTN Group at the parent level. Second, it remains to be seen whether the MoMo entities will be spun off and listed as separate publicly traded companies, allowing investors to directly participate in the fintech growth story. Third, to enable a more accurate valuation of the business, shareholders require greater transparency through segment-level financial disclosures for the MoMo operations. The resolution of these issues will influence shareholder value realization and determine the degree to which MTN’s fintech opportunity is accessible to public market investors.

What This Means for Shareholders

The outcome of these unresolved questions have implications for shareholders across the MTN ecosystem, particularly as the Group moves ahead with its proposed fintech platform structure.

For MTN Group (JSE) shareholders, there is clear exposure to the consolidated value of the fintech business through Mastercard’s minority investment, the capture of growing fintech revenues, and the potential upside from a future IPO of the Group’s consolidated fintech platform. However, for shareholders in MTN OpCos, the situation is more complex. The absence of detailed segment-level financial disclosures may create a valuation gap. The market cannot fully see or appropriately value the fintech earnings embedded in each OpCo. This misalignment between the Group’s fintech value realization strategy and the limited visibility provided to OpCo shareholders may raise concerns about whether local investors will capture the full benefits of the fintech growth opportunity.

Conclusion

MTN (MoMo) has shown that fintech in Africa is no longer a theoretical story. MTN has built the rails, and Mastercard’s investment validates the reality and value of that infrastructure, shows a path to exit for a fintech investment. The debate is not about whether MoMo has value, it is undeniable. The critical question now is who owns that value and how can it be unlocked?

If you are an investor in MTN, what matters now is making sense of how MTN is restructuring its businesses, what it is (and isn’t) telling the public, and how profits from mobile money will be shared. As the market starts to recognize the true value of MTN’s fintech side, those who have taken the time to understand who really owns what and how it is all set up will have the best shot at benefiting from the upside.

Disclaimer: This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute financial advice. Please consult your financial advisor before making any investment decisions.

item.title: As a Stanbic Shareholder, Here’s What I’m Seeing in Uganda’s Banking Sector (2024)
item.description: This is not investment advice!
item.content:encoded:
Home← All writingWorkRSS

WRITING / ARCHIVE

As a Stanbic Shareholder, Here’s What I’m Seeing in Uganda’s Banking Sector (2024)

Originally published on Substack: 2025-04-21 · Original publication ↗

I’ve been a minority shareholder in Stanbic Bank Uganda for a while now. And like many retail investors, I occasionally take an interest in their performance, most times I just wait for the dividend and eat the money. When I take an interest in the performance, it is to occasionally answer the question:

Should I sell, hold, or accumulate?

The 2024 audited results offered a great opportunity to benchmark Stanbic’s performance against some of its top-tier peers: Absa Bank Uganda, Bank of Baroda Uganda (BOBU), and dfcu Limited. So I reviewed each bank’s 2024 numbers, compared performance themes, and took note of risks and opportunities. What follows is both an analysis of the sector—and a bit of insight into how I think as a long-term investor.

1. The 2024 Scorecard: How the Peer Banks Stack Up

2. My Stanbic Watchlist: Strengths & Risks

From the review, Stanbic remains the most dominant and resilient bank compared to peers.

Here’s how I see it:

Strengths

  • Strong Profitability: UGX 478 billion in profit and a 24.3% ROE—this is hard to beat.

In 2024, Stanbic Bank Uganda reported a net profit of UGX 478.1 billion, comfortably leading the banking sector in absolute earnings. That’s more than double Absa’s UGX 178 billion and over six times dfcu’s UGX 72.1 billion. But Stanbic’s strength lies not just in scale—but in efficiency and capital productivity.

The bank delivered an impressive Return on Equity (ROE) of 24.3%, making it one of the most profitable banks on the Uganda Securities Exchange. Using the DuPont decomposition, we can see what’s driving this return: exceptional net profit margin (44.8%), supported by balanced leverage (equity multiplier of 5.34). Unlike BOBU, which relies more heavily on financial leverage (6.93×), Stanbic’s return is margin-led, reflecting stronger operational performance rather than gearing-driven amplification. This makes the quality of its ROE more sustainable.

  • Diversified Income: 35.7% of revenue from non-interest sources (FX, digital services, insurance) - One of Stanbic Bank Uganda’s key strategic strengths is its revenue diversification—with 35.7% of total income in 2024 coming from non-interest sources. This is well above the market average and points to a mature, resilient business model that isn't overly reliant on traditional lending.

📈 Why This Matters (as a shareholder)

Stability Across Cycles: When interest rates fall or lending slows, NII provides a buffer to sustain earnings.

Margin Expansion: Non-interest income often has higher margins than lending and requires less capital to generate.

Competitive Moat: Building strong NII streams requires tech infrastructure, client relationships, and regulatory trust—a high barrier to entry for smaller or newer banks.

As a shareholder, I see Stanbic’s NII not just as a revenue line—but as a strategic shield against shocks, and a growth engine with upside in the digital economy.

  • Clean Loan Book: NPLs at just 1.5% vs dfcu’s 4.4%.

Over the last decade, Stanbic Bank Uganda has consistently maintained one of the lowest non-performing loan (NPL) ratios in the market, improving from 3.5% in 2015 to just 1.5% in 2024. This long-term trend underscores Stanbic’s conservative credit culture, disciplined underwriting, and robust loan monitoring systems. In contrast, dfcu has struggled with elevated NPLs—averaging over 5% for much of the past decade, and only recently declining to 4.4%. Peers like Absa and BOBU have also carried higher NPL levels throughout the period, despite stable books. As shown in the chart below, Stanbic has become a benchmark for asset quality in Uganda’s banking sector. For shareholders, this matters: a clean book reduces provisioning costs, supports earnings stability, and frees up capital for dividend payouts and new lending—particularly in higher-risk but higher-growth segments like SMEs.

  • Dividend Consistency: UGX 5.86/share is reasonable and backed by earnings.

Stanbic Bank Uganda’s 2024 dividend of UGX 5.86 per share—split between an interim UGX 2.73 and a final UGX 3.13—continues a long-standing track record of consistent payouts. Since its IPO, Stanbic has paid dividends almost every year, even during downturns, setting it apart on the USE for reliability. The 2024 payout is backed by strong fundamentals, with a net profit of UGX 478.1 billion and a payout ratio of approximately 39%, reflecting disciplined capital management. For shareholders like me, this translates to a cash yield of ~12.5%, making it not only an attractive income play but also a sign of Stanbic’s commitment to delivering value from real, repeatable earnings. It’s the kind of dividend I can trust—earned, sustainable, and shareholder-focused.

Risks to Monitor

  • Cost Efficiency: Cost to Income Ratio (CIR) at 47.2% is decent, but Absa and BOBU are leaner. I’d like to see this trend lower over the next 2 years.

Stanbic’s cost-to-income ratio (CIR) of 47.2% in 2024 is respectable for a universal bank of its scale, especially given its wide physical and digital footprint. However, peer banks like Absa (45%) and BOBU (39.5%) are operating leaner—generating more income per shilling spent. While Stanbic’s CIR has remained stable over recent years, I’d like to see a downward trend toward 44–45% in the next 1–2 years. With continued investment in digital infrastructure and improved operational leverage, there’s real potential to unlock more margin without compromising service delivery. For a shareholder, cost discipline is just as important as topline growth—it directly impacts profitability and dividend capacity.

  • Market Share Pressure: Absa is gaining fast in digital and card business. Stanbic needs to defend its retail edge.

Stanbic remains the market leader in digital banking by volume and revenue—but Absa is gaining fast. As shown in the charts, Absa’s digital transactions and revenue have surged since 2020, growing faster than Stanbic year-on-year. While Stanbic’s scale gives it an edge, Absa’s growth reflects strong momentum in mobile, card, and fintech-driven retail channels.

To maintain its lead, Stanbic must move decisively—investing in digital experiences, SME solutions, and customer stickiness. In a market where convenience and speed drive loyalty, the biggest bank can’t afford to be the slowest mover.

  • FX Dependency: A lot of non-interest income comes from FX trading—vulnerable to regulation or external shocks.

As the charts below show, foreign exchange trading remains the largest and most consistent contributor to Stanbic’s non-interest income (NII), growing at an impressive 11.4% CAGR between 2017 and 2024. However, this strength also presents a concentration risk. FX income is highly sensitive to regulatory interventions—such as tighter spread limits or transaction disclosure rules—that could erode margins. It’s also exposed to external shocks like currency stability, declining trade flows, or geopolitical disruptions that may reduce volume. While FX has powered earnings in good times, it is less predictable in stressed environments. Encouragingly, faster-growing streams like bancassurance (22% CAGR) and digital fees (~12%) signal a shift toward a more balanced and resilient NII mix—critical for sustaining performance regardless of macro conditions.

3. How Other Banks Are Playing the Game

Absa is the fastest riser—innovative, efficient, and now generating over 37% of its income from non-interest sources. They’re gaining market share.

BOBU wins on discipline and efficiency. With a cost-to-income ratio of 39.5%, they convert more revenue into profit than anyone else. But they don’t take big swings—no real SME or digital push yet.

dfcu is still rebuilding. They posted a profit this year and paid the highest dividend per share—but it’s too early to call a turnaround. With NPLs at 4.4% and CIR at 64%, they’ll need to cut costs and grow smarter.

4. What I’m Watching for in 2025

As a shareholder, I won’t rush to exit—but I won’t blindly hold either. Based on the foregoing, here’s what I’ll be watching for before deciding whether or not to accumulate more:

  • Can Stanbic get its CIR closer to 45% or below?

  • Will digital services and SME lending keep growing market share?

  • Does the dividend remain sustainable amid competition?

  • Is NII stable, especially if FX markets tighten?

5. Final Thought: Why I’m Holding—for Now

This year’s numbers reaffirm my belief that Stanbic is still a quality asset in a growing market. Their fundamentals are strong, and they’re well-positioned across retail, SME, and corporate banking. But as a shareholder, I know performance is not guaranteed. I’ll keep tracking the trends—and if Stanbic keeps improving efficiency while holding market share, I’ll be happy to accumulate more.

Thanks for reading.
If you’re also a Stanbic shareholder—or follow the Ugandan banking sector—let me know what you’re seeing.

Professional overthinker. Occasional optimist. Building a platform for #InvestinAfrica—driving impact through capital, innovation, and technology.

item.title: You Don’t Need to Buy Land Now. You Just Need the Option.
item.description: Why land options could unlock housing, roads, energy and urban growth—if we use them right.
item.content:encoded:
Home← All writingWorkRSS

WRITING / ARCHIVE

You Don’t Need to Buy Land Now. You Just Need the Option.

Originally published on Substack: 2025-04-19 · Original publication ↗

Africa needs to invest $130–170 billion annually in infrastructure just to meet basic growth and development needs1. But only about half of that is actually financed and delivered each year.

Why?

Yes, financing gaps matter. But there’s a deeper, often-overlooked problem: land access.

  • Housing projects are delayed years due to land titling issues.

  • Road and energy corridors get stuck in compensation disputes.

  • Developers sit on cash but can’t secure land in time or at the right price.

Land is the choke point—and yet we continue to treat it as an afterthought.

This article is for:

  • Project Developers who need clean, ready-to-develop land but can’t risk millions upfront.

  • Governments and Public Agencies trying to implement infrastructure masterplans but battling land bottlenecks.

  • Landowners and Families who want to monetize their land—without being cheated or forced to sell now.

The tool? Land options. Simple in theory. Powerful in practice. Criminally underused.

A land option gives a buyer (developer or public body) the right—but not the obligation—to buy land at a fixed price within a set timeframe. In return, the landowner is paid a non-refundable option premium.

It’s like putting land on layaway: you pay a little now to secure the right to pay the rest later—after you’ve secured planning approval, financing, or project green lights.

The key components of a land option are:

  • Option Premium: Typically 2–8% of the land value2,3

  • Option Period: Usually 6–36 months

  • Strike Price: Pre-agreed land sale price

  • Condition: Buyer exercises only if project proceeds

Case Studies Across Africa

1. Kigali, Rwanda – Urban Expansion Planning

The city government mapped key future zones and optioned strategic land parcels along planned roads. Landowners got a 3% premium and guaranteed market-price purchase later. Planners got certainty. Developers got a green light once infrastructure was in place4.

2. Lekki, Nigeria – Private Land Assembly

Developers aiming to build housing estates optioned plots across 200 acres, spreading risk while negotiating with dozens of families. As land values rose, they locked in 2020 prices in a 2023 market5.

  • Average land price in Lekki: ₦35 million/plot

  • Option premiums: ₦1.5–₦2 million, 3–5% of plot value

  • Net savings per plot after exercising: ₦4–₦6 million

3. Kenya – Urban Development and Energy Projects

In Kenya, developers have applied land options and similar agreements to secure land rights while minimizing upfront costs.

In urban real estate, the Tatu City development—a 5,000-acre Special Economic Zone near Nairobi—used phased acquisition and option-like deals with multiple landowners. Initial premiums were estimated at 3–5% of land value, with full payment deferred until planning and infrastructure approvals were in place6.

In renewable energy, the Kipeto Wind Power Project in Kajiado County engaged local communities through pre-lease agreements, offering KES 20,000–50,000 upfront for land access and committing to annual lease payments once construction began6.

These flexible land access models helped de-risk projects and align community interests—without requiring full land purchase from day one.

Why land options matter

Problem vs Solution solved via land options:

  • Land is expensive to buy upfront: Pay a small premium to secure it for later

  • Delays due to title or planning: Use option period to sort out paperwork

  • Landowners reluctant to sell immediately: Give them cash now + a fixed price guarantee

  • Investors want certainty before buying: Lock in land before committing to full investment

A 5-Step Framework for Using Land Options in Projects

Step 1: Identify Strategic Land Needs

Use Geographic Information System (GIS) tools or masterplans to target land near roads, utilities, or growth corridors7.

Step 2: Engage Landowners

Offer a transparent deal: a small premium now, with a clear strike price later. Build trust.

Step 3: Structure Legal Agreements

Use standardized templates.

Define:

  • Premium %

  • Duration

  • Conditions for exercising

  • What happens if it lapses8

Step 4: Secure Approvals & Financing

Use the option period to finalize planning permission, Environmental and Social (E&S) clearance, and financing.

Step 5: Execute or Exit

If all goes well—exercise. If not—the landowner keeps the premium and can re-market the land.

Use Case: Affordable Housing

A housing developer in Uganda needs 10 acres for 200 homes near a new industrial park.

  • Land price = UGX 1.5 billion

  • Option premium = UGX 90 million (6%)

  • Option term = 12 months

The developer uses the 12-month window to:

  • Apply for government housing subsidies

  • Finalize engineering plans

  • Pre-sell units to buyers

Once ready, they pay the UGX 1.5 billion and start construction—without losing capital if approvals fall through.

Aside, land is just one of the obstacles to affordable housing, for a more wholistic model on affordable housing for Africa, I share some thoughts on making home ownership affordable in Africa here.

What's the Potential?

  • Public Sector: Pre-option land around infrastructure projects to control urban sprawl and speculative land grabs.

  • Private Developers: De-risk early-stage investment in energy, transport, and real estate projects.

  • Landowners: Monetize idle land while maintaining ownership—until a good deal comes along.

Land shouldn’t be what holds Africa’s infrastructure future hostage—it should be what unlocks it. From housing estates in Uganda to energy corridors in Kenya and urban expansion in Nigeria and Rwanda, land options are quietly proving their worth as a flexible, low-risk tool for getting projects off the ground. Whether you are a developer trying to de-risk early-stage investment, a government planning growth corridors, or a landowner looking to earn from idle property—this tool belongs in your playbook. Now is the time to bring it into the mainstream, share success stories, and shape a smarter way forward. If you’re exploring a project, let’s connect so we can all structure better, build faster, and unlock value together.

Footnotes

  1. African Development Bank (AfDB), 2023. Africa’s Infrastructure Development Needs.

    https://www.afdb.org

  2. Centre for Affordable Housing Finance in Africa (CAHF), 2022. Transaction Support for Affordable Housing Projects. https://housingfinanceafrica.org

  3. Cadman, D. & Topping, R. (2021). Property Development (6th ed.). Taylor & Francis.

  4. UN-Habitat, 2021. Urban Expansion Planning in Rwanda and Uganda.

    https://unhabitat.org

  5. Interviews with Nigerian developers, Lekki corridor, 2022–2023 (on file).

  6. Cities Alliance & Kenya Ministry of Housing, 2022. Urban Land Access Mechanisms in Secondary Cities; Tatu City – Wikipedia; Kipeto Wind Power Project – Energy, Sustainability & Society (2024)

  7. World Bank, 2020. Doing Business in Africa: Land Access and Urban Development Challenges. https://www.worldbank.org

  8. RICS (2019). Valuation of Development Land and Option Agreements – Professional Guidance. https://www.rics.org

Professional overthinker. Occasional optimist. Building a platform for #InvestinAfrica—driving impact through capital, innovation, and technology.

item.title: The Ghosts of Drawdowns Past, Present, and Yet to Come
item.description: Understanding Investment Risk Through a Dickensian Lens
item.content:encoded:
Home← All writingWorkRSS

WRITING / ARCHIVE

The Ghosts of Drawdowns Past, Present, and Yet to Come

Originally published on Substack: 2025-04-19 · Original publication ↗

"I wear the chain I forged in life," said Marley. Likewise, investors bear the burden of their drawdowns—unless they learn to manage them.

The markets reminded us—once again—that they don’t move in straight lines.

Last week brought a mix of investor jitters: sticky inflation data, renewed rate-hike concerns, and earnings volatility sent the S&P 500 wobbling, just as many were starting to feel comfortable. It wasn’t a crash by any means—but it was enough to stir up that old familiar feeling: “Should I be worried?”

It’s in these moments that looking back can be instructive. And few tools are better for perspective than a good old-fashioned drawdown chart.

This one, shared by Harald Berlinicke, CFA, captures just how deep and painful major market corrections can be.

To note:

  • The Global Financial Crisis? A brutal -56.8% slide.

  • The COVID-19 shock? A sharp -33.9% in a matter of weeks.

These aren’t just numbers on a chart. They’re the moments that made your stomach drop—the ones that test your plan, your patience, and sometimes your sleep.

Enter Dickens: The Ghosts of Drawdowns

If Charles Dickens had written A Christmas Carol for investors, the spirits wouldn’t warn of stinginess—they’d warn of poor risk management.

Because every investor, at some point, is visited by the ghosts of drawdowns:

  • 👻 The Ghost of Drawdowns Past (who never forgets a loss),

  • 👻 The Ghost of Drawdowns Present (navigating the market now), and

  • 👻 The Ghost of Drawdowns Yet to Come (looming in the uncertain future).

Each ghost reflects a different risk appetite—and a different way of managing the emotional and financial impact of market downturns.

So, whether you're cautious like Scrooge at the start, balanced like Bob Cratchit, or bold like a reformed Scrooge on Christmas morning, understanding your drawdown mindset is key to surviving and thriving through market cycles.

Let’s meet the ghosts.

👴 The Ghost of Drawdowns Past — The Conservative Investor

Who they are: Cautious, loss-averse, focused on capital preservation.
Strategy:

  • 🧱 Heavy in bonds and cash

  • 🛑 Uses stop-losses and exits early

  • 💰 Keeps large cash buffers

  • 🕰️ Short to medium-term horizon
    Motto: “Preserve at all costs.”

🎩 The Ghost of Drawdowns Present — The Moderate Investor

Who they are: Balanced, steady, seeking growth without recklessness.
Strategy:

  • ⚖️ Diversified between stocks and bonds

  • 🔄 Rebalances regularly

  • 🏦 Maintains modest cash buffer

  • ⏳ Medium to long-term horizon
    Motto: “Stay steady, stay sane.”

🎁 The Ghost of Drawdowns Yet to Come — The Aggressive Investor

Who they are: Bold, growth-focused, unfazed by volatility.
Strategy:

  • 🚀 Heavy in equities, alternatives, and growth assets

  • 💼 Uses tactical hedging, but rarely stops out

  • 🪙 Minimal cash—sees dips as buying opportunities

  • ⏳ Long-term or generational outlook
    Motto: “No risk, no reward.”

So… Which Ghost Walks With You?

Drawdowns aren’t just statistical dips—they’re emotional tests.
Knowing your risk appetite helps you design a portfolio you can live with—not just when things go well, but when the market turns cold.

"I will honour investing in my heart, and try to keep it all the year." — Not Dickens, but close.

Managing drawdowns isn’t just about weathering losses—it’s about clarity, control, and confidence. Have you ever faced a drawdown that reshaped how you think about investing?

Drop a comment or send me a message—I’d genuinely love to hear your story.

Let’s learn from each other.

item.title: Nobody Talks About This Path to Homeownership in Africa — But It Could Change Everything
item.description: How to turn renters into owners
item.content:encoded:
Home← All writingWorkRSS

WRITING / ARCHIVE

Nobody Talks About This Path to Homeownership in Africa — But It Could Change Everything

Originally published on Substack: 2025-04-18 · Original publication ↗

What if renting your dream home today could guarantee you own it tomorrow — without a big down payment, perfect credit score, or a 25-year mortgage?

Sounds too good to be true? It’s not. It’s a model hiding in plain sight — and it could be the breakthrough Africa’s affordable housing sector desperately needs.

The Dream of a Home

Across African cities, from Kampala to Nairobi to Lagos, families dream of owning a home. But for most, that dream is pushed further out of reach with every passing year.

The cost of land is rising. Construction materials are expensive. Banks are hesitant to lend. And even those who earn enough to pay rent consistently often find themselves locked out of homeownership because they lack one thing — a large upfront deposit.

The result? Housing developments cater to the top 10%, while 90% of working households are left to rent indefinitely, with no clear path to owning a place they can truly call home.

Rethinking the Model

So how do we turn renters into owners?

The answer may lie in a smarter, more inclusive version of rent-to-own — reimagined for Africa’s realities.

Instead of asking families for a 20% deposit on day one, we start with a smaller option premium — say 5% of the home’s value. This gives the tenant the right, but not the obligation, to buy the home within a 1–5 year window.

During this option period, tenants pay a monthly rent that includes rent credits — contributions that accumulate toward their future deposit or down payment. Think of it as built-in savings.

Even better, these rent credits can be tracked and invested. If the tenant decides to buy, they use the funds toward a mortgage. If they choose not to buy, a portion may be retained to compensate the property owner — while the rest can be returned or reinvested elsewhere.

It’s a model that provides both flexibility and commitment — essential for markets with informal incomes, fluctuating cash flows, and credit gaps.

More Than a House: A Platform for Inclusion

But why stop at rent credits?

This model can become a full financial inclusion platform.

Within the regular monthly payments, we can bundle in life insurance, disability cover, or health insurance — offered at scale and lower cost. Over time, tenants build credit histories, financial discipline, and a better risk profile for lenders.

It’s not just about shelter. It’s about shifting from survival to security.

And there’s a strong case for targeting this model toward public servants and low-to-middle income earners — teachers, nurses, local government workers — whose steady income and pension contributions make them ideal candidates for structured homeownership.

The Cost Question

Of course, this only works if the houses are affordable in the first place.

So we must ask: What kind of home can be built for $25,000 or less? What construction technologies — prefab, modular, or 3D-printed — can deliver decent homes at scale?

How do we lower costs through bulk procurement, standardized designs, and efficient delivery models?

Governments, too, have a role to play — providing affordable land banks, supporting infrastructure, and de-risking projects through guarantee schemes or anchor funding.

So, What Happens Next?

This is more than just an idea — it’s a framework ready to be tested.

It’s a model that works backward from what people earn and saves them from being punished for what they don’t have yet — a perfect credit score or lump sum deposit.

It encourages discipline, offers security, and most importantly, gives dignity.

Let's Build the Future Together

If you’re a developer, financier, policymaker, or investor — let’s explore a pilot. If you’re a SACCO, employer, or pension fund — this could be the path to secure housing for your members. If you're a fintech or insurtech, this is a chance to power the rails of inclusion.

Originally published on Linkedin.

Professional overthinker. Occasional optimist. Building a platform for #InvestinAfrica—driving impact through capital, innovation, and technology.

item.title: Solar Investment in Uganda: Policies, Incentives, and Market Response
item.description: Originally published on Substack.
item.content:encoded:
Home← All writingWorkRSS

WRITING / ARCHIVE

Solar Investment in Uganda: Policies, Incentives, and Market Response

Originally published on Substack: 2025-04-11 · Original publication ↗

Introduction

Uganda presents an interesting opportunity for solar energy investment, with abundant sunlight, a growing demand for electricity, and government-backed incentives to support renewable energy expansion. For an investor interested in solar power development, Uganda offers both grid-connected and off-grid investment opportunities, particularly in rural electrification and commercial solar solutions.

If you’ve been thinking about investing in solar power in Uganda, here’s what you need to know about the policy environment, tax incentives, market trends, and response to date.

Uganda’s Solar Market: A Snapshot

Uganda sits in the solar belt and receives an average of 5.1 kWh/m²/day of solar radiation¹, making it one of the best locations for solar power generation in Africa. However, despite this potential, solar energy still accounts for a small share of the national electricity mix.

  • Total Installed Electricity Capacity (2024): 2,048.1 MW, with solar contributing ~54 MW to the grid².

  • Electricity Access: 28% of the population is connected to the grid. Another 28% relies on off-grid solar solutions (PAYGo home systems, solar mini-grids)³.

  • Annual Electricity Demand Growth: 14%, projected to increase per capita consumption from 80 kWh today to 1,750 kWh by 2050⁴.

Clearly, solar is underutilized but holds immense potential, especially for off-grid households, small businesses, and commercial users.

Government Initiatives & Policies Driving Solar Growth

Uganda’s government has made renewable energy development a priority, and solar energy features prominently in national policies:

1. Energy Transition Plan (ETP) – 2023

  • Targets universal electricity access by 2030 and net-zero energy emissions by 2065⁵.

  • Requires $8 billion in clean energy investments annually over the next decade.

  • Focuses on expanding solar and other low-emission electricity sources.

2. Electricity Connections Policy (ECP)

  • Aims to add 300,000 new connections annually, with a third coming from off-grid solar solutions⁶.

3. GET FiT Solar Facility (2014)

  • A donor-funded initiative that subsidized solar projects to lower generation costs and boost solar adoption⁷.

4. Renewable Energy Policy (2007)

  • Provides tax exemptions, grants, and financing schemes to promote solar energy investments⁸.

Tax Incentives & Financial Support for Solar Investments

For an investor, the Ugandan government offers several financial incentives to encourage solar energy adoption:

1. VAT Exemptions on Solar Equipment

  • Zero VAT on solar panels, inverters, batteries, and solar water heaters⁹.

  • Tax-free imports of specialized solar equipment to reduce costs.

2. Import Duty Exemptions

  • No import duty on solar energy equipment and components.

3. Investment Capital Allowances

  • Investors can deduct capital expenditures on solar projects to reduce taxable income¹⁰.

4. Feed-in Tariffs (FiTs)

  • Provides guaranteed payments per kWh for electricity generated from solar projects¹¹.

  • Designed to create a stable revenue stream for independent solar producers.

PAYGo Solar: The Growing Off-Grid Market

One of the most exciting solar opportunities in Uganda is the Pay-As-You-Go (PAYGo) model, which has made solar energy accessible to rural and off-grid communities.

Key Players in Uganda’s PAYGo Market:

  • M-KOPA Solar – Leading PAYGo provider in East Africa (500,000+ customers)¹².

  • d.light – Serves 30M homes across 72 countries.

  • SolarNow – Offers SHS, solar appliances, and solar water pumps.

  • Fenix International (ENGIE Energy Access) – Focuses on PAYGo ReadyPay solar solutions.

PAYGo Pricing Estimates:

  • Basic SHS: $100–$200, with payments as low as $0.50/day over 1–2 years¹³.

  • Larger systems (TVs, refrigerators): $300–$500, with flexible payment plans.

Large-Scale Solar Projects & Investment Opportunities

Uganda has several commercial solar projects in various stages of development:

  • Xsabo Lira Solarline (50 MW, $45M investment) – Expected completion Dec 2024¹⁴.

  • Xsabo Nkonge Solarline (20 MW, $22M investment) – Expected completion June 2024.

  • Ituka Solar Power Station (24 MW, $19M investment) – Expected completion 2025.

Investment Options:

  1. Utility-Scale Solar Farms – Investing in large grid-connected projects.

  2. Off-Grid Solar Ventures – Partnering with PAYGo companies to expand solar access.

  3. Solar Equipment Distribution – Local assembly and supply chains to reduce costs.

  4. Solar for Productive Use – Funding solar-powered irrigation, cold storage, and microgrids.

References & Sources

  1. Energypedia – Uganda Energy Situation.

  2. Uganda Electricity Regulatory Authority (ERA) – Installed Generation Capacity.

  3. GOGLA Report 2024 – Uganda PAYGo and Off-Grid Solar Market Update.

  4. International Energy Agency (IEA) – Uganda Energy Transition Plan (2023).

  5. Uganda Ministry of Energy – National Energy Policy.

  6. World Bank & GET FiT Program Reports – Uganda Renewable Energy Policy.

  7. Uganda Investment Authority – Tax Incentives for Renewable Energy.

  8. Uganda Renewable Energy Association – Tax Exemptions for Solar Equipment.

  9. GOGLA Market Report – PAYGo Market and Consumer Trends in Uganda.

  10. EAIF (Emerging Africa Infrastructure Fund) – Solar Power Project Investments in Uganda.

item.title: The Rise of Carbon Markets in East Africa: Opportunities and Challenges
item.description: Originally published on Substack.
item.content:encoded:
Home← All writingWorkRSS

WRITING / ARCHIVE

The Rise of Carbon Markets in East Africa: Opportunities and Challenges

Originally published on Substack: 2025-04-10 · Original publication ↗

🔁 This article is part of a 10-part series on Carbon Markets in East Africa—a deep dive into climate finance, opportunity, and action across the region. To read the introduction to the series and the full article lineup, see here.

Introduction

As the global climate crisis deepens, carbon markets have become one of the most promising tools for mobilizing finance toward climate action. Carbon markets allow countries, companies, and organizations to buy and sell carbon credits. They help put a price on carbon emissions, encouraging businesses and countries to reduce their climate impact. Properly designed, they help reduce emissions where it's most cost-effective while channeling resources to communities and countries that need them the most.

Carbon credits are permits that represent the reduction or removal of one tonne of carbon dioxide (CO₂) or its equivalent in other greenhouse gases. They are used to: 1) Offset emissions by companies, governments, or individuals who want to reduce their climate impact; and 2) Support projects like reforestation, renewable energy, or clean cooking that help cut or absorb emissions. For example, if a company emits 1,000 tonnes of CO₂ but buys 1,000 carbon credits from a forest protection project, it is considered "carbon neutral" for that amount.

East Africa finds itself in a unique and urgent position. The region contributes only a small fraction to global GHG emissions (less than 3%), yet it is among the most vulnerable to climate impacts such as droughts, floods, and shifting agricultural seasons. According to the ND-GAIN Index (2024), East African countries such as Burundi, Uganda, and Rwanda rank among the bottom third globally in climate vulnerability—out of 182 countries assessed. At the same time, many East African countries rank low on human development indicators, out of 193 countries assessed, and face serious economic challenges. Despite these pressures, they have committed to ambitious emissions reduction targets under their nationally determined contributions (NDCs)—often relying on international finance to deliver on these goals.

The table below illustrates this climate paradox: low emissions, high vulnerability, and bold commitments. It underscores why carbon markets in East Africa are not just financial tools—they are also a matter of equity, climate justice, and shared global responsibility.

Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) are each country's official climate action plan under the Paris Agreement. They explain: 1) How much the country plans to reduce its greenhouse gas emissions; 2) What actions it will take to adapt to climate change; and 3) What support (like finance or technology) it might need to meet these goals. Every country sets its own targets and updates them every five years to reflect more ambition over time.

For the region, carbon markets offer a dual opportunity: to attract vital climate finance and to support a transition toward low-carbon, climate-resilient development. However, despite increasing global demand and local enthusiasm, East Africa’s carbon market ecosystem remains young, fragmented, and uneven across countries.

1. Why Carbon Markets Matter for East Africa

According to the World Bank, carbon markets could channel over $100 billion annually to developing countries by 2030. Africa, with its natural assets and low emissions profile, could supply up to 30% of the world’s carbon credits by 2030 under favorable policy and institutional conditions (McKinsey, 2022).

The East Africa region is home to some of the world’s most significant carbon sinks, including: The Congo Basin peatlands in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), storing ~29 billion tonnes of carbon (UNEP, 2021), The Albertine Rift forests and wetlands in Uganda and Kenya’s extensive mangrove and savannah ecosystems. Moreover, East Africa holds some of the world’s highest renewable energy potential, with Africa accounting for 60% of the best solar resources globally but possessing only 1% of installed solar PV capacity (IEA, 2022). In the Greater Horn of Africa, hydropower contributes around two-thirds of electricity generation, while geothermal accounts for nearly one-fifth (IEA, 2024). Additionally, smallholder farmers—who manage approximately 80% of sub-Saharan Africa’s farmland and contribute up to 70% of the continent’s food supply (Farm Africa, 2024; IFAD, 2024)—represent a critical force for scaling climate-smart agriculture and sustainable land use across the region.

2. Current Market Landscape in East Africa

The market data shows a dynamic yet uneven carbon market landscape across East Africa. Countries like Kenya, Uganda, and Rwanda have made significant strides in scaling project pipelines and aligning with international mechanisms, while others like Burundi and South Sudan are in earlier stages of engagement.

Kenya, continues to lead the region, with nearly 300 registered carbon projects. These span geothermal and wind energy, reforestation, and clean cooking initiatives. Kenya is also the first in the region to publish regulations aligned with Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, positioning it as a policy frontrunner.

Article 6 of the Paris Agreement allows countries to cooperate in meeting their climate goals, mainly through carbon markets: Article 6.2, Lets countries trade carbon credits (called ITMOs) to meet their targets; Article 6.4, Sets up a UN-supervised global carbon market for public and private actors; and Article 6.8, Supports non-market approaches like cooperation and knowledge sharing. Article 6 helps countries reduce emissions more cost-effectively while promoting international climate action.

Uganda, with approximately 250 active projects, is building momentum through forestry and energy access projects. The government’s engagement in pilot Article 6 programs reflects early-stage ambition. The 2021 Climate Change Act still requires operationalization for scale-up.

Rwanda, maintains over 200 active projects and is among the first in Africa to issue multiple Letters of Authorization (LoAs) for Article 6.2 transactions. It is also piloting a national digital MRV platform.

Tanzania, possesses strong natural capital but lags in regulatory preparedness. With only ~48 active projects, the country is finalizing its Article 6 framework. Private developers continue to innovate, especially in REDD+ and land use.

Burundi and South Sudan, remain nascent markets. Each has fewer than 5 known carbon projects, largely in early-stage clean energy or forestry. While there is international donor interest, formal Article 6 engagement is minimal.

Democratic Republic of Congo, stands out for the scale of its forest coverage. Although specific project numbers are elusive, more than 54 million hectares of land are under carbon-related activities. DRC is active in bilateral Article 6 dialogues but lacks formal market infrastructure.

3. Opportunities for Growth

A. Natural Resource Endowment

East Africa boasts over 130 million hectares of forest cover, according to the FAO, and major wetlands and savannahs with high carbon sequestration potential. The Congo Basin alone stores an estimated 29 billion tonnes of carbon in its peatlands (UNEP, 2021).

B. Energy Transition

East Africa is advancing its clean energy transition, with Kenya generating 92.3% of electricity from renewables and Uganda exceeding 1,000 MW in installed renewable capacity (EPRA, 2024; ERA, 2024). These developments support energy-related carbon credit opportunities.

Beyond grid power, a major untapped market lies in shifting households away from biomass fuels like firewood and charcoal. Over 900 million people in sub-Saharan Africa still lack access to clean cooking (WLPGA, 2024), and meeting this need requires $8 billion annually in investment (OPEC Fund, 2024).

Solutions like improved cookstoves, biogas, LPG, and electric cooking are expanding across the region, many supported by carbon finance.

BURN Manufacturing’s clean cookstoves are projected to avoid 12 million tonnes of CO₂ and reach 6.5 million people, funded largely through carbon credit revenues (EIB, 2024).

Scaling these alternatives offers a powerful carbon market opportunity—combining emissions reductions with health, gender, and development benefits.

C. Climate-Smart Agriculture

Agriculture is a cornerstone of East African economies, contributing approximately 30–40% of GDP within the East African Community (EAC). Implementing sustainable practices such as agroforestry and soil carbon enhancement not only bolsters climate resilience but also offers significant opportunities for carbon sequestration. Countries like Kenya, Uganda, and Rwanda have initiated projects utilizing methodologies like Verra's VM0042 Improved Agricultural Land Management, aiming to quantify and monetize these environmental benefits.

Project Examples:

1) Kenya Agricultural Carbon Project (KACP): Launched in 2014, KACP became the first initiative to earn carbon credits under the Verified Carbon Standard (VCS) for soil carbon sequestration. Engaging 60,000 farmers across 45,000 hectares, the project achieved a reduction of 24,788 metric tons of CO₂ in its initial issuance;

2) Boomitra Carbon Farming in East Africa: This project spans Kenya, Rwanda, Tanzania, and Uganda, focusing on improved cropland management. With a projected annual removal of approximately 300,000 tCO₂e, the initiative is set for a 20-year crediting period starting from October 2019.

D. Youth and Innovation

The region is home to over 100 climate-tech startups (AfriLabs, 2024), especially in Kenya and Rwanda, exploring blockchain-based MRV, satellite monitoring, and digital platforms for credit traceability and smallholder farmer inclusion.

4. Challenges to Market Maturity

Despite its promise, East Africa’s carbon market landscape faces several challenges:

A. Regulatory Uncertainty

Only a few EAC countries have passed climate change legislation that explicitly governs carbon markets. While most countries still lack national registries or Article 6 readiness frameworks.

  • Kenya passed the Climate Change Act (2016); implementing a national carbon registry

  • Rwanda has passed Law N°48/2018 on the Environment; implementing a national carbon registry

  • Uganda has passed the National Climate Change Act (2021); implementing a national carbon registry

  • Tanzania operates under the Environment Management. Act No. 20 of 2004 but recently passed the Environmental Management (Control and Management of Carbon Trading) Regulations, 2022; have a national carbon registry with a pipeline of 75+ projects

  • DRC operates under the Environment Protection Law 2011, but no dedicated climate change law; no national carbon registry

  • Burundi, no dedicated climate change legislation, completed a REDD+National Strategy and Action Plan; no national carbon registry

  • South Sudan operates under the The Environmental Protection Act, 2001, but no dedicated climate change policies or law, completed a National Adaptation Plan (NAP) for Climate Change in 2021; no national carbon registry

  • DRC operates under the Environment Protection Law 2011, but no dedicated climate change law; no national carbon registry

B. Fragmented and Costly Verification

High transaction and verification costs (exceed $100,000+ per project), with long lead times (12–24 months). This creates barriers for community-led and small-scale projects and make carbon markets inaccessible. This limits local ownership and equity. A possible solution is to establish a regional carbon project aggregation and digitized MRV platform that reduces costs and improves access for small-scale and community-led projects.

Case Study:

Aggregation Model – Ghana Improved Cookstove PoA: Ghana’s Improved Cookstove Programme of Activities (PoA) shows how aggregation can reduce costs and open up carbon markets for small-scale projects. By bundling multiple clean cooking initiatives under a single carbon framework, the program cut transaction costs by up to 70% and enabled local stove producers and NGOs to access carbon finance. Over 100,000 cookstoves were distributed, generating hundreds of thousands of carbon credits, with shared MRV processes and streamlined verification cycles reducing lead times and costs. This model offers a practical blueprint for East Africa to scale community-led carbon projects efficiently and equitably.

C. Limited Market Infrastructure

East Africa currently lacks a regional carbon exchange or aggregator platform, making it difficult to discover fair prices for carbon credits or to bundle small-scale projects into investable portfolios. Without this infrastructure, countries often rely on third-party international project developers to access carbon markets. While these actors bring technical expertise, their involvement often leads to value leakage, where a significant portion of the carbon revenue leaves local communities and countries.

A potential solution is to establish a regional carbon exchange or aggregator platform that enables price transparency, project bundling, and direct access to buyers. Such a platform could help small, community-led projects overcome high transaction costs by pooling resources and standardizing verification processes. It would also improve local ownership and ensure a greater share of the carbon finance stays within East Africa. Governments, private actors, and development partners could co-invest in building this infrastructure as part of a broader effort to scale high-integrity carbon markets in the region.

D. Integrity and Greenwashing Concerns

As global demand for carbon credits grows, so does scrutiny—particularly on projects in Africa—over risks of greenwashing and weak environmental claims. Buyers increasingly seek high-integrity credits that demonstrate real, additional, and lasting emissions reductions, along with strong social and environmental safeguards.

To stay competitive, East African projects must align with emerging global standards such as the Core Carbon Principles (CCPs) from the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market (ICVCM) and and the Claims Code of Practice from the Voluntary Carbon Markets Integrity Initiative (VCMI) frameworks to stay competitive. These frameworks promote transparency, rigorous verification, and credible use of carbon credits. Adopting them will help East African countries build trust, attract more investment, and ensure that carbon finance delivers genuine climate and community benefits.

E. Capacity and Awareness Gaps

Many national agencies and local developers in East Africa lack the technical skills needed to design and finance carbon projects, especially in areas like MRV and structuring for carbon markets. A 2021 review by the Eastern Africa Alliance on Carbon Markets found that most countries still rely on outdated CDM-era systems and need significant upgrades to participate effectively in Article 6 (Perspectives Climate Group, 2023). The African Carbon Markets Initiative also highlights the urgent need to build local capacity and scale up African project developers (PMI Climate, 2023). Without targeted support, local actors risk being sidelined, and much of the carbon market value could be lost to external intermediaries.

5. The Way Forward

To unlock carbon market potential, EAC countries must take coordinated action:

National-Level Actions

  • Finalize and implement national carbon market frameworks aligned with updated NDCs and Article 6.2/6.4 mechanisms of the Paris Agreement.

  • Establish or enhance domestic carbon registries with digital traceability tools to improve transparency and avoid double counting.

  • Develop benefit-sharing frameworks to ensure fair and inclusive distribution of carbon revenues, especially at the community level.

  • Integrate ICVCM and VCMI standards into national systems to build trust and meet the growing demand for high-integrity credits.

Regional Collaboration

  • Create a regional carbon exchange or aggregator platform (e.g. East African Carbon Exchange – EACEX) to support price discovery, pooled project access, and matchmaking between buyers and sellers.

  • Harmonize MRV protocols and integrity standards across EAC countries to reduce duplication, lower verification costs, and boost buyer confidence.

  • Coordinate Article 6 engagement through shared infrastructure and joint negotiations to strengthen regional leverage in international markets.

Capacity Building

  • Invest in hands-on training for public agencies, developers, and communities on carbon methodologies, MRV systems, and project finance structuring.

  • Support local climate tech startups and service providers through innovation hubs, accelerators, and blended finance vehicles.

  • Provide targeted technical assistance for community-led and nature-based projects, helping them meet verification and registration requirements.

  • Build long-term institutional capacity through partnerships with universities, vocational institutions, and regional climate research centers.

Conclusion

Carbon markets offer East Africa a chance to access new financing streams, drive climate-smart innovation, and position itself as a global supplier of high-quality carbon credits. But to do so, the region must overcome governance, institutional, and technical barriers—and invest in readiness now.

A coordinated, high-integrity approach will be essential to ensure that carbon finance delivers real emissions reductions, supports sustainable development, and benefits local communities equitably.

item.title: The World Is Reordering. Africa Must Be the Centre
item.description: Originally published on Substack.
item.content:encoded:
Home← All writingWorkRSS

WRITING / ARCHIVE

The World Is Reordering. Africa Must Be the Centre

Originally published on Substack: 2025-04-10 · Original publication ↗

Ray Dalio’s Changing World Order reminds us that no global power stays on top forever. In his analysis, the rise and fall of empires follows a familiar rhythm: economic strength fuels influence and military power, but debt, inequality, and internal division eventually erode that dominance.

See chart below.

As the United States faces political fragmentation, and China rises as a challenger, the world is moving into a new, multipolar reality. For Africa, this presents a rare window—not just to adjust to change, but to shape it.

Africa should no longer be a passive observer in global affairs. With a population set to reach 2.5 billion by 2050—over 60% of whom will be under 25—Africa holds the last great demographic advantage. It is home to critical mineral resources, the world’s highest solar potential, and vibrant digital ecosystems that have leapfrogged traditional infrastructure. Yet its role in the next world order will depend not on what it has, but on what it does with it.

To claim a central role, Africa must build a capable political economy and invest in state capacity. That includes long-term policymaking, institutional stability, infrastructure planning, and capital market development. Some countries are already showing the way: Rwanda’s state-led innovation, Kenya’s fintech dynamism, and Ghana’s growing fiscal maturity are examples of what intentional governance can achieve. But elsewhere, corruption, volatility, and over dependence on donor financing still dominate, for example see effects of USAID wothdrawal.

So what, where is Africa's action plan?

The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) provides a once-in-a-generation platform for integration. It links 54 countries in a $3.4 trillion market. However, policy without infrastructure is paper. Trade needs roads, rail, ports, and digital rails to flow. That’s where innovations like the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS) become vital.

PAPSS allows real-time cross-border payments in local currencies, bypassing the need for USD and reducing friction. It strengthens Africa’s financial sovereignty and accelerates intra-African trade. But PAPSS is just the plumbing. The continent must now build the architecture: logistics corridors, energy networks, data infrastructure, and industrial capacity.

This African economic transformation cannot be achieved without the infrastructure as the foundation, currently, only 16% of African trade is intra-continental. This is largely due to fragmented transport and poor connectivity. Also, industrialisation which is key for this economic transformation remains constrained by unreliable power—only 43% of Sub-Saharan Africa has access to grid electricity. Even thriving digital economies still rely on physical systems: fibre optic networks, cold storage, reliable logistics, and secure hubs.

Africa’s renewable energy potential presents a solution to the unreliable power problem. While the solar potential in Africa is acknowledged, there is potential that goes far beyond solar. Untapped hydropower, powerful wind corridors, geothermal resources in the Rift Valley, and growing interest in green hydrogen suggest Africa could one day become a clean energy exporter. But these opportunities must be captured through intentional and directed investment, not left to chance.

Africa therefore needs to move up the value chain—from resource extraction to green manufacturing and innovation. That means refining minerals, assembling batteries, and leading in climate-smart technology. This won’t happen without capital—and lots of it.

Africa’s own capital base—over $200 billion in pensions, sovereign wealth, and insurance—is underused. Mobilising this capital into infrastructure, private credit, and industrial ventures is necessary. But it’s not enough. To truly reposition Africa in the global hierarchy, the continent needs an estimated $1.2–$1.5 trillion over the next decade.

Blended finance is the most strategic tool to bridge this investment gap. By combining concessional, philanthropic, and commercial capital, Africa can de-risk high-impact sectors and attract long-term private investment. Vehicles like Africa50 and Room2Run prove that structured capital can unlock 4–6x the value in private flows.

Africa must stop asking for inclusion—and start asserting its centrality. It has the numbers. It has the natural resources. It has the youth, the markets, and increasingly, the digital architecture. But the next global centre won’t be inherited. It must be built—through infrastructure, financial innovation, governance reform, and visionary investment.

The world is reordering. For the first time in modern history, Africa is not just being shaped by this change—it has a chance to shape it.

item.title: Carbon Markets in East Africa
item.description: My Deep Dive into the Region’s Climate Finance Future
item.content:encoded:
Home← All writingWorkRSS

WRITING / ARCHIVE

Carbon Markets in East Africa

Originally published on Substack: 2025-04-04 · Original publication ↗

Learning in Public, Building with Purpose

At the start of this year, I made a commitment to myself and my network—to learn deeply, build thoughtfully, and share openly in the areas that matter most to me and the future I want to help shape.

That commitment revolves around five themes:

  1. Blended Finance – including climate finance and carbon markets

  2. Personal Investing – across asset classes, with a long-term lens

  3. AI and Frontier Technologies – understanding tools that shape how we build and decide

  4. SME Finance – bridging the capital access gap for entrepreneurs in emerging markets

  5. Personal Growth – resilience, stewardship, and purposeful leadership

This series is part of that learning journey—rooted in climate finance, with a focus on carbon markets in East Africa, where opportunity and uncertainty are rising in equal measure.

Making Sense of a Complex, Emerging Market

The idea of carbon markets is everywhere—but the details are fuzzy for most people, including those working in climate, policy, or investment.

In East Africa, countries like Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda, and the DRC are being positioned as suppliers of high-quality carbon credits to global buyers. Forests, wetlands, savannahs, cookstove projects, clean energy, and regenerative farming are all part of the growing pipeline.

But:

  • Are we ready?

  • Who benefits?

  • What risks are we taking on as countries, as communities, as entrepreneurs?

  • Can carbon credits be a source of transformational finance—or just another extractive mechanism in green clothing?

This 10-part article series is an attempt to unpack those questions—and to look at both the promise and pitfalls of carbon markets in our region.

From Research to Writing to Reflection

I’m writing this series as part of my own process: learning through research, reflection, conversation, and practice. I’ve been fortunate to work across investing, development finance, and ecosystem building in Africa, and I increasingly see carbon markets as a place where those threads intersect—with real potential for impact.

The articles draw on current data, policy trends, real projects, and first-hand insights. They follow a structured approach—to make them useful, readable, and relevant for practitioners, investors, developers, and policymakers alike.

Each article stands alone, but together they paint a picture of a region in transition—full of risk, reward, and responsibility.

🧭 The Series: 10 Articles, 10 Deep Dives

  1. The Rise of Carbon Markets in East Africa

  2. Unlocking Climate Finance: From NDCs to Action

  3. Who’s Winning? A Country-by-Country Breakdown

  4. How East Africa Can Become a Global Hub for Voluntary Carbon Markets

  5. Climate-Smart Agriculture and Carbon Finance

  6. Global Carbon Market Shifts and What They Mean for East Africa

  7. The Business of Carbon: How Investors Can Profit from Africa’s Carbon Credit Boom

  8. How East Africa’s Carbon Markets Can Attract Institutional Investors

  9. Greenwashing or Real Impact? A Deep Dive into Carbon Credit Projects in East Africa

  10. Carbon as Collateral: The Future of Climate-Linked Finance in Africa

🌱 Why I’m Sharing

Because I believe:

  • Learning is more powerful when shared

  • Finance must be rooted in context, equity, and integrity

  • Africa’s voice and leadership must be central—not peripheral—in the climate economy

So this series is part climate research, part investment insight, part accountability to my own growth.

I hope it sparks ideas, challenges assumptions, and opens up new conversations.

✅ Let’s Learn and Build Together

If you're working in or curious about:

  • Climate finance, policy, or investing

  • The intersection of development, data, and ESG

  • How carbon markets might shape Africa’s next decade

…then I invite you to follow along, ask questions, and share your thoughts.

Article 1 drops early next week, starting 07/04/2025:
🟢 “The Rise of Carbon Markets in East Africa: Opportunities and Challenges”

Let’s build understanding—and better markets—together. 🌍

#ClimateFinance #CarbonMarkets #AfricaInvests #LearningInPublic #BlendedFinance #ESG #CarbonCredits #GreenGrowth #ClimateAction #PersonalGrowth #Investing #EastAfrica #ClimateEconomy

item.title: Bond Yield rate Vs Bond Coupon rate
item.description: Bond investing basics
item.content:encoded:
Home← All writingWorkRSS

WRITING / ARCHIVE

Bond Yield rate Vs Bond Coupon rate

Originally published on Substack: 2025-04-04 · Original publication ↗

I want to inquire about something small on bonds... The bond yield rate and the coupon rate — what should appeal more to me as a wanainchi investor?"

Clarifying bond investing basics.

Coupon Rate = Your regular income.

It’s the fixed interest a bond pays you based on its face value.

Example: If you buy a UGX 100,000 bond at 15% coupon rate, you’ll earn UGX 15,000 per year (UGX 7,500 every 6 months). Simple.

Yield (Yield to Maturity) = Your actual return.

This matters when you're buying a bond at a discount or premium (like on the secondary market). It tells you what return you're actually earning, based on what you paid.

Coupon rate is like rent — it’s the fixed income you get every period. Yield is like return on investment — it tells you if what you paid for that rental house was worth it

So which should matter more?

> For cash flow, look at the coupon. For return on investment, focus on the yield.

>Coupon = what they pay you, Yield = what you earn
